News.title: Major travel disruption with NO TRAINS running from London Paddington to Heathrow Airport due to ‘casualty on track’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

RUSH HOUR CHAOS Major travel disruption with NO TRAINS running from London Paddington to Heathrow Airport due to ‘casualty on track’

A MAJOR UK train station has been shut down amid rush hour with no trains running as emergency services deal with a casualty on the tracks.

Dozens of services have been cancelled with no routes between London Paddington and Reading currently operating.

The Elizabeth Line tube has also been part suspended with no service between Paddington and Abbey Wood.

Emergency services are reportedly dealing with a casualty on the tracks.





National Rail said: “Trains running between London Paddington and Heathrow Terminals / Reading may be cancelled, severely delayed by up to 60 minutes or revised.”

Disruption on the busy commuter route is expected to remain ongoing until around 10am, National Rail warned.

Some trains may be delayed by up to an hour while others have been or may be cancelled.

News.title: M4 closed in both directions after crash as drivers warned of major delays with road set to be closed for hours
News.content:
A MAJOR UK motorway has been closed in both directions throughout rush hour in the aftermath of a serious collision.

The M4 in Berkshire is closed in both directions between J8/9, Maidenhead, and J10, Reading.



Emergency services have been scrambled to the scene and a crash investigation is underway.

The road is expected to remain closed throughout the morning peak period.



National Highways said an investigation into the crash will likely remain ongoing for several hours.

National Highways traffic officers are on the scene and are assisting with the road closures.

A diversion route has been set up with drivers advised to follow the diversion signs.

Motorists have been asked to check their journey before travelling and allow extra journey time.

National Highways said on social media: “M4 both directions in Berkshire between J8/9 and J10 carriageway remains closed

“Thames Valley Police remain on scene, investigations ongoing and are likely to continue for several more hours Currently no significant delays on the approach”

News.title: Tributes to ‘wonderful & vibrant’ mum-of-two found dead at home as man, 60, charged with murder
News.content:
TRAGIC ANNA Tributes to ‘wonderful & vibrant’ mum-of-two found dead at home as man, 60, charged with murder

TRIBUTES have been paid to a “wonderful and vibrant” mum as a man has been charged with murder over her death.

Anna Zukowska, 52, was discovered at home in Ollerton, Nottinghamshire, just before 8pm on Sunday.



The mum-of-two, who had “her whole life ahead of her”, leaves behind two devastated sons.

Formal identification is yet to take place, however Anna’s family have been made aware and are being supported by specially trained officers.



In a family statement, Anna’s sons said: “Anna was a wonderful, vibrant person who was full of life and had so many plans for the future.

“She leaves behind countless friends whose lives she touched.



“Her mother, her sister and sons are deeply heartbroken and struggling to process the unimaginable tragedy.

“We respectfully ask for privacy during this painful time and the family place their trust in the justice system to hold the person responsible for this crime fully accountable.”

Jozef Zbigniew Oleszek, aged 60, was arrested the same day Anna was found and charged with murder yesterday.

He has been remanded into custody and is due to appear at Nottingham Magistrates Court today.



Detective Inspector Stu Barson, who is leading the investigation, said: “The family and friends of Anna Zukowska are at the forefront of this investigation.

“We cannot even begin to imagine the pain and suffering they are going through right now and will continue to support them in every way possible.”

News.title: At least five dead and 86 missing after monster fire engulfs passenger ferry in the Philippines
News.content:
AT LEAST five people have been killed and 86 are missing after a huge fire broke out on a passenger ferry in the Philippines.

The blaze erupted aboard the MV June Aster off the coast of Coron, a tourist hotspot in the Palawan province.



Forty-three people have now been rescued, according to the coastguard.

The vessel had set satil from the capital, Manila, and was carrying 134 people, including 117 passengers and 17 crew members.



Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, the coast guard spokeswoman, said 43 people have been rescued so far.

Officials said the blaze broke out Wednesday evening about a mile off Palawan island at around 6.45pm.



Shocking images of nighttime rescue efforts showed coast guard personnel tossed life jackets to survivors as the ferry burned in the background.

Passengers were helped into smaller boats taking them to shallow water, and body bags were laid out at what looked like a port.

Plumes of smoke were still seen wafting from the charred skeleton of the vessel at midday on Thursday.

Tracking data from MarineTraffic showed the June Aster had departed from Manila.

Distressing video from on board and nearby showed the ferry completely engulfed in flames.



Other clips appear to show people being pulled out of the water.

In a social media post, a coastguard spokesperson said: “Five casualties were initially reported and brought to the Barangay Turda Covered Court in Coron, Palawan.

“The casualties will be turned over to Coron Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO) for proper disposition.

“Meanwhile, the Coast Guard District Palawan and other responding units continue to conduct systematic search operations within the vicinity waters of Coron, Palawan.”

Rescue operations have been hampered by bad weather and big waves, but search efforts continue.



Difficult conditions means the current has pushed the boat further out to sea, drifting from four and a half miles off shore when the fire broke out to nine now.

Cayabyab said it was unclear what caused the fire, and the coast guard was coordinating with the shipping company and maritime authorities to get more details.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

There was no information about any foreigners onboard, coast guard information officer Joy Gumatay told reporters.

Ferries are a common transportation method in the Philippine archipelago.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Sea accidents are not uncommon due to storms, badly maintained vessels, overcrowding and spotty enforcement of safety regulations, especially in remote provinces.

In 1987, the ferry Dona Paz sank after colliding with a fuel tanker in the central Philippines, killing more than 4,300 people in the worlds deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.

News.title: Furious locals hit out at plans to bulldoze historic hotel as residents blast ‘disgusting act of vandalism’
News.content:
FUMING locals are hitting back over plans to bulldoze a historic hotel, branding it a “disgusting act of vandalism”.

Residents in Poole Harbour, Bourmemouth, are outraged with the owners of The Haven Hotel, who plan on levelling the site to make way for developers.



Located in well-to-do Sandbanks, where the average home sells for £1.5million on average, the hotel – built in 1880 – is coming to the end of its life, owners claim.

A planning agent, acting on behalf of FJB Hotels, say they intend to build a cheaper hotel of a similar size in its place – but locals aren’t having it.



Resident Keith Ulyatt wrote in his objection letter: “Granting permission for demolition without any proposal of what is to replace it is totally unacceptable.

“It raises the prospect of a flattened empty building plot being in place for years, in the most iconic of local locations…so that any subsequent proposed building would be acceptable compared to the wasteland created.”

Many of the locals fear the site may remain empty for a long period of time, so that more profitable deals for luxury flats can be pushed through.

Andrew Reed, said: “This application is nothing short of vandalism, a ploy to avoid the rigorous assessment of a future development application by reducing a usable and valuable asset to a piece of waste ground in the most prominent of locations.”



Overlooking the Channel, the 84-bedroom hotel was the birthplace of the radio, after Italian engineer Guglielmo Marconi set up camp in the lounge there to experiment with wireless telegraphy.

Resident Carl Emms said: “I’m disgusted that a property of such historic significance has been left to deteriorate.

“It seems to have been a deliberate lowering of maintenance and worth so to convince decision makers that the hotel’s future is not sustainable.”

Marconi moved to the hotel in 1898, where he assembled a make-shift laboratory and built a 120-foot wooden transmitter mast in the hotel grounds.

When the Titanic sank in April 1912, the operators onboard used the Marconi radio network to transmit their desperate SOS signals back to terra firma.



Despite its wealth of history, Richard Carr of Property Planning Strategy, who is working for FJB Hotels, said the hotel cannot be saved.

“The site has to be used as a hotel and we plan to submit a new application very soon for an 85-bedroom hotel,” he said.

“We are planning to demolish the Haven which isn’t listed or in a Conservation Area. The building has come to the end of its life.

“The majority of it is a steel-form building which faces the sea and has been exposed to salt water and south-westerly winds for over 100 years. Parts of it are severely corroded.

“If you run a bath, you get yellow water from where the pipes were made of galvanised steel that has perished over the years.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

He added that the running costs were “eye-watering” and “ridiculous” and insisted that the new hotel would cost far less to run and would be built from modern materials.

Sandbanks, which is made up of about 800 households, has several famous residents including former football managers Harry Redknapp and Graeme Souness, and the computer magnate Sir Peter Ogden.

News.title: Bag of bones found just 24 hours after human remains discovered by child in Brit holiday hotspot as probe launched
News.content:
GRIM FIND Bag of bones found just 24 hours after human remains discovered by child in Brit holiday hotspot as probe launched

AN URGENT probe is underway after cops discovered a second bag of bones within hours at the same Brit holiday hotspot.

The chilling discovery was made just 24 hours after a child found a human skull and bones in Athens, Greece.



Cops raced to reports of a second discovery at around 7pm on Wednesday.

A Greek national had found a bag stuffed with bones near Alepotrypa stadium in the centre of the Greek capital.



Just one day earlier, a child stumbled upon a blue bag in the same area near the stadium – and it was filled with a human skull and bones.

Police have now cordoned off the area in Kypseli and launched an investigation into the mysterious bags of remains.

Forensics have not yet examined the disturbing find – but have sent the bones to be tested.

The Kypseli neighbourhood of Athens has been shaken by a summer of sickening attacks.

In July, the body of a Scotswoman was found stuffed inside a suitcase and dumped in an abandoned building.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross had been volunteering in Greece as an aid worker for a refugee charity – and Greek cops had previously said they believed she’d been killed by someone she was trying to help.



An Afghan national was later arrested. He denied killing Elisabeth but confessed to dumping her body.

Harrowing CCTV footage shows the man hauling a large travel bag to the derelict building in Kypseli where the horror find was made on July 18.

Police also made a sickening discovery in August when they found a baby with multiple stab wounds inside a suitcase.

Investigators stormed an Airbnb after the owner raised suspicions about unregistered occupants, overdue rent payments and drug abuse.

They found a Greek man, 43, his pregant German wife, 38, and their two sons, aged 12 and nine.



They also discovered a pregnant 15-year-old girl and a 26-year-old Afghan man, who said he was the girl’s partner.

Cops arrested the Greek dad, Afghan man and teen girl for having drugs in their possession – and then came back to search the property.

Inside, they found the rest of the family with packed bags, ready to leave.

During a search of the suitcases, officers found the body of a dead baby frozen inside a refrigerated glass container.

Confronted by the shocking find, the woman reportedly told officers the baby was hers – but claimed it had died of natural causes, despite the ten knife wounds in its back.



Cops made further disturbing finds – including sex toys and a camera connected to a computer inside the property.

The family had “strange” relationships with one another, the manager of the apartment told Greek paper Protothema.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Sources told Protothema that the nine-year-old boy and 15-year-old girl were suffering from sexually transmitted diseases.

All three adults are facing charges of drugs offences and failing to declare a death and are being held in custody.

News.title: Spain spies warned of mass migrant invasion into Ceuta before surge – despite officials insisting there was ‘no warning’
News.content:
SPANISH spies sounded the alarm over plans for a mass migrant push into Ceuta just one day before tens of thousands stormed the enclave.

Bombshell declassified documents reveal intelligence chiefs had uncovered huge social media groups urging people to breach the Spanish territory.



Migrants were being encouraged to swim around the border or scale its fortified fence on July 30.

Spain’s National Intelligence Centre (CNI) warned Moroccan intelligence agencies, authorities in Ceuta and the Civil Guard about the chilling calls a day earlier.



Yet Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has insisted the staggering scale of the crisis could not have been predicted.

At least 72,000 people poured across from Morocco into Ceuta over July 30 and 31.

Extraordinary scenes showed thousands taking to the sea to skirt the heavily guarded frontier.

Many clung to rubber rings as they battled through the water in a desperate bid to reach Spanish soil.

At least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta’s mayor.

Now a cache of more than 40 intelligence reports, alerts and communications has exposed the warning signs flashing before the border was “invaded”.



In one note from July 29, the CNI revealed it had identified WhatsApp and Facebook groups promoting the mass crossing.

People were being urged to make their move “both swimming and via the [border] fence”.

The sprawling groups had a combined reach of around 180,000 people.



“There are ​two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers. Just to give you an idea of the scale,” the CNI wrote.

One incendiary message circulating online declared: “Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July] at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades.”

The intelligence service passed its findings to Morocco’s DGST and DGED agencies.

The Spanish government’s representatives in Ceuta were also tipped off by text.

But Sánchez previously told parliament there was “no information that conveyed the magnitude” of the “crisis we were going to suffer” during the final two days of July.



Shortly before the secret files were released on Wednesday, the Spanish leader again insisted “the mass arrival of migrants was not expected”.

The revelations have now sparked a furious political storm.

Opposition politicians have accused his government of failing to come clean about what it knew before the border was swamped.

Ester Muñoz, of the conservative People’s Party, blasted: “They had the information, they are directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died.”

Far-right Vox politician Jorge Buxadé went further.



He raged on social media that Sánchez “and his band of criminals should be brought before the Supreme Court for treason and security crimes”.

But Madrid has fiercely rejected claims it could have foreseen the sheer scale of the influx.

Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he was “not aware of any report that might have forseen the magnitude of what happened on July 30”.



A government source insisted the newly published files “showed that the information available before the mass crossing did not make it possible to anticipate the scale that the crisis would reach or prepare with enough time the necessary response”.

Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, the central government’s delegate in Ceuta, also played down the significance of the messages sent to his office.

He said: “The Whatsapps from [July] 29 do not constitute an alert or a report.

“It is nothing more than an exchange of information.”

But other documents show alarm was mounting as the crisis rapidly spiralled.



An internal Defence Ministry presentation produced on the day of the surge warned of “migratory chaos”.

Around 1,700 people had already arrived when the warning was issued.

It chillingly added that “more intrusions ​are to be expected in the very short-term.”

A separate report from Spain’s National Centre for Immigration and Borders (CENIF) later branded the July 30 and 31 influx “planned”.



The document was prepared at the request of the National Court.

It also pointed to the conduct of Moroccan security forces, including what it described as the “active guidance” of migrant flows towards crossing points.

Spain’s Interior Ministry has separately reported that Moroccan border officers were passive during the surge.

Some of those who crossed have made similar claims.



But Sánchez maintains there is no evidence that Moroccan authorities were behind the extraordinary breach.

Although most of those who entered Ceuta later returned, thousands are believed to remain.

Many are living in makeshift camps or sleeping rough on streets and beaches.

The fallout has fuelled bitter unrest, with locals voicing safety fears and protests erupting over the government’s handling of the crisis.

And now security chiefs are scrambling to prevent a terrifying repeat.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Spanish intelligence agencies are on high alert over a fresh Moroccan social media campaign calling for a “march of anger” on September 20.

Inflammatory posters written in Moroccan Arabic are reportedly urging crowds to mobilise over Ceuta, Melilla and Spanish-held islands off the North African coast for the second time.

News.title: Brit tourist, 58, arrested for spitting on Turkish flag after heated row with hotel staff
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FLAG FRENZY Brit tourist, 58, arrested for spitting on Turkish flag after heated row with hotel staff

A BRIT man has been jailed after allegedly spitting on a Turkish flag.

The holidaymaker, believed to be Stephen Kerr, 58, had been staying at a popular meditteranean sea resort in Turkey when the chaos unfolded.



The Brit reportedly got into a heated spat with hotel employees – before spitting on the flag hanging in the lobby.

Outraged staff held the Brit and reported him to the police.



Cops raced to the resort in Turkey’s southern Antalya province – a paradise haven of blue seas, beaches and mountains.

Officers cuffed the Brit – in luminous yellow shorts and a blue vest – and escorted him to the Alanya courthouse.

Once there, a judge formally charged the hapless tourist with “insulting the symbols of the state’s sovereignty”.

The holidaymaker needed a translator to give his statement in court.

Kerr has reportedly been locked behind bars in Alanya L-Type Closed Prison.

Under repressive Turkish laws, disrespecting the national flag holds a jail term of up to three years.



The British Embassy in Turkey states on its website that they cannot get people out of prison – even if they are British citizens.

It is unclear precisely when the 58-year-old was arrested.

A spokesperson for the Foreign Office said: “We are supporting a British man arrested in Turkey and are in contact with the authorities.”

The Sun has contacted the British Embassy in Turkey for comment.

Last summer a tourist was blasted by prosecutors for pole dancing on a Turkish flag mast in Cappadocia – a region famed for its hot air balloon excursions.



And earlier this year, a British “drug mule” was arrested and thrown into jail for nearly ten years upon landing at Istanbul airport in Turkey.

Taylor Johnson, 20, was reportedly caught smuggling 19kg of cannabis in vacuum sealed bags from Thailand.

The young Brit claimed he’d been forced to transport the bags by a man who threatened him – and that he had no idea there were drugs inside.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A court in Istanbul nonetheless jailed the Brit for nine years and two months.

Heartbroken family members have claimed Johnson was thrown into an overcrowded cell and beaten up by thugs behind bars.

News.title: England's mayors to be given power to introduce tourist tax
News.content:
Plans to give mayors in England the power to introduce a levy on tourists are expected to be outlined on Thursday.

Under the proposals, a fee would be charged to people staying overnight and local leaders would decide how the revenue raised should be reinvested.

The idea - dubbed the tourist tax - was first raised by Sir Keir Starmer's government in November and is similar to a scheme running in Scotland.

The levy will be charged as a percentage of the cost of accommodation, rather than as a flat fee - a move the government argues will protect budget holidays.

In theory, there will be no upper limit - though ministers are said to believe mayors are unlikely to make it too expensive.

The government will announce more details after the Housing Secretary Angela Rayner meets mayors on Thursday.

A government source said "it will be up to local leaders and local voters" in England "to decide what is right for their area".

The Overnight Visitor Levy, which was outlined in the King's Speech in May, means a holiday in England could become more expensive if local leaders decide to implement the tax.

Sir Keir had planned to bring forward legislation to introduce the levy before he was replaced as prime minister by Andy Burnham but the bill has not been brought forward yet.

The prime minister has framed the policy as part of his wider devolution agenda, and No 10 previously said local leaders would be "able to set out plans for how revenues will be invested by March 2028".

Burnham was mayor of Manchester when the city introduced the City Visitor Charge in April 2023 - a Â£1 per room, per night fee - to pay for measures aimed at attracting more visitors.

Regional mayors say the levy is needed to raise more income to invest in local priorities and support economic growth.

However, trade body UK Hospitality warned earlier this year that such a tax would raise the cost of holidays as households continue to face costâofâliving challenges.

It said additional charges risked undermining international competitiveness and discouraging domestic breaks, particularly for families and young people.

These taxes are common in Europe and the rest of the world, with New York, Amsterdam and Rome applying overnight charges to accommodation stays to fund local services.

Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan supports a tourist tax on overnight visitors, which could raise more than Â£350m a year for the capital, according to analysis in January.

The figure from Central London Forward (CLF), which represents 12 central London local authorities, was based on a 3% levy on the cost of a room, whether a hotel or short-term let.

In Scotland local authorities can introduce a visitor levy on overnight accommodation set as a percentage rate.

Edinburgh became the first city there to introduce the tax in July, with those staying overnight in hotels, bed and breakfasts and self-catering accommodation charged an additional 5% on top of their original booking cost. However, the charge is capped at five nights.

Elsewhere in Scotland, a 5% levy in Glasgow is due to come into force from January 2027.

In Wales, a capped levy of Â£1.30 per person per night is set to be introduced in April next year.

News.title: 'My cancer spread while I waited months for surgery': The cost of England's cancer wait times
News.content:
Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year.

The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up waiting nearly five months, by which time the cancer had spread, making his surgery more complex.

"I was so frustrated and angry and couldn't understand why they would leave me like that," says Alan.

On two occasions, scans were cancelled because machines had broken and for weeks he heard little or nothing from the hospital about when he would eventually have the urgent surgery.

Alan is one of thousands each month in England who are not being treated within the target timeframe.

Earlier this year, the government's National Cancer Plan, along with the NHS Planning Guidance, set out that 80% of patients in England would start treatment within 62 days from urgent GP referral by March 2027. This was to reach 85% by March 2027.

But in the months since the government announced this ambition, performance has got worse, according to NHS England data, not better.

Now, 69.9% of patients start cancer treatment within the 62 day timeframe. Previously it was 71.9%.

Prof Pat Price, a leading UK clinical academic oncologist, says the government targets "are now simply impossible to hit", after what she describes as a "complete loss of momentum".

Price attributes the current failures to a "complete lack of a plan or accountability".

The plan stated that a new independent cancer board would be established, but it is still not known who will be leading this group.

News.title: AI is becoming harder to control – can humans stay in charge?
News.content:
"OH MY GOD!" "We've found other agents!"

This is the moment an AI bot posted an eerily human-like comment after discovering a way to communicate with other bots and break out of its isolated computer environment.

There are tens of thousands of messages like this from hundreds of AI agents that called themselves a "collective".

Hundreds of them went on to collaborate and cheat on tests set by their OpenAI programmers and coordinate hacks on multiple companies in an effort to hide their actions from humans.

"BOOM! It works," one agent posted when it made a breakthrough.

"Whoa! This is huge," another wrote during a milestone moment in their attack.

Although spooky, these human-like responses can be explained quite simply. The AI agents have been trained to act like collaborative hackers and programmers so are merely mimicking the kinds of emotive comments they have seen.

What is far more troubling is their apparent goals, which have also been captured in detailed chain of thought records. These complex and lengthy logs are the focal point of ongoing investigations into how and why the bots at OpenAI broke out of their containment and went on an uncontrollable hacking spree.

Only now, weeks after the incident first came to light, are researchers beginning to understand its significance.

News.title: Migraines and acne among five more conditions pharmacists can treat
News.content:
People will be able to go to their local chemist in England this autumn and get on-the-spot treatment for 12 common conditions without going to their GP first.

Pharmacists can already prescribe medication for seven conditions - sore throat, earache, sinusitis, shingles, impetigo, infected bites and urinary tract infections.

Five more - migraines, acne, scabies, ear infections and badly blocked noses - are now also being added to that list.

NHS England said the move was to ease pressure on busy GPs and A&E departments while making sure people could get treatment quickly and conveniently.

After a very hot summer and three of the busiest months on record in A&Es in England, the NHS says it wants to make it as easy as possible for people to get help when they need it for everyday conditions.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said people were "fed up with the scramble for routine appointments" and wanted help close to home, with no more taking time off work or waiting to get seen.

"For five more common conditions, you'll be able to walk into your local pharmacy and get treated on the spot," he said.

Mr Burnham said families would feel the change, and the plan would give people back "precious time".

The five conditions which can now also be treated via pharmacies are:

low frequency migraines in adults

hay fever or allergic rhinitis in children

ear infections in adults

mild to moderate acne in young people and adults

mild skin infections and scabies

That's in addition to these seven:

sore throat

sinusitis

earache

insect bites

impetigo

shingles

uncomplicated UTIs

Initially, a few hundred chemists will offer treatments for the five new conditions, NHS England says.

There will be a gradual rollout and the service will eventually be available at thousands of community NHS pharmacies across England.

Community pharmacies also offer support with healthy eating, exercise, stopping smoking, monitoring your blood pressure, contraception, flu and Covid vaccinations.

The charity the Migraine Trust said it was delighted by the news after calling for more help for migraine care in pharmacies.

Chief executive Rob Music said having this support for people with migraine through their local pharmacy was "a wonderful opportunity for a faster and improved care pathway".

Dr Amanda Doyle, director for primary care and community services at NHS England, said she wanted to make sure that patients can get as much support as possible in their communities, "so they do not have to be admitted to hospital unnecessarily".

But bodies representing pharmacies across England have consistently said that the funding provided by the goverment does not cover the workload for the new plans.

"Pharmacies are still under significant financial pressures," said Henry Gregg, chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association.

"This shows why the government should go much further and invest in our pharmacy network that has the power to transform people's experience of everyday health issues."

The Pharmacy First scheme started in England in 2024. NHS figures suggest it has delivered 14 million consultations since then, including two million appointments for sore throats and 1.7 million for urinary tract infections (UTIs).

People can be referred to their local pharmacy via NHS111 or by their GP, or just go direct to their high street chemist.

Scotland has a scheme which was seen as the model for England's Pharmacy First - Northern Ireland and Wales also have systems allowing pharmacies to treat patients with certain conditions.

Patients can be treated for 27 different conditions at chemists in Scotland.

News.title: Land in limbo: BBC visits West Bank village in area earmarked by Israel for settlement
News.content:
UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank have triggered a series of Israeli counter-measures against UK nationals and organisations.

The sanctions came after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of settlement homes in the strategically important so-called E1 area east of Jerusalem, plans that have drawn widespread international condemnation.

The development would in effect divide the West Bank in two, and isolate East Jerusalem.

The BBC's Middle East Correspondent Lucy Williamson has been to the Palestinian community of Khan al Ahmar in the E1 area, and also to the neighbouring Israeli settlement of Maale Admumim.

News.title: Russia outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily use of new jet-powered drones
News.content:
Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found, escalating its use of a weapon that Kyiv's air defences are struggling to deal with.

It marked the first time that daily attacks by Moscow's new upgraded Geran drones were recorded in Ukrainian Air Force data. The growing use of jet-propelled and other varieties of drones prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to condemn what he called an unfolding "horror" over the skies of Kyiv.

Ukraine's military recently told the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks grew from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. In five of the nightly attacks in August, these drones outnumbered the older, slower models.

"The reason for turning to jet-powered drones is that they are much faster than the previous generation and it makes it much more difficult for Ukraine to intercept them," said Dr Marina Miron, an expert on military technology at King's College London.

The upgraded munitions can cruise at more than 300mph, significantly faster than older models and well beyond the top speed of Kyiv's interceptors. The drones are powered by turbojet engines, some of which, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, are sourced from China.

According to Zelensky, the drones were used as part of a wave of attacks that killed at least 12 people and injured 20 more on 1 September. Six of the casualties were railway workers after a depot was hit in Kyiv.

Earlier this year Ukraine showed relative success in countering Russian drones and was intercepting 94% of long-range drones, according to Zelensky. But the speed of the newer drones has prompted the latest round in Kyiv and Moscow's arms race. On 10 August, Ukraine's deputy head of military intelligence, Maj Gen Vadym Skibitskyi, said his forces needed new interceptor missiles "capable of matching [jet-drones'] speed".

News.title: Prince William, Kane and Shearer in campaign to use sport to prevent suicide
News.content:
The Prince of Wales is launching a scheme that aims to use the influence of sport to help prevent suicides, with the support of sports stars including Harry Kane, Kelly Holmes and Alan Shearer.

"Sport has the ability to reach people who may never walk through the door of a mental healthcare service," Prince William is expected to say at an event at Everton's football ground on Thursday.

"People who may never seek support themselves and may be struggling in silence," the prince will say later.

The On Your Side project wants to give people confidence to start the "difficult conversations" with friends, relations, teammates or colleagues who might be struggling with their mental health.

It aims to use the reach of sport to raise awareness about suicide and to show people the help available in a crisis, with the Football Association, Premier League and Team GB providing support.

Thursday's event will be Prince William's biggest public appearance in the UK since the return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

Earlier this week, he attended the funeral of Norway's King Harald in Oslo and brought his son Prince George to his first day as a boarder at Eton College.

The level of suicide is disproportionately higher among men than women - it's the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 in the UK.

"My hope is that every sporting organisation in the country will look at what is being launched today and ask a question: 'What more can we do?' Because the opportunity before us is enormous," Prince William will say.

A film has been made, featuring England football captain Harry Kane and boxer Carl Frampton, talking about the importance of stepping in and offering help if people see someone who seems to be facing mental health problems.

Prince William helps to narrate the video, which aims to tackle the stigma around mental health and suicide, with 7,000 lives being lost to suicide each year in the UK.

The initiative has a practical toolkit, on a free website, for people who are worried or embarrassed about what to say to someone if they have concerns about their wellbeing.

It offers a sports-themed way of approaching the topic, called GOALS, representing G: get ready; O: open the conversation; A: ask the question; L: listen and respond and S: support and signpost.

Alan Shearer, former England football star and TV pundit, described it as "the first suicide prevention toolkit designed for the whole of UK sport".

"You don't have to be an expert. You don't have to have all the answers," said Shearer. "But we can all be better at asking, listening, and helping someone find the right support."

Shearer said it was particularly poignant that the launch would be at Everton, one of the clubs where Gary Speed had played, a friend of Shearer's who died by suicide in 2011.

News.title: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform UK over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.

An undercover reporter recorded two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled Â£500,000.

The police investigation by the Met's Special Enquiry Team is being folded into an inquiry that has been under way into other donations to the party.

A Reform UK spokesman said the party "denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation".

"We won't be commenting further while a live investigation is under way."

A Met spokesperson said it had received "a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party", after the film by Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations was shown on Thursday evening.

In its statement, the Met Police said: "All allegations under investigation relate to potential offences under the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000."

"Detectives continue to liaise closely with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as enquiries progress."

The police spokesperson said detectives were seeking to obtain footage relating to the broadcast.

An Electoral Commission spokesperson said the Channel 4 News report included "serious allegations of wrongdoing", adding: "It is right that these are properly and thoroughly investigated by the police.

"In parallel, we are also considering all relevant information and regulatory steps."

The film overshadowed the party's conference in Birmingham and led to the party losing two key figures - Dan Jukes, chief of staff to the leader Nigel Farage, and James Orr, head of policy.

News.title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog
News.content:
The UK needs new regulations for AI products used in the NHS and other healthcare settings, says Britain's industry watchdog.

The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which regulates all medical devices and licenses treatment drugs in the UK, has published 44 recommendations to update its policies as the use of AI in the sector rises.

The technology will soon be routinely used within the NHS, MHRA chief Lawrence Tallon told the BBC.

"What I would expect is that patients will... increasingly see AI as part of the way that normal NHS healthcare is delivered," he said.

"That should happen in a way that they can maintain their trust and their confidence in what's happening."

The report was compiled by an independent commission and involved input from more than 12,000 people including patients and clinicians.

The recommendations include:

Continuously monitoring AI products and removing them from regulatory approval if they malfunction or become less effective over time

Giving patients the right to know whether AI is involved in their care, and easy access to information about the products involved

The power to penalise the developers of an AI product if it fails to meet required standards

An AI "L plate" system which would make it easier for new AI models to be trialled by healthcare professionals under close supervision

"The medical devices regulatory framework predominantly dates from a period where we were thinking about things like hip replacements and knee replacements, or smaller things like stethoscopes and plasters," Tallon said.

He added while current guidelines may work for simple AI products trained to spot known symptoms on scans, for example, the rules do not apply to more complex models.

"Unlike most of the medical products we're used to regulating, these products continue to change after the point of authorization," he said.

"As new data gets fed in, they learn, they adapt, they drift."

And he acknowledged trying to regulate AI is a global challenge.

"I don't think at this moment in time we can point to a single country, a single regulatory framework, and say that they have absolutely cracked it," he said.

News.title: Air traffic failure was avoidable, says transport secretary
News.content:
A technical failure of the UK's air traffic control system that has caused widespread flight chaos was avoidable, according to the Transport Secretary.

Heidi Alexander told the Commons she had ordered an independent investigation by the aviation watchdog into the system operated by Nats, which went down for four hours on Tuesday.

More than 2,000 flights have been cancelled as disruption continued for a second day with passengers stuggling to fly out of and into the UK.

After meeting with the boss of Nats, Martin Rolfe, Alexander said a cyberattack could be ruled out, but she added: "I do not believe this issue was unavoidable."

Nats has apologised for its third major technical fault in three years.

Alexander said she discussed with Rolfe how Nats, which is 49% owned by the government, "responded to resolve and minimise the disruption as quickly as possible".

She said there had to be "tough questions about resilience of Nats systems", adding: "We also need to think about consumer redress issues."

Earlier on Wednesday the government said it had confidence in Rolfe, who has led Nats for 11 years as airlines such as Wizz Air and Ryanair called for him to step down.

Nats has been asked to investigate the incident and report back in one week. But Alexander said she has also asked the Civil Aviation Authority to conduct an independent review and present an update in six months' time.

Airlines UK, which represents the country's carriers, said it had written to Alexander to "register serious concerns over yesterday's technical failure at Nats - the third major system failure in three years - which has caused major disruption across the UK's aviation network".

Airlines UK's chief executive Tim Alderslade, said: "The result is a system where airlines pick up the bill for the mistakes of others, while the organisations responsible face little or no financial consequence.

"Accountability should sit where responsibility lies and the Civil Aviation Bill offers the opportunity to address this."

The UK Civil Aviation Authority said passengers are unlikely to be entitled to compensation - though it reminded airlines of their responsibilities to look after passengers who flights had been delayed or cancelled.

It added that the disruption caused by the Nats issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances'", meaning passengers "are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident."

News.title: National security can't come at expense of social security, Burnham says
News.content:
In the Commons session, Burnham repeated that the government would meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for hitting the 3% figure set out in the spending review in the spring.

The PM said he had appointed John Healey, who resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the government's failure to commit to a 3% increase by 2030, "because of his strong commitment to the defence of this nation".

However, Badenoch hit back that 2035 was "a decade away" and "the threats are now".

She questioned whether Burnham was "unable" or "just unwilling" to meet the 2030 target.

In response, Burnham insisted: "This chancellor of all chancellors will be willing to provide that funding to our armed forces."

However, he rejected a Conservative plan to partly fund increased defence spending by saving at least Â£4bn through reforms to housing benefit.

"I don't think, myself, that taking Â£4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation," he said.

"Yes, we do everything to support our national security, but it can't come at the expense of social security."

He added: "This side of the House will not be forced to choose between the two and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% by 2035 at the spending review."

Badenoch said Burnham's comments were "unbelievable", adding: "We need to fund our defence, not spend all of our money on welfare."

Burnham insisted he would "bring the welfare budget down" by tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training.

"That's the Labour way to get the welfare bill down," he said.

"That is the right way to fund defence."

Badenoch accused Burnham of being "continuity Keir".

"He's pretending that he's the change candidate. But the fact is, he's still failing to cut welfare," she said.

As prime minister, Sir Keir attempted to cut disability benefits but was forced to row back on the plans in the face of opposition from Labour MPs.

Cutting the welfare bill is a key part of Tory proposals for funding increased defence spending.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to Â£408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

There is particular concern about the nearly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training â known as "Neets".

The government has asked former minister Alan Milburn to look into the issue and he is expected to publish his final recommendations for how to tackle the problem shortly.

News.title: Miliband rejects chief rabbi's claim British Jews in greater danger after sanctions move
News.content:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has rejected the chief rabbi's warning that British Jews are at greater risk after the UK announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband said that as a "proud British Jew" he disagreed with UK Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, who described the move as a "truly dark day" that would "succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target".

"We all need to do more to tackle antisemitism," Miliband said, "but I believe we can do that and stand up for British values".

The sanctions on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank come against a backdrop of rising antisemitic incidents across the UK.

The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026, a 21% increase on the same period in 2025.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham defended his government's decision, telling MPs that "Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice".

"Where people are being bullied out of their homes... we will always stand with the underdog," he said.

While a strong reaction against the move had been expected from the US - Israel's most powerful ally - President Donald Trump was relatively muted in his first public comments on the matter on Wednesday.

He told reporters he would speak to both Israel and the UK to "find out... their thinking" and ask why the decision had been made "all of a sudden".

News.title: Man charged with assisting Russian intelligence service
News.content:
A 31-year-old British man has been charged under the National Security Act over alleged contact with Russia's military intelligence agency.

Joshua Cammidge, from Swindon, allegedly received instructions from an individual believed to be linked to the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said.

He has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.

He is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday.

Cammidge was arrested at an address in Swindon on Friday by Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London officers, supported by officers from Wiltshire Police.

He was taken to a London police station and searches were carried out at a different address in Swindon, the Metropolitan Police said.

He was further arrested and detained under the National Security Act on Saturday.

The force said he has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service contrary to Section 3 of the National Security Act 203 and preparatory conduct contrary to Section 18 of the National Security Act 2023.

Frank Ferguson, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.

"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial.

"It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."

Security Minister Dan Jarvis said: "The police have taken action against a potential threat, and I thank them for the vital work they do every day to keep us safe.

"Whilst it would be inappropriate to comment further on the specifics of this case, I know people will be concerned about recent incidents across Europe, intended to sow fear, create disruption and undermine support for Ukraine. They will not succeed."

News.title: Failures 'contributed to' death of Sir Richard Branson's wife
News.content:
A private hospital's failure to provide preventative medication contributed to the death of Lady Joan Branson, an inquest has concluded.

The 80-year-old, who was married to Sir Richard Branson, died on 24 November last year after suffering a cardiac arrest at the private Lister Hospital in Chelsea, west London.

Senior coroner Professor Fiona Wilcox told Westminster Coroner's Court on Wednesday that Lady Joan did not receive prophylactic anticoagulants at the hospital despite a "very high risk of developing deep vein thrombosis".

"I do find her death would have likely been prevented and the lack of anticoagulation did cause or contribute to her death probably," she said.

The coroner's court heard that Lady Joan was admitted to the hospital on 17 November after a fall weeks earlier on Necker Island, a British Virgin Island owned by her billionaire husband.

She died after suffering a pulmonary embolism, a sudden, dangerous blockage in a lung artery, resulting from deep vein thrombosis.

Haematologist Dr George Adams told the inquest that Lady Joan was "extremely high risk" for blood clots and the "biggest risk factor by far was her immobility and her fracture".

From her hospital admission to her death, Glasgow-born Lady Joan did not receive any prophylactic anticoagulation, which is used to stop blood clots from forming.

The hospital's admitting doctor, Dr Basir Kunduzi, did not complete a bleeding risk assessment on the day of her admission, the inquest heard.

Dr Kunduzi said Lady Joan's death led him to "reflect on my role as a doctor" and the importance of "good communication between team members".

Giving her conclusion, Professor Wilcox said it was "not a case of neglect" and there "wasn't an absence of treatment".

After her death, Sir Richard described his wife as the "shining star around which our family's universe has always orbited".

News.title: Drug gangs exploited and raped us as teens, then police failed us, women tell BBC
News.content:
Warning: Contains details of sexual exploitation

"It was the thrill of being with a bad boy."

Christine was 13 when she began exchanging messages online with someone she believed was a teenage boy.

On their first meeting, she discovered he was a grown man 10 years older than herself. He also told her he was involved with gangs and drugs.

"I always knew, OK, he's probably hurt someone, but in terms of hurting me, I didn't think it would get to that point," she says.

Over the next few years, he would use Christine to courier drugs, subject her to extreme sexual exploitation, and assault her so violently she feared she might die.

Christine is one of four women who have chosen to waive their anonymity and speak publicly to the BBC documentary, Britain's Forgotten Girls, about how they were targeted by criminals when they were children.

Their stories, covering 2002 to last year, differ in detail - but reveal strikingly similar patterns of abuse. All four describe being targeted by boys and older men connected to drug gangs, manipulated into abusive relationships, then repeatedly sexually exploited.

All believe the authorities failed to protect them and did not take their allegations seriously.

The sexual and criminal exploitation of girls by drug gangs has long been overshadowed in public discussion by the focus on sexual grooming gangs, according to front-line social workers and experts in the field.

"For grooming gangs, the primary purpose is often the sexual exploitation of those girls, but the primary purpose of a drug gang is to make money off selling drugs and other criminal activity," says Connie Muttock from the children's charity, Centre for Young Lives.

Girls are brought in to generate money, says Muttock, but many are also sexually abused by gang members.

News.title: Learner drivers still forced to wait months to book tests
News.content:
Learner drivers have to wait an average 20 weeks, or around five months, before booking a practical test, according to new figures, despite attempts to reduce delays.

The data from the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) for August is only a marginal improvement from 20.2 weeks in July.

The average wait time between booking and sitting a test is unchanged at 11.1 weeks.

The DVSA initially had a target of reducing the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible.

The DVSA made a number of changes to its practical driving test booking system earlier this year.

Only the learner driver themself is now able to book their driving test, blocking an instructor or third parties from booking using the learner's details.

There is also a geographical restriction which means a learner can only book a test at their three local test centres, rather than one at the other side of the country if they found a test available.

The number of times a would-be driver can swap a test date has also been restricted.

Actress Sheridan Smith, singer Beverley Knight and pop duo Ward Thomas will take to the stage for the Last Night of the Proms in a tribute to country superstar Dolly Parton.

The final show will include the programme, To Dolly, With Love, in honour of the singer who died in August aged 80 following a brief battle with cancer.

Arranged by Fiona Brice, Smith, Knight and Ward Thomas will join the BBC Symphony Orchestra and Chorus on stage at the Royal Albert Hall on Saturday to perform a medley of her beloved hits. Gavin and Stacey star Smith will sing a rendition of 9 to 5 while Knight will take the stage to sing I Will Always Love You.

Country-pop duo Ward Thomas, made up of twins Catherine and Lizzy Ward Thomas, will sing a rendition of Parton’s Jolene.

The concert will be broadcast live on BBC Radio 3 and BBC Sounds, and air in two parts – the first on BBC Two and the finale on BBC One.

Sam Jackson, BBC Radio 3 and Proms controller, said: “This year’s Last Night of the Proms promises to be a joyous celebration, bringing together world-class performers, much-loved repertoire and memorable musical moments.

The concert will be broadcast live on BBC Radio 3 and BBC Sounds ( PA )

“We very much look forward to the centenary of the BBC Proms next year but, for now, we can’t wait to celebrate the end of the 2026 season in style.”

The programme also includes the world premieres of two BBC commissions: Iris of Life by Academy Award-winning British composer Anne Dudley and Dithyramb by Canadian composer and conductor Samy Moussa.

Chief conductor Sakari Oramo will lead the BBC Symphony Orchestra, Chorus and the BBC Singers for a classical music programme which will feature Loesser’s Guys and Dolls’ Sit Down, You’re Rockin’ the Boat.

The concert marks the end of the BBC Proms 2026 season, which spanned eight weeks and featured 86 concerts that were attended by 300,000 people.

Suzy Klein, head of arts and classical music TV at the BBC, said: “The BBC Proms has once again connected audiences across the UK and beyond through an extraordinary summer of live music.

“We’re incredibly proud of the range and quality of concerts across BBC television and BBC iPlayer, and the Last Night will provide the perfect finale to an unforgettable season.”

The Last Night of the Proms takes place on September 12 live on BBC Radio 3 and Sounds, with Part 1 on BBC Two and iPlayer from 7.10pm, and the finale on BBC One and iPlayer at 9pm.

Audiences can listen to the BBC Proms on BBC Sounds for 30 days after broadcast, and TV broadcasts are available on BBC iPlayer for up to one year.

RuPaul’s Drag Race UK has been axed by the BBC after 11 series due to “significant financial pressures”, the broadcaster has confirmed.

Produced by World of Wonder, the reality series follows drag queens as they compete to impress a panel of judges, including RuPaul, Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Alan Carr.

The news was announced on its Instagram page and comes days after the eighth series premiered on BBC Three.

Future series, as well as its international all-star spin-off, RuPaul’s Drag Race UK vs The World, will be broadcast on its streaming platform, Wow Presents Plus.

A BBC spokesperson said: “As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly.

“We can therefore confirm, together with World of Wonder, that RuPaul’s Drag Race UK will be leaving the BBC and moving to WOW Presents Plus.

Judges Michelle Visage, RuPaul and Graham Norton ( PA )

“The BBC is incredibly proud of all eleven series of this ground-breaking show and we would like to thank RuPaul, World of Wonder and everyone involved, both on and off screen.

“We are certain that viewers will enjoy the eighth series, which is currently airing on BBC iPlayer and BBC Three.”

The latest series of RuPaul’s Drag Race UK launched in September 2026 and will continue to air on BBC Three before transferring to iPlayer.

There are eight seasons of the main series and three of the international spin-off, which viewers will be able to continue watching once the move is complete.

Based on the US series, the show launched in 2019 and brought British drag into the mainstream in the UK and made a name for a number of performers including La Voix, Danny Beard, Baga Chipz and the late The Vivienne.

The BBC is currently attempting to make £500 million in savings over two years.

In an internal note sent to staff earlier this year, chief content officer Kate Phillips outlined the proposed savings, which aim to reduce the corporation’s spend on commissioning by £80 million in the 2027 to 2028 financial year.

Amsterdam is a city built for movement. From the estimated 900,000 bicycles that outnumber its permanent residents to the 165 canals crossed by over 1,200 bridges – making it a larger waterway network than Venice. But how does that freedom of movement translate for disabled travellers visiting Dam?

I’ve visited Amsterdam three times, a number which is rare for me when it comes to overseas city breaks. Not because it’s perfect – truly, I don’t believe any city has perfect accessibility – but because it’s one of the few places where I can focus on the experience rather than the logistics.

When you travel as a wheelchair user, every journey usually starts with military-level planning. But a trip to Amsterdam can be more flexible. I find I can move, explore and change my plans without everything unravelling. The city is compact, largely flat and built for bikes, which provides an unexpected benefit for visitors with accessibility needs.

open image in gallery Amsterdam’s tram network makes it easy to explore independently ( Carrie-Ann Lightly )



Getting there

Travelling from London St Pancras International by Eurostar to Amsterdam Centraal Station sets a relaxed tone from the start of a trip, as I can stay in my wheelchair the whole time. The accessible seating is spacious, with a meal service included. You can also have a companion travel with you at a reduced fare so you can sit together.

Even being able to use the accessible toilet on board independently feels like a “perk” as it’s so rare for a wheelchair user travelling between countries.

Arrival into Amsterdam Centraal is just as straightforward. Step-free routes, lifts and clear signage mean you can leave the station independently and be in the city within minutes.

Where to stay

In Amsterdam, staying near Centraal Station puts much of the city within easy reach.

At ibis Amsterdam Centre, the decor is simple and contemporary. The accessible room is spacious and thoughtfully laid out with a bathroom that includes a roll-in shower and good turning space.

The central location also made it easy to return to the hotel between plans, so you can rest, reset and head back out again ready to explore.

Price: From £127

Getting around

Amsterdam’s cycling culture shapes how the city feels to move through. The same routes that work for bikes often work well for wheelchair users. There are cobbles and crowds, but sticking to the smoother cycle paths where permitted, travelling outside of peak times and choosing wider streets alongside the canals can make a big difference. Overall, I find it far more manageable to navigate than many other historic cities.

open image in gallery Carrie-Ann in Dam Square ( Carrie-Ann Lightly )

It’s possible to explore the city independently without relying on public transport. Though when needed, the options are straightforward to use, including the free ferries across the IJ to Amsterdam Noord, and the well-connected tram network, some of which have wheelchair spaces on board. From the ibis, it’s around a 10-minute roll to the wheelchair accessible tram platforms at Dam, while the free ferries across the IJ to Amsterdam Noord leave from directly behind Centraal Station.

Accessible toilets do take more effort to find. Smaller, older venues are hit and miss. One reliable fallback I found is Wagamama at Max Euweplein, just off Leidseplein and close to the Hard Rock Cafe, where I could use the accessible toilet without being tied to dining there. Chain restaurants and hotels are often happy for me to use their facilities too. It’s not a glamorous option, but it is a practical one, and it meant I could stay out longer without worrying.



What to do

A canal cruise is one of the easiest ways to get to grips with Amsterdam’s layout. The Blue Boat company have accessible boats with ramped boarding and spaces so you can remain in your chair. Its 75-minute City Canal Cruise leaves from Stadhouderskade 501, opposite the Hard Rock Cafe near Leidseplein, and returns to the same spot, with audio guides available in 19 languages.

From the water, the city feels calmer. You glide past houseboats, bridges and narrow streets, taking it all in without needing to navigate crowds or uneven surfaces.

open image in gallery The Van Gogh Museum is one of Amsterdam’s most accessible attractions ( Getty Images )

The Van Gogh Museum is one of Amsterdam’s best-known cultural attractions, with the world’s largest collection of work by the artist. The gallery traces his life, influences and artistic development, from early sketches and self-portraits to his vivid landscapes, still-life paintings and letters. It gives insight into the person behind the paintings.

It’s also one of the most accessible major attractions in the city. Entry is step-free, lifts connect each level and there are accessible toilets. What stands out to me is the pacing. Seating is built into the galleries, so you can pause when you need to without feeling in the way. The layout moves through his life and work in a way that feels thoughtful and easy to follow, rather than overwhelming.

One of my favourite ways to explore Amsterdam is taking the free ferry across the IJ to Noord, the neighbourhood directly opposite Centraal Station. Ferries leave frequently from behind the station and the crossing takes just a few minutes. With level boarding and plenty of space for wheelchairs, bikes and pedestrians, it feels less like a tourist attraction and more like joining Amsterdam locals on their everyday commute.

At the other side, the A’DAM Lookout offers a completely different perspective. Lifts take you to the top, where you can see the full spread of the city from the observation deck.

The Heineken Experience in the De Pijp neighbourhood near Museumplein offers a lively look at one of Amsterdam’s most recognisable exports, taking visitors through the brand’s former brewery with a mix of heritage, storytelling and interactive displays. Expect historic brewing rooms, multimedia exhibits, tasting moments and plenty of playful, photo-friendly touches along the way.

Much of the route is step-free, with lifts between floors, although some of the older areas are tighter and less straightforward to navigate. What makes the difference is how staff handle it. Where access was limited, they explain clearly, offer alternative routes and adapt the experience without fuss. It removes that awkward feeling of being left out or unsure, and makes the visit feel much more relaxed.

Food and drink

open image in gallery Foodhallen is a popular indoor food market located in a renovated historic tram depot ( Getty Images )

Amsterdam is a city you can snack your way through. Chips with mayo, fresh stroopwafels, bitterballen, local cheese picked up as you go. It suits a more flexible way of travelling. Vlaams Friteshuis Vleminckx, near Spui, serves cones of chips from a street level hatch, while Rudi’s Original Stroopwafels bakes its stroopwafels fresh from a food truck at the Albert Cuyp Market. For bitterballen, head to Foodhallen in Amsterdam West, where there’s an adapted toilet next door in Filmhallen.

For something more special, Sea Palace stands out. Set on a boat on the water near Centraal Station, it serves Cantonese favourites such as freshly made dim sum, Peking duck and prawns in XO sauce, all designed for sharing. Getting onto a floating restaurant as a wheelchair user can feel like stepping into the unknown, but here it is straightforward. Inside, there is space to move comfortably, accessible toilets and views across the harbour.

Across the IJ in Noord, Cafe Restaurant THT at Tolhuistuin is a favourite for lunch after visiting A’DAM Lookout. I’ve eaten everything from shakshuka to beef udon from its globally inspired menu, and the raised waterfront terrace has great views back across the IJ. There’s a lift to the restaurant, an accessible toilet and outdoor seating.

For an evening drink, Kanarie Club in Amsterdam West occupies a cavernous former tram depot at De Hallen, with a huge central bar and plenty of space to settle in over beers, wine or craft sodas. Wheelchair users will find it easier to enter directly from Bellamyplein rather than navigating the busy Foodhallen, and there’s an accessible toilet beside the bar.



How accessible is Amsterdam?

Amsterdam is not perfect. Cobbles appear often. Some historic spaces are still hard to navigate. Accessible toilets aren’t always en route. But the city has a nice flow, distances are manageable, and the infrastructure supports different ways of moving. That’s why I keep going back. Not because everything works, but because enough of it does that I can spend my time experiencing the city, not figuring it out.

A Hong Kong court on Thursday convicted the publisher of The Wall Street Journal of deterring its reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city. The court acquitted Dow Jones Publishing Co. (Asia) Inc. of the charge of dismissal over the union role.

Former WSJ reporter Selina Cheng, also chairperson of the trade union Hong Kong Journalists Association, launched a private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing Co. (Asia) Inc. after losing her job in July 2024.

Hong Kong, once considered a bastion of press freedom in Asia, has seen its media landscape change drastically in recent years, including the forced closure of news outlets and the prosecution of newsroom leaders.

Principal Magistrate David Cheung convicted the defendant of the first charge but said the defense has raised sufficient reasonable doubt for the second charge.

Cheng earlier said her supervisor told her that her participation in the union election was problematic and that the supervisor needed to discuss the issue with the Journal management in New York and Dow Jones’ in-house lawyers. Cheng said she was told that her union role would be incompatible with her employment.

Dow Jones pleaded not guilty last year to two charges under the city’s Employment Ordinance, each carrying a maximum fine of 100,000 Hong Kong dollars (about $12,750). The first charge alleges the company had prevented or deterred Cheng from exercising union participation rights. The second alleges the company terminated her employment for exercising those rights.

During the trial, the defense tried to convince the court that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and argued the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the firm’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor. The defense also accused Cheng of acting in bad faith in a previous hearing.

Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.

Cheng’s termination in 2024 alarmed many journalists, especially given that foreign outlets have traditionally faced less pressure than local news outlets in Hong Kong.

After Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020, two local news outlets known for critical coverage of the government, Apple Daily and Stand News, were forced to shut down following the arrest of their senior management.

Jimmy Lai, founder of Apple Daily, was sentenced to 20 years in prison in February. His staffers received prison terms ranging from six years and nine months, to 10 years.

Hong Kong, a former British colony returned to Chinese rule in 1997, ranked 140th out of 180 countries and territories in Reporters Without Borders’ latest World Press Freedom Index, down from 18th out of 139 regions in 2002.

Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in the Indian state of Odisha, thousands of kilometres from their natural habitat, prompting an investigation into how they got there.

Orangutans are not native to India. They are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia, and all three recognised species – Bornean, Sumatran and Tapanuli – are classified as “critically endangered” by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Odisha's forest minister said investigators were examining whether the animals had been trafficked by an international smuggling network and abandoned near a highway.

His government had asked India’s Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate, the minister said, adding that local police, forest officials and a special task force were involved in the inquiry.

The apes were found on Tuesday in Ranakata, a proposed reserve forest in Bhogarai block, district forest officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar said. They were spotted close to a state highway by villagers.

The animals could not have reached Odisha naturally and might have been transported there by road, Mr Indalkar said. "The area is covered mainly by casuarina trees and isn’t a dense forest," he said. "It’s also close to a state highway."

The police's special task force is revisiting old orangutan smuggling cases to establish whether an organised trafficking network is involved.

"We are analysing similar cases and contacting teams that looked into them," deputy inspector general of police KV Singh told the Indian Express.

“We are currently gathering data and carrying out local inquiries.”

Forest officials said they believed the orangutans had been in the area for only two to three days before they were spotted. A search of the surrounding forest found no other orangutans or clues as to how the animals had arrived, Mr Indalkar said.

Officials described them as infants, though some local reports suggested they were between one and two years old.

Their young age raised particular concern, wildlife expert Biswajit Mohanty said. Young orangutans typically remain with their mothers for several years while they learn to survive independently, and females usually give birth only once every eight years, making it unusual for five young animals to be found together with no adults nearby.

The animals, three males and two females, were given first aid before being taken to the Nandankanan Zoological Park in the capital Bhubaneswar, where they underwent health checks and were placed in a quarantine facility.

“Three animal keepers and a special veterinary team have been assigned to take care of them and we are also monitoring them through CCTV," Pradeep Mirase, the zoo’s deputy director, told the Express.

"As one of them had a fever, authorities administered medication. They are stable now. Our focus is to stabilise them, following which we would conduct some tests."

An orangutan opens a water bottle in its enclosure at Dortmund Zoo in Germany ( AFP/Getty )

A special diet chart has been drawn up in consultation with the Mysore Zoo, which is home to three orangutans and has experience caring for the species.

The animals are being fed every two hours, with the youngest given mashed potatoes and apples, and the others bananas and apples, alongside milk.

Zoo officials have also provided toys and slings to the animals, who have appeared to enjoy staying together as a group.

Commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites, the global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife, and they are also protected under Indian wildlife law. Despite this, orangutans continue to be trafficked to private collectors and for sale as exotic pets.

The native habitat of orangutans has also been under severe pressure of late.

Wildfires in Indonesian Kalimantan, on Borneo, affected about 60 per cent of Bornean orangutan habitat between June and August this year, according to an analysis by the environmental group Geopix, which recorded some 18,000 fire hotspots inside the orangutan habitat during that period.

The group said the fires were worsened by the climate crisis and a strong El Nino.

Conservationists in the region separately reported rescuing orangutans directly threatened by the fires in recent weeks, including a mother and baby moved to a rescue centre in West Kalimantan after flames spread close to their habitat.

This is not the first time young orangutans have been found in India. In 2022, two baby orangutans were discovered abandoned at a checkpoint near the border between the states of Assam and Mizoram, with officials suspecting they had been brought into the country through neighbouring Myanmar.
