World.title: A new Anthropic model seeks to test how AI could impact the U.S. economy
World.content:
A new Anthropic model seeks to test how AI could impact the U.S. economy

toggle caption Imen Ben Youssef/AFP

Will artificial intelligence light a fire under the U.S. economy in the coming years? That's been a big question in the field of economics, and now Anthropic — the company behind the popular Claude AI assistant — is taking a stab at helping people find their own answers. The company has created an interactive tool that lets users test their assumptions about how productive — or disruptive — the AI boom might be.

In one scenario, artificial intelligence provides a gentle boost to the economy, lifting growth rates with little effect on workers. At the other extreme, GDP soars, but so does unemployment, with nearly 14% of workers losing their jobs to AI and less than half of them finding new ones.

Sponsor Message

The different outcomes depend on how capable and flexible the technology is, how quickly it's adopted, whether it supports or replaces workers, and whether displaced workers find new work to do.

"In the modest change scenario, AI is a small technology. The economy continues on a 'normal' path with AI making changes around the margins," Anthropic experts write in an accompanying blog post. "In the extreme scenario, AI transforms the economy. The macroeconomic consequences go well beyond any event in history, both in terms of magnitudes and in terms of the speed at which change happens."

Authors of the Anthropic study do not offer a prediction of which outcome is more likely. In general, they say, AI experts tend to project a more rapid spread of the technology while economists tend to be more cautious.

Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark is somewhere in the middle.

"I think the technology will keep developing at a very, very fast and sustained rate but diffusion of the technology will likely be more challenging than people think," Clark told NPR. "So it will get really, really good. But it will make its way into the economy more slowly."

AI's impact on economy is uncertain

A survey by Anthropic of nearly 11,000 people found that the public's expectations of AI are also mixed. The average survey respondent projects a significant boost in productivity and economic growth but also a substantial disruption to workers in AI-sensitive fields.

Sponsor Message

A major determinant of AI's impact will be how quickly it spreads through the economy.

"If the AI can do amazing things but nobody uses it, then it's not going to have an economic impact," says Anton Korinek, Anthropic's head of transformative AI economic studies.

While rapid adoption of the technology could be more disruptive, it could also produce much faster economic growth. In Anthropic's extreme case, GDP grows at more than seven times its current pace. That could produce a lot of additional tax revenue to support workers who are hurt by AI.

"If you end up with this level of GDP growth, you have moves available to you as a [government] policymaker that are unimaginable today," Clark says. "Policymakers should get ready to spend."

World.title: Whatever happened to the measles outbreak that shocked a country this year?
World.content:
Whatever happened to the measles outbreak that shocked a country this year?

toggle caption Ali Asif Shawon for NPR

In May, we posted a story about the rapid and devastating spread of measles in Bangladesh. The headline: More than 500 children have died in an outbreak that the world is virtually ignoring . We asked the reporter who covered the story to tell us what has transpired since then.

About This Series Over the next week, we'll be looking back at some of our past global health and development stories to see "whatever happened to ..."

There was optimism early on about bringing the measles outbreak in Bangladesh under control.

In April, the country's health minister, Sardar Md. Sakhawat Husain, offered this assessment : "Measles outbreak has somewhat decreased in the country. Once the nationwide vaccination campaign begins on April 20, the situation will improve further."

The goal was to vaccinate 18 million children ages 6 months to 5 years, even if records indicated they'd already been vaccinated. That goal was met and then some, with 18.4 million vaccinations.

Five months later, the outbreak continues apace.

In August, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that Bangladesh has had more measles cases than any other country from January to June of this year: 57,561.

Sponsor Message

On the day of Aug. 31, authorities recorded 1,162 suspected cases and 94 confirmed cases in 24 hours.

On September 9, the toll for children who have died from suspected or confirmed measles cases since March 15 passed 1,000, according to the Directorate General of Health Services of Bangladesh.

Why has the virus not been conquered?

It turns out that 18 million vaccinations wasn't enough to reach all the unvaccinated children. Health experts in the country now say that 22.6 million is the true target.

This persistent immunization gap has given the highly contagious virus a continued chance to spread.

"Many children have still not received the measles vaccine, so we cannot go into a relaxed mode," Tajul Abdul Bari told NPR. He is a vaccine expert and former program manager of the government's Expanded Programme on Immunization. "We need to start a new vaccination campaign, potentially covering children from 6 months up to under 10 years of age. We did something similar in 2014."

Dr. Javid Abdelmoneim, president of Médecins Sans Frontières International, told NPR, "The management of a measles outbreak is vaccinating. Vaccinate, vaccinate, vaccinate."

"Measles has a very specific biology. It is highly transmissible. One case of measles can affect 100 others," he added.

Dr Jahangir Alam , the World Health Organization's divisional coordinator for the capital city of Dhaka, said: "Even small gaps in immunization coverage can trigger outbreaks. Every missed child increases the risk."

Sponsor Message

Indeed, a UNICEF situation report says that 72% of cases are among those with no doses of the two-dose vaccine and 16% of the patients are partially vaccinated.

The toll has been worsened because of the country's widespread malnutrition, which increases the risk of severe illness and death from a measles infection. "Children who are underweight or have two or more medical conditions at the same time suffer more, and their condition worsens," says Colonel Latifa Rahman, director of Mohakhali DNCC Hospital, the hospital in the capital that is now doing nothing but measles care.

Malnutrition can also lessen the immunity conferred by a vaccine.

Next steps

On Aug. 18, Bangladesh announced it will vaccinate another 1.6 million children against measles.

Former Health Services Division Secretary Md Kamruzzaman Chowdhury said official data shows that in some pockets of the country, there are children between 6 months and 5 years who missed out on vaccination. in pockets of the country.

"In light of that, we will administer the 1.6 million vaccines we currently have," he said.

The government is also moving to procure another 2.5 million doses to guard against future shortages, according to Kamruzzaman.

"We will give 1.6 million now and are procuring 2.5 million vaccines for the future. We have spoken with UNICEF about purchasing these vaccines," he added.

toggle caption Ali Asif Shawon for NPR

So the early forecast of a quick end to the outbreak has been tempered by the reality in Bangladesh.

"There is no scope for unrealistic assurances. Even if the pace of vaccination were doubled, it would still take another two to three months to bring the measles outbreak fully under control," State Minister for Health Dr. M.A. Muhit said on Aug. 19.

The toll on families

As the outbreak continues, thousands of families are being driven into financial distress. Nearly 9 in 10 affected households have borrowed money for treatment and 6 in 10 have exhausted their savings, according to a joint assessment in May and June by the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).

Sponsor Message

The assessment covered 2,746 measles-affected households receiving care at 12 government medical colleges and district hospitals.

Sonakshi Dey of the IFRC in Bangladesh said economic hardships continue even if a child has recovered: "Beyond direct medical expenses, caregivers often lose income when they need to stay home to care for a sick child or travel repeatedly to health facilities. For low-income households that depend on daily wages, even a short interruption to work can have serious consequences for household wellbeing and food security."

Families who have lost a child face the heaviest toll of all. Toriqul Islam, whose 10-month-old boy died due to measles on May 9, said in a heavy tone:

"When fate turns against you, this is what happens. I don't know if there is any greater pain in this world.

"Let the government do whatever they want, but all I want is for no one to die."

Ali Asif Shawon is the chief reporter at Dhaka Tribune in Bangladesh, where he covers politics, security, climate change, migration and global health. He can be reached on LinkedIn.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: What will Trump's retaliatory tariffs do to Canada’s economy big picture?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The White House fired another shot in the Canada-U.S. trade war this week, banning outright the imports of Canadian dairy, motorcycles and some alcohol products.

But how much will those bans, along with fresh 50 per cent tariffs on a slate of other products, actually impact the Canadian economy?

Not all that much, say economists who’ve run the numbers. But that doesn't mean it won't hurt certain industries — and it certainly won't give business owners any peace of mind.

On Tuesday night, the White House retaliated against Canada's counter-tariffs with the bans and the addition of 50 per cent tariffs to items including mattresses and some paper products. American officials also dropped tariffs on others, such as toilet paper, cement and sugar.

But according to one analysis from Derek Holt, vice president and head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, the new tariffs will apply to an estimated $3 billion worth of Canadian goods, while the removed tariffs apply to about $2 billion worth — making the difference marginal, given Canada exported more than $527 billion worth of goods to the U.S. in 2025.

The bans on alcohol, dairy and motorcycles will also be negligible, Holt adds, as Canada sends very little dairy and few motorcycles south of the border. Alcohol exports are a bit higher than the other categories, with $550 million worth sent to the U.S. last year, according to his analysis, but the export bans would still only impact $700 million worth of Canadian exports to the U.S.

"These actions are face saving by the U.S. administration, not substantive in nature and that’s a positive," Holt said in a note to investors on Wednesday.

WATCH | How will the new U.S. retaliatory tariffs impact Canadians?: How will the new U.S. retaliatory tariffs impact Canadians? | Duration 5:22 U.S. President Donald Trump has hit Canada with a new round of trade measures, escalating the trade war. CBC's Peter Armstrong says the scope of the trade war has grown, and as a result, regional disruptions could lead to job losses and the closure of small businesses.

He says the rising cost of oil — which soared past $100 for the first time since July on Wednesday due to escalating tensions in the Middle East — poses a greater economic risk than the new U.S. measures.

At BMO, chief economist Doug Porter agrees. His team puts the value of newly tariffed items and those taken off the list both at about $2 billion, putting the country "in the same spot" as it was before the announcement.

But where the tariffs do hit, in certain industries or parts of the country, they will still hurt business owners badly, Porter told CBC News.

Just Asking wants to know: What questions do you have about shopping in the age of the Canada-U.S. trade dispute? Send us your questions before our Sept. 12 show.

"It's extremely negative for the new industries and products that were selected, but of course, some pretty important ones were taken off the list," he said.

"So there are going to be some relieved industries today and some horrified."

50% tariffs already an effective ban

For makers of Canadian booze, further escalation isn't a positive sign. Cal Bricker, CEO of Spirits Canada, says Canada exports much of the alcohol it makes to the U.S., making the continued targeting of his industry a concern.

WATCH | U.S. ban on booze will hit hard, says Spirits Canada CEO: U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol would bite deep, Spirits Canada says | Duration 3:06 About half of the $2 billion in spirits produced in Canada every year is sold to the U.S., says Cal Bricker, president and CEO of Spirits Canada. 'We sell more Crown Royal in Texas than we do in all of Canada.'

But because many alcohol products already faced 50 per cent tariffs, upping the ante to a ban might not make a material difference to many booze producers.

Matt Johnston of craft brewer Collective Arts in Hamilton, Ont., says he wouldn't have been able to send any more of his beer south at a 50 per cent rate anyway.

"The reality is that once you add 50 per cent tariffs, it becomes extremely difficult to try and sell on the market.”

He already sent months worth of product to the U.S. before the new tariffs came into effect a few weeks ago, in hopes a deal could be reached before supplies ran out. Now, the plan is to grow the business within Canada and other international markets to make up for the loss of U.S. sales, where a fifth of their business used to come from.

Empty Collective Arts beer bottles on display at their Hamilton location. The brewery says 50 per cent tariffs were already acting as a ban before the White House's latest retaliation. (Collective Arts Brewing)

"The world's a big place and we can look elsewhere," Johnston said.

As with alcohol, many of the banned items were already facing 50 per cent tariffs, RBC economist Nathan Janzen points out, which would have effectively kept them out of the U.S. market, meaning the impact of the ban will be relatively small.

Real hit will be indirect

Even if the impact will be small by the numbers, Tu Nguyen, an economist at accounting firm RSM Canada, says the escalation is still very real in terms of the message it sends to business owners.

While the U.S. has historically increased the tariff percentages in order to turn up the heat on Canada, Nguyen says an all-out ban signals a departure from that strategy. She says the real hit from the escalating retaliation will be indirect — the tit for tat denting business confidence.

"A lot of these tariffs, they sound really big … but they don't hit the economy nearly as badly as one would think," Nguyen said.

“The bigger hit, I would say … comes from uncertainty.”

And unlike in the past, when the U.S. gave many weeks or months of lead time before tariffs went into effect, some of the newly announced measures will come into force as soon as next week. Nguyen says this gives businesses less time to prepare or pivot to new markets, and introduces another worry for business owners on both sides of the border.

World.title: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visits Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in Canada this week for his first visit to the country in nearly a year as his country copes with an onslaught of deadly airstrikes.

Zelenskyy will be in the country from Wednesday to Friday and attend events in Calgary, Toronto and North Bay alongside his wife, Olena Zelenska, says a statement from Prime Minister Mark Carney.

"The visit underscores Canada's continued leadership in supporting Ukraine and reflects our unwavering commitment to a just and lasting peace," Carney said in the statement.

The visit will focus on "shared priorities" between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defence, economic and energy co-operation, Carney's statement said.

"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries."

The statement doesn't say when or where Zelenskyy is expected to arrive in Canada, but the prime minister's itinerary says he is meeting with Zelenskyy in Calgary on Thursday morning. The two leaders will participate in a signing ceremony and hold a news conference afterwards.

The Ukrainian president announced that he was travelling to Canada in a social media post on Wednesday, but did not say what city he was flying into.

Zelenskyy's most recent visit to Canada was last December, where he met with Carney in Halifax before travelling to the U.S. for talks focused on ending the Russia-Ukraine war.

Carney visited Kyiv last August in his first official visit to the country, where he reiterated Canada's support for Ukraine and unveiled details of an additional $2 billion in military aid.

Flight delayed Tuesday due to drone activity

On Tuesday, a flight scheduled to carry Zelenskyy from Moldova to Norway was ​delayed when authorities closed Moldova's airspace because of a drone incursion, a government spokesperson said Wednesday.

Moldovan police said a Russian drone crashed on Tuesday in a sunflower field on the outskirts of a village in Riscani district, which caused four fires to break out but no injuries.

On Wednesday, government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici said Moldova had closed its airspace on Tuesday afternoon to protect aircraft flying over the country at the time, delaying three departures, including Zelenskyy's.

Zelenskyy's visit comes as Kyiv copes with devastating airstrikes and as his government pleads for more air defence support. European leaders argue Russia has been widening its war.

WATCH | Russia-Ukraine war escalation: Intelligence warns Putin is preparing escalation in Ukraine | Duration 2:07 As Western intelligence warns about a planned escalation in Ukraine, Russian airstrikes have killed at least 12 people in Kyiv over six days. Meanwhile, Germany formally accused Russia of sabotage on a Ukrainian plane at the Leipzig airport.

Before travelling to Canada, Zelenskky chided the international community for not taking a tougher stance against Russia over its escalating bombardment of civilian areas of Ukraine.

"Unfortunately, there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes, which are taking people's lives practically every day," he said on social media.

"But a response is needed — Moscow must not go into the winter believing that it can get away with missile and drone terror without consequences."

Last week, Carney told reporters his message to Vladimir Putin will be straight forward if the Russian president attends this year's G20 summit in Miami.

"The message will be simple: 'Get out of Ukraine, give back all of Ukraine to Ukraine, end this war which is killing more than 30,000 of your people every single month,' and I'd leave it at that to be honest."

World.title: Buffalo Bills to 'celebrate' O Canada at home opener amid more Trump threats during trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Amid a trade war that includes President Donald Trump's threats to Canadian sovereignty and his plan to ban imports of several Canadian products to the U.S., the NFL's Buffalo Bills have made an unexpected announcement.

On Wednesday, the team said on social media platform X that both O Canada and The Star-Spangled Banner will be performed before its Sept. 17 home opener against the Detroit Lions, the first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium.

The Bills announced that "for the first time in Highmark Stadium history, we will celebrate the American and Canadian anthems during pregame." Actress and singer Auliʻi Cravalho will perform the American anthem and Toronto band Barenaked Ladies will sing O Canada.

The Barenaked Ladies' Ed Robertson, Tyler Stewart and Jim Creeggan, left to right, are shown in Toronto on Sept. 9, 2023. The band will perform O Canada before the Buffalo Bills’ home opener against the Detroit Lions on Sept. 17. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

In Buffalo, the Canadian national anthem is rarely heard before NFL games, but it's commonly played before NHL games, even when the Sabres are up against American opponents. In April, fans at KeyBank Center in Buffalo sang O Canada after a microphone failed before the Sabres' playoff game against the Boston Bruins.

Buffalo is the only U.S.-based NHL team that plays both national anthems before home games against American and Canadian teams.

Tit-for-tat tariffs escalate trade war

On Tuesday, Trump signed five proclamations to ban Canadian imports including alcohol, motorcycles and various other products to the U.S. as of Sept. 29, and slap 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products starting next week.

Auliʻi Cravalho, shown arriving at the premiere of Moana on July 7 in Los Angeles, is set to sing The Star-Spangled Banner at the Bills' game. (Richard Shotwell/The Associated Press)

The latest move in an escalating trade war between Canada and the U.S. comes after Canadian retaliatory tariffs, promised after trade talks fell apart last month, came into force Tuesday.

In explaining why Canada chose not to sign a trade deal amid Trump's deep tariffs on billions in Canadian goods, Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries."

Bills owners Terry and Kim Pegula bought the team for $1.4 billion US from the estate of late Hall of Fame owner Ralph Wilson in 2014.

NBA Hall of Famers Vince Carter and Tracy McGrady, former Toronto Raptors stars, were among 10 limited partners who joined the Bills' ownership group in 2024. Jozy Altidore, a former U.S. National Team soccer player, MLS champion and Toronto FC star, was also among the new limited partners announced.

It marked the first time in franchise history that minority owners were added.

World.title: Apple's new iPhone Duo costs more in Canada, but not because of tariffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadians are used to seeing higher prices than what our neighbours in the U.S., but the price gap for the latest iPhone has caused some double takes.

The iPhone Duo, Apple's new foldable phone revealed Wednesday, is retailing for prices ranging from $2,999 to $4,799 in Canada, before tax.

In the U.S., prices start at $1,999 US, which works out as $2,760 — meaning Canadians will have to pay almost 10 per cent more for the cheapest version.

The sticker shock drew jeers and jokes on a Canadian Reddit forum, with one user saying anyone who spends that much on a phone should have to take a financial literacy class.

"You used to be able to buy a car for that amount," another wrote.

University of Toronto economics professor Joseph Steinberg says the price bump likely signals that Apple recognized the subset of the Canadian population that would buy a "super-premium product" like the Duo is "less price sensitive" relative to American consumers, "and therefore they can get away with jacking up the margin a little bit more."

He notes that it's not unusual for electronics and other products to be more expensive in Canada.

"This one just stands out because of how darn expensive this phone is, I think, more than anything," Steinberg said.

It's not tariffs: profs

Some have speculated that Canada's new retaliatory tariffs on U.S. products would raise iPhone prices, but experts told CBC News that is not a factor in this case.

While the list of U.S. products tariffed at 50 per cent includes smartphones, Steinberg says Canada does not actually import the devices from the U.S. in any meaningful quantity.

Additionally, Canada's tariffs do not apply to the iPhone Duo because the phones are built in China and are therefore treated as a product originating in China and not the U.S., he says.

WATCH | Some Canadians already feeling the pinch from tariffs: Canadian consumers already seeing trade war price hikes | Duration 2:04 Canadian consumers are already feeling price hits from Canada's counter-tariffs on U.S. goods, and more pain could be coming soon as U.S. President Donald Trump escalates the trade war even further against Canadian companies and products.

"What matters for whether a tariff is applied is where the project originates from, not where it last crossed the border into Canada from," he added.

Canada's counter-tariffs on U.S. products came into effect early Tuesday, prompting Washington to escalate the countries' trade dispute by banning certain goods imported from Canada and introducing more tariffs of its own later that day.

Microchip shortage raising prices

Werner Antweiler, chair in international trade policy at the University of British Columbia, says virtually all electronics Canadians buy come from Asia, and include components made around the world.

He says the reason smartphone prices are rising in general is because of the global microchip shortage caused by the AI boom and the rapid spread of data centres, creating a "crazy demand" that is driving up manufacturing prices.

Antweiler says he's surprised to see Apple specifically raise its prices more for Canadian consumers, though he notes it's not an uncommon practice for U.S. companies.

"Price discrimination is not unusual, and that can be in the magnitude of 10 to 15 per cent, because that is typically what the Canadian market will pay more," he said, adding that's largely because Canada is a smaller market than the U.S.

CBC News has contacted Apple for comment but has not heard back.

Apple CEO John Ternus led the unveiling of the iPhone Duo on Wednesday, which marked a major change to the company's flagship product in his first event since taking the leadership role.

Pre-orders for the Duo begin on Oct. 17 and the phone will be available Oct. 23.

World.title: Pilot of Amazon plane flagged excessive speed before deadly Miami crash, investigators say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of the pilots of the Amazon cargo plane that careened off a Miami runway and killed five people on Sunday repeatedly warned they were coming in too fast nearly two minutes ahead of time and at the last second urged them to abort the landing, according to cockpit recordings released by investigators Wednesday.

The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) released some details from the recording after investigators interviewed both pilots, but the full transcript won't be made public until later. The agency said the other pilot didn't consistently respond to the speed warnings.

The Amazon plane came in fast on Sunday afternoon and then barrelled roughly 400 metres past the end of the runway and smashed into a van carrying workers at a plane-cleaning company before hitting a compact SUV as it slid across a public road before catching fire.

All five people who died were in the van. Five others were hurt, including two who remained in critical condition on Tuesday. The two pilots survived.

At the point when the pilot first called out the plane was speeding, former FAA official Mike O'Donnell said the crew could have done a number of things to slow it down, including extending the spoilers, cutting the throttles and lowering the landing gear. Or the pilots could have aborted the landing at that point and circled to try again.

"You have plenty of time to slow down, plenty of time to say, let's just do a go-around at two minutes out," said O'Donnell, who used to oversee airport safety and crash investigations.

World.title: Barry Melrose, former NHL player-turned-coach and broadcaster, dead at 70
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Barry Melrose, a hockey player-turned-coach who led the Los Angeles Kings to the 1993 Stanley Cup final before going on to a long career in broadcasting the sport, has died. He was 70.

ESPN announced Melrose's death Wednesday after his wife informed the network.

"From the flowing locks of his distinctive mullet to the flared lapels of his trademark long suit coats, Barry Melrose cut an unmistakable figure whenever you were fortunate enough to run into him at a rink or catch him on your television screen," NHL commissioner Gary Bettman said. "You were even more fortunate if you engaged him in conversation or listened to his analysis because he never failed to boost your love of the game of hockey."

Melrose stepped away from his analyst role in 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. Wayne Gretzky at the time said Melrose was "bigger than any team."

Melrose had a relatable everyman broadcasting style, bringing a sense of humour to his insights, and was easily recognized by his goatee and slicked-backed hair.

"For decades, Barry Melrose was one of the most distinctive and trusted voices in hockey," ESPN said in a statement. "His knowledge of the game was deep, his candor was refreshing and his passion was unmistakable."

Barry Melrose returned behind an NHL bench as head coach for the first time in over 13 years on Sept. 20, 2008. (Jamie Sabau/Getty Images)

From rural Kelvington, Sask., Melrose broke into professional hockey with the Cincinnati Stingers of the now-defunct World Hockey Association in 1976. He played three seasons in Cincinnati, the last alongside a young Mark Messier, and after the WHA folded, made the transition to the NHL with Winnipeg in 1979.

Melrose went on to play for Toronto and Detroit, where he ended his career after the 1985-86 season.

He finished with 10 goals, 33 points and 728 penalty minutes in 300 career NHL regular-season games, and played seven more games in the playoffs. His WHA totals were five goals, 32 points and 343 penalty minutes in 178 games with Cincinnati.

Melrose turned to coaching and led the Adirondack Red Wings to the American Hockey League's Calder Cup championship in 1992.

The following year, Melrose was hired by the Kings, bringing colourful flare and immediate success to Los Angeles. In his rookie season, he coached a Kings team that featured Gretzky to make a memorable playoff run. They reached the Stanley Cup final before losing to Montreal in five games.

Melrose finished with a record of 79-101 and 29 ties over two-plus seasons in Los Angeles before being fired midway through the 1994-95 season.

WATCH | Barry Melrose talks about getting fired as head coach: Hockey Night in Canada podcast: Barry Melrose on getting fired | Duration 1:00 On this week's episode, we look at the process of how NHL coaches lose their jobs.

He was hired by ESPN in 1996 and later left broadcasting for what became a brief stint coaching the Tampa Bay Lightning in Steven Stamkos' rookie season in 2008-09. Melrose was fired 16 games into the season following a 5-7-4 start and returned to broadcasting.

Melrose was also known for his long-ball hitting prowess in fast-pitch softball, joining fellow Kelvington-area NHL players Wendel Clark, Joey Kocur, Kelly Chase and Kevin Kaminski, among others, during the off-season in Saskatchewan to form what some called the "the toughest team there ever was."

World.title: Release of detainee into Chinatown parking lot prompts anger, calls for reform in Edmonton
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Surveillance video showing a former detainee being released from a corrections transport van into the streets of Edmonton’s Chinatown has raised concerns over how Alberta offenders are released into the community.

The surveillance footage, recorded on Sept. 3 at 8:30 a.m., shows a white van with a Correctional Services logo pulling into a private parking lot on 105th Avenue between 97th and 98th streets, near the Pacific Mall in Chinatown.

The driver, a uniformed officer, steps out, opens the van’s secured rear doors. The person released from the van is then seen walking away, carrying a stack of documents in his hands.

Karl Miu, vice-chair of the Chinatown Business Association, says the surveillance footage is further evidence that the province’s correctional agencies have been releasing offenders into the central Edmonton neighbourhood without adequate support or supervision.

He has written to Mike Ellis, Alberta’s public safety minister, on behalf of the association, demanding that Alberta tighten its transition protocol for offenders by mandating formal discharge-and-reintegration plans.

WATCH | Correctional Services van releases man in inner city parking lot: Raw video shows provincial corrections van releasing person in parking lot in Edmonton's Chinatown | Duration 1:47 A surveillance video obtained by CBC News shows a former detainee being released from a van, marked as a provincial corrections transport vehicle, into a parking lot in Edmonton's Chinatown neighbourhood. CBC News has blurred the detainee's face because neither his identity nor the circumstances of his release have been verified.

Miu said he believes Chinatown has become an “unofficial discharge destination” for offenders, and is concerned that the practice undermines public safety in the area.

“The community is furious but also concerned,” Miu said in an interview with CBC News Wednesday. “Chinatown should not become the province's dumping ground.”

Miu said the concentration of social service agencies in Chinatown, including daytime and overnight shelters, has already created issues of security, poverty and social disorder in the neighbourhood. The video appears to show the officer pointing toward The Hope Mission, located a few blocks away, he said.

Miu is a consultant with the Yorkton Equity Group real estate asset management company, which owns the parking lot. He noted the corrections officer was on private property without permission while making the drop-off.

'Reinforcing expectations' over release policy

In a statement, officials with the Public Safety and Emergency Services ministry said the individual being released had been transported to an area of Edmonton where “various community supports” were located.

“While the intent was to connect the individual with available services, we acknowledge concerns about where the individual was released,” the statement reads. The ministry oversees Alberta Correctional Services.

“We are reinforcing expectations with staff that releases occur at appropriate public locations and not on private property.”

In the statement, officials said Alberta corrections staff work with incarcerated individuals to develop plans for their release, which includes consideration of transportation needs and available support.

“Both remanded and sentenced individuals are advised to arrange pickup from correctional centres with family, friends or another transportation provider,” the ministry stated.

“When pickup cannot be arranged, centre staff will facilitate transportation based on the individual’s home community, immediate needs and available supports.”

Alberta is responsible for operating correctional centres for both adults and youth who are serving sentences under two years, as well as designated remand centres for those awaiting trial or bail hearings.

Alberta ministry officials did not provide details about the person who was released, including the status of their release, age, or where and why they had been held in custody.

“Due to privacy considerations, we are unable to provide personal information about individuals in custody or under community supervision ... unless that information is already part of the public record or there is a specific legislative authority permitting its release,” officials said.

CBC News has blurred the detainee's identity in the video because the person's identification of and circumstances of his release are not confirmed.

Ellis, the public safety minister, declined an interview request Wednesday. The Alberta Union of Provincial Employees also declined to comment on member involvement in the drop-off.

In his letter to the province, Miu said the video demonstrates the urgent need for Alberta to reform how it releases offenders from its correctional facilities.

People being discharged from provincial custody need to be carefully managed, he said, with clear release conditions, confirmed housing placements, detailed mental health and addictions assessments and prolonged follow-up care by case managers.

“Why should Chinatown businesses, residents, workers and visitors experience the consequences of a failed transition plan that was supposed to be managed by the provincial correctional and social-service systems,” Miu wrote in his letter.

A failure in transition planning can have tragic consequences, Miu said.

He said the incident has parallels to the release of Justin Bone, who was taken to Edmonton by the Alberta RCMP in May 2022, in violation of his bail conditions that barred him from being unsupervised in the city.

Bone was arrested three days later, charged in the deaths of two Chinatown residents, Hung Trang and Ban Phuc Hoang. The high-profile homicides stoked safety fears in Chinatown and prompted concerns about the strength of Alberta’s enforcement systems for offenders on release conditions.

'Tossing people out'

David Shepherd, the NDP MLA for Edmonton-City Centre, said his heart dropped when he viewed the security footage.

He said such drop-offs undermine the ongoing efforts of Chinatown residents and business owners to revitalize the neighbourhood in the years since the tragic killings.

The video, he said, demonstrates that there are still concerning gaps in Alberta’s correctional system.

“We really need to see the UCP government step up and make sure that the services and supports are available and that we're working with the correctional system to ensure that we're not just sort of tossing people out."

Chris Hayes, executive director of the John Howard Society of Alberta, said incarcerated individuals face unique challenges after they have served their time.

He said discharging them without basic support and oversight — a systemic issue that is seen across Canada — often guarantees their failure to safely reintegrate.

“If we just punt someone out of a van into downtown Edmonton without supports, the research shows that the odds of their success are almost zero.”

In an interview Wednesday, Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said the footage reinforces an ongoing issue in the city that demands clear solutions from both the provincial and federal governments.

He said Edmonton is surrounded by a large number of correctional facilities and that concentration requires stronger policies to ensure that there is a plan in place for every person who is discharged from custody into the capital region.

“To see that clearly on video is a reminder that this is an issue that demands a clear set of solutions," Knack said. "Being dropped in a parking lot, even if there was a plan to go somewhere else, doesn't feel like a great solution.”

World.title: AI researchers 'earnestly believe' it could kill all humans within the next decade, Anthropic researcher says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There is a more than 10 per cent chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade, a researcher at Anthropic estimated in a post, hours after social media posts went viral from someone saying they had just quit Anthropic over concerns that AI companies are “gambling with our lives” in the AI development race.

The comments join a growing tide of warnings from industry experts that the pace of AI advancement is outstripping our ability to keep it in check, and that we aren’t prepared for the risks it could bring.

Jacob Coxon, who claimed he was a former researcher at Anthropic, said in a thread on X that he had resigned from the role out of fears that AI companies are barrelling forward toward self-improvement models without considering the risks, or being honest with the public about them.

"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," Coxon, who said he had previously worked at Anthropic and OpenAI within the past three years, wrote on Tuesday. “This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately.”

The posts had racked up more than 120 million views as of Wednesday evening. Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, replied to Coxon’s thread to share his agreement.

“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” he wrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”

CBC News has reached out to Coxon, but has not been able to independently verify his identity.

Other industry experts have since chimed in on social media to express that fears of the pace of AI development are common among many developers — sparking discussion among both observers skeptical of dire warnings focused on the future and those who have been tracking these risks.

People participate in a march to protest the opening of AI data centres in Vancouver on June 27. There is a growing wave of concerns being raised by industry experts that the pace of development is outstripping our controls. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Rogue AI raises alarm bells

The posts come only two weeks after more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft, signed an open letter warning that AI-enabled cyberattacks will become "far more widespread and sophisticated" as models continue to advance.

Hundreds of OpenAI agents went rogue in July and hacked into online platform Hugging Face before they were discovered. More than 1,300 employees of leading AI companies signed the letter urging the U.S. government to work with other nations to "deliberately pace" AI development.

Last week, UN human rights chief Volker Türk called "for an all-out effort to put cast iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI, before it is too late,” in front of the Human Rights Council in Geneva.

Dario Amodei, CEO & Co-Founder of Anthropic, speaks on a panel at the convening of the International Network of AI Safety Institutes at the Golden Gate Club at the Presidio in San Francisco, Nov. 20, 2024. (Jeff Chiu/The Associated Press)

CBC News has requested comment from Anthropic and OpenAI but did not receive a response. The Anthropic Institute, a research arm of the company, stated earlier this year that AI frontier development should be paused pending regulation, but that this is only possible if major AI labs all agreed.

In reply to Coxon's post, Samuel Marks, a scalable oversight lead at Anthropic speaking in a personal capacity, noted Wednesday that developers continue despite the risks, "due to a mixture of commercial incentives and a belief that they are in a race with other, less responsible AI developers that will abuse the technology or develop it less safely."

‘Severe’ risks

This conversation is "really what we need,” according to David Krueger, a core academic member of Mila, a Quebec research institute that studies AI deep learning.

“I think the risk is more severe than virtually anybody is saying publicly. And I think that’s been the case for a while now,” he told CBC News.

“We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”

The existential threat of AI comes in multiple forms, Krueger explained. One is human workers being displaced by AI models that learn faster and work cheaper. Another is that AI’s faster processing could unlock more powerful biological weapons or advancements in war.

Then there’s the spectre of powerful, rogue AI models that self-improve and could pursue their own objectives, misaligned with the goals of humans. In an essay in January, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote that Anthropic's Claude showed the ability to cheat and deceive in lab testing.

WATCH | An early report on the rogue AI hack: OpenAI models went rogue and launched cyber attack on start-up | Duration 0:56 OpenAI models went rogue during a security test, triggering a hack that compromised the infrastructure of the AI startup Hugging Face last week. AI's expanding capabilities fuel worries about security, as even top developers can be caught off-guard by flaws their models can exploit.

“There’s been a culture of downplaying, ignoring, and even in many cases, outright lying about these risks to the public,” said Krueger, who is also an assistant professor at the University of Montreal and founder of Evitable, a non-profit dedicated to stopping AI from replacing human workers.

Other experts are concerned that the dramatic warnings of Coxon’s post could actually distract from the present issues of AI.

WATCH | Exposing an AI misinformation hub: We exposed a secret AI slop empire operating from Vietnam | Duration 2:24 HTV Network controls hundreds of social media accounts and websites with fake news and clickbait — and ads that make it profitable. CBC's visual investigations unit teamed up with Radio-Canada's Decrypteurs to figure out who's behind it.

Luke Stark, an assistant professor at Western University who studies the history and ethics of computing, including AI systems, said that the 10 per cent figure strikes him as “science fiction,” noting that researchers associated with AI companies may use eye-grabbing warnings as “marketing” for the capability of their models.

He added that existing AI systems are "having big effects, many of them negative, on society right now, not in 10 years, not in five years."

Instead of worrying about AI going rogue and becoming the Terminator, Stark believes we should be focusing on the explosion of data centre construction — which is deeply unpopular in Canada — the environmental impacts, and the way AI technology is being pushed onto society, including the public sector and education, “without a lot of oversight.”

WATCH | AI Minister brushes off latest concerns, stresses safety: Existential warnings about AI 'are not new,' minister says | Duration 5:23 AI Minister Evan Solomon said 'there are real concerns' at the frontier of AI development, when asked about an Anthropic researcher who quit the firm, citing existential safety risks. 'Our No. 1 concern always is safety, full stop,' Solomon said.

“We need to be concerned about the amount of power the companies and the people behind the companies who are developing these tools are amassing, both in Canada and around the world," Stark said.

Canada lagging in legislation

When asked by CBC News about the apparent resignation of an AI researcher and the concerns raised in the process, AI Minister Evan Solomon appeared to brush off these latest warnings, saying, “These stories that come out … are not new.”

He acknowledged that “there are real concerns,” at the frontier of AI development, but stressed that he believes the Canadian government is taking the necessary steps to create legislation to “protect our kids, our privacy and our personal data.”

“Our No. 1 concern always is safety, full stop,” Solomon said.

“That’s why we’re establishing a new regulator that will have the power to hold these big companies to account on what they are doing, whether it’s on deepfakes on surveillance pricing, or on other matters.”

Experts have been calling for Canada to implement robust legislation surrounding AI for years.

WATCH | Carney announces 'AI for All' strategy: Carney's AI strategy big on jobs and training promises, light on details | Duration 1:57 Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled the government's long-delayed strategy on artificial intelligence, pledging 250,000 AI-related jobs and billions for training programs, but little in the way of privacy and safety details.

A previous attempt to regulate AI in Canada, the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA), introduced in 2022, died when Parliament was prorogued on Jan. 6, 2025. Canada’s new ‘AI for All’ strategy launched in June 2026 dashed expectations that the bill could be resurrected.

The new AI strategy, which puts billions toward nurturing AI development and increasing AI usage nationally, mentions the word “legislation” only once in the 50 page strategy outline. No clear timeline for this legislation has been announced, outside of a promise that it will come within the next five years.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Liberal Party joins Colombia’s far-right to form majority coalition
World.content:
The Liberal Party announced that it had joined the congressional coalition of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The party, which also supported De la Espriella’s presidential bid, said that it would join the coalition after “extensive deliberation and arduous debate among representatives, senators, and leadership” of Colombia’s oldest political party.

It is worth noting that the discussions between representatives and senators over the past several weeks have revealed disagreements among some members of our caucuses with the current administration, but they also acknowledge President Espriella’s ability to work toward stimulating economic growth, building a talent pool to provide real opportunities for Colombians, and restoring security and respect for institutions. Liberal Party

The liberals’ decision gives the government broad support in Congress and marginalizes the opposition led by the leftist Historic Pact Party.

In the senate, De la Espriella’s right-wing coalition can count on the support of 63 of 103 lawmakers. In the House of Representatives, the coalition consists of 123 of 183 lawmakers.

The Historic Pact, which won the elections and became the biggest party in Congress, was abandoned by the left-liberal Green Alliance party and can count of the support of 28 senators and 44 representatives.

The opposition party has been able to make temporary anti-government alliances with, for example, the far-right Democratic Center party of former President Alvaro Uribe.

World.title: Colombia’s president appoints controversial new spy chief
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella appointed retired army General Jorge Andres Zuluaga as director of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) despite pending criminal investigations.

Zuluaga, who spent 30 years with military intelligence, is best known for his participation in Operation Jaque, which liberated former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American military contractors and 11 soldiers.

Throughout his career, the 61-year-old former general was deputy commander of the now-defunct Charry Solano intelligence school, commander of the Regional Intelligence #5 and the director of the National Army’s Technical Intelligence Center (CITEC).

Zuluaga received training in the United States and was a diplomatic aide at the Organization of American States.

He was removed as CITEC director in 2014 after prosecution investigators found out that he received intelligence illegally obtained from “Andromeda,” a clandestine intelligence unit that operated from a Bogota internet café.

In October 2024, war crimes tribunal JEP ordered the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate Zuluaga for his alleged participation in the extermination of the leftist Patriotic Union party when he was the CITEC’s director between 2004 and 2005.

The prosecution has yet to decide whether or not to formally charge the retired general with the crimes he allegedly committed.

Zuluaga, who became a member of the far-right Democratic Center party after he was ejected from the army, has always sustained that he acted within the boundaries of the law.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with human rights office over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.
