World.title: Mobility: Europe must move from targets to the conditions for delivering them
World.content:
First example: heavy-duty vehicles. Seventy-eight percent of European land freight travels by road: almost everything on our shelves has traveled by truck. The technology needed to electrify these flows is available, as is the regulatory framework; the challenge is economic. Higher purchase prices, uncertain residual values, charging infrastructure that still needs to be deployed, slow electricity-grid connections and hesitation over a technology that is advancing rapidly: no single stakeholder can bear these risks alone.

The answer lies in distributing those risks more effectively, and even transforming risks for some into opportunities for others. Battery leasing, residual-value guarantees, shared charging infrastructure and securing volumes through contracts: the ecosystem already has some of the solutions it needs.

Public action becomes decisive where the market cannot act alone or cannot act quickly enough, particularly on electricity-grid connections and interoperability. It must also provide confidence in the direction of travel: not by imposing constraints across the board, but by making the trajectory credible, facilitating the initial stages of voluntary transformation and supporting those willing to take the first risks.

These are the actors who should be supported, before others are allowed to enter a market that has become clear and attractive. Europe must not reconsider its destination every time implementation becomes difficult, because nothing discourages investment more than regulatory instability. Instead, it must create the conditions needed to reach that destination.

Otherwise, uncertainty about scaling up the transition will fuel opposition to the direction itself. The choice is simple: distribute risk to create the market or remain trapped in diesel for too long.

Second example: the affordable small car. Europe has produced icons such as the 2CV, the Fiat 500 and the Beetle. Then our cars grew larger: some models now weigh twice as much as their predecessors with the same name, and their prices have followed the same upward trajectory.

World.title: Zelenskyy’s big bet: Ukraine can outlast Russia
World.content:
With that aim in mind, Ukraine mounted in August one of its heaviest waves of strikes on Russia since the war started more than four years ago.

The campaign expanded quickly to target not just conventional military facilities but also oil refineries, factories, and the vast warehouses of Russia’s online retail behemoths, Wildberries and Ozon. And ordinary Russians have expressed frustration at the domestic fuel shortages, the disruption of air travel and the upending of Russian e-commerce. Ukraine has scaled up domestic production of its attack drones as it tries to make the war unsustainable for Moscow.

But there is little evidence yet that the disruption poses any serious threat to Putin’s hold on power. Coups have been forecast before. European spymasters, Ukrainian officials and Russian exiles have issued numerous predictions that Putin’s days are numbered, that Russians will turn on him or he’ll be ousted in a Kremlin uprising by oligarchs and Russia’s elite.

Nonetheless, Putin has endured.

What Ukraine’s air campaign does appear to have done is make the war harder for ordinary Russians to ignore. That’s significant given how the Kremlin has succeeded largely in silencing public dissent and has Russian-based media on a tight leash.

“I don’t think the authorities’ approval rating can fail to decline when people go outside and see a huge column of smoke rising over the city, or when they arrive to a gas station and there’s no fuel, while on television they’re being told that Russia is a great oil power,” said Ian Matveev, a Russian political analyst and an associate of the late Russian dissident Alexei Navalny.

World.title: August declared the hottest month ever recorded
World.content:
Copernicus said the record temperatures were "due to global heating from burning fossil fuels," combined with rising sea surface temperatures in the Pacific linked to a strong El Niño climate pattern.

"Combined with record global sea surface temperatures and the warmest summer on record for western Europe, these observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which carried out the research for Copernicus.

The sweltering August capped a record-breaking European summer of heatwaves, wildfires and droughts, as planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions around the world continue to rise.

Global greenhouse gas emissions from human activities last year rose 0.7% to reach a record 54 billion tons of CO2 equivalent, the European Commission said Monday — an annual rate that would likely lock in 1.5 degrees of warming by the end of the decade.

The United States led the upward trend, increasing its climate pollution by 2.2% in 2025.

In China, the world's top climate polluter, emissions rose 0.1% in 2025, while in India they fell 0.2%. The EU's emissions also fell by 0.2% in 2025, the Commission said.

World.title: Green leader Zack Polanski aims to catapult himself into the Commons via Starmer’s old seat
World.content:
Holborn and St. Pancras has had a Labour MP since its creation in 1983. The Greens would need to overturn Starmer’s 11,572 vote majority.

For the two main parties in contention in the race to replace Starmer, there is a lot at stake.

What’s at stake for Labour?

This is Andy Burnham’s first test in a parliamentary by-election since becoming prime minister over the summer. For Labour, holding onto Holborn and St. Pancras would send a message that Labour’s image has been successfully divorced from Starmer’s unpopularity. It would also be an encouraging sign voters have accepted him as the new prime minister and are prepared to buy into his plan for government.

The selection on Wednesday night of Camden Council Leader Sagal Abdi-Wali as the Labour candidate — who came to the U.K. as a refugee from Somalia — could also help the party’s chances.

Reform UK spokesperson Zia Yusuf attacked Abdi-Wali’s background when she emerged as the frontrunner, and Labour will likely make the argument for progressive voters to back Abdi-Wali in a show of strength against Nigel Farage’s party.

However, losing a seat that has been deemed safe for so long would be damaging for both Burnham and the party, as it would suggest that the reputational damage Labour suffered under Starmer had stuck.

World.title: ‘Step backwards’: Union leader warns Burnham against political donations cap
World.content:
He wrote to ministers this week calling for a “comprehensive plan” to ensure workers have a say on AI practices at their own workplaces. He said: “I think at some stage it will require primary legislation.”

Nowak met Burnham face-to-face on Monday and said they discussed his promises to “reindustrialize” Britain and bring more public sector contracts in-house, as well as the TUC’s push for the government to deliver the Employment Rights Act — Labour’s flagship set of workplace reforms — “in full.”

Some unions will use next week’s Congress, where either Burnham or a senior Cabinet ally is expected to speak, to press the government for a second employment rights bill to go further than the first Act. This would prompt a backlash from many business groups, which argue the new law, passed last December, is already adding burdensome red tape.

Nowak suggested he would back a second bill as part of a future general election manifesto, given many policies from the first Act haven’t been implemented yet. “I think it’s entirely legitimate to say, at the next election, what is Labour’s manifesto going to say about employment rights?” he said. “The idea that the Employment Rights Act is the finished article in terms of U.K. employment law, that nothing else needs to change, I think clearly is not the case.”

Elsewhere, Nowak said the government “could listen more” to unions when drawing up trade deals, as they have “real concerns” about a recent pact with the Gulf Co-Operation Council and ongoing talks about upgrading the U.K.’s free trade agreement with Turkey. “I’ve got concerns about any trade deals that say nothing about labor standards, say nothing about respect for union rights, and say very little about environmental standards — and I’ve made this point directly to [the] government,” he said.

He also said that Burnham’s agenda to move power and resources out of Westminster is not a “panacea,” adding: “I think it’s part of the solution. It’s not the solution in and of itself. Simply devolving powers without devolving responsibilities and real resources I don’t think is going to benefit anybody.”

World.title: EU Commission scrambles to keep pace with Moldova's accession push
World.content:
The European Commission is redirecting internal resources to Moldova's enlargement process, after Chișinău's reform pace outstripped the department's capacity to keep up with it, EU officials told Euronews.

 

The Moldovan government has pushed through required reforms so quickly that the Commission is now playing catch-up, reallocating existing resources to keep tabs on progress.

"Moldova's impressive record of EU reforms is paying off. I had a good call with new Prime Minister Vasile Tofan during which we discussed the next steps on Moldova's EU accession path," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos wrote on X on Tuesday.

The Commission's enlargement department, already stretched thin by simultaneous progress across several candidate countries, has had to shift resources towards the best-performing ones.

Forging ahead

Chișinău has pushed hard on EU-required reforms since Maia Sandu became president in 2020, installing a pro-EU government with a comfortable parliamentary majority.

"The reforms that we are undertaking in the last five years are really unprecedented," Cristina Gherasimov, Moldova's Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration, told the press at the margins of a ministerial meeting on Friday.

"Our formula for these reforms to be successful is the political will and the determination of our people to work strongly in favour of the current window of opportunity that exists in the European Union," she said.

The Commission, in turn, must verify that candidates are getting the reforms right, meaning it has to match its expertise to the pace each country can realistically sustain.

Kyiv is also advancing its reform agenda, which gained fresh momentum when Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi took office in July. However, the country's war effort and budgetary strain continue to weigh on its accession bid.

On Tuesday, the IMF released a report analysing the potential economic benefits of EU membership for the Western Balkan countries and Moldova, excluding Ukraine because of its "much larger size and ongoing military conflict."

This rapid technical progress sits awkwardly against the political reality in the Council of the EU, where Ukraine and Moldova's accession tracks remain linked.

Political coupling

"Coupling" refers to the informal practice of linking two countries' accession processes.

Grouping countries is particularly useful during ratification, since it allows member states to ratify a single accession treaty — as was the case when Romania and Bulgaria joined the bloc in 2007.

Ukraine and Moldova began their accession tracks together in 2022, just days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In December 2023, EU leaders opened accession negotiations with both countries simultaneously.

Kyiv's process was then blocked for two years by a veto from Viktor Orbán's Hungary, rooted in bilateral disputes over the treatment of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine's eastern Transcarpathia region.

Momentum returned after Péter Magyar's Tisza party ousted Orbán from power in April, prompting Budapest and Kyiv to open negotiations to resolve the bilateral disputes. In June, Hungary lifted its veto on the first negotiation cluster.

The second of six clusters opened in July. Since then, however, Hungary has slowed the process again, as over a decade of anti-Ukraine rhetoric under Orbán makes rapid progress hard for many Hungarians to accept.

Although the friction is a purely bilateral matter between Ukraine and Hungary, the coupling means Moldova has been caught in the slipstream.

Expected departure

The coupling was driven by major geopolitical considerations. Moldova has long had a Russian military presence in Transnistria, meaning that when war broke out in 2022, the country found itself behind the front line, with Russian troops on its own territory.

The coupling matters deeply to Kyiv too, which sees the prospect of future EU membership as a lifeline anchoring the country outside Russia's sphere of influence.

Since Moldova joined the enlargement track alongside Ukraine, the argument goes that Chișinău forging ahead alone while Kyiv is bogged down in bilateral disputes would send the wrong political signal.

That is why Ukraine's main enlargement supporters, notably the Baltic states, have pushed to maintain the coupling throughout the cluster-opening phase.

But the technical side of accession, the reforms themselves, does not have to wait for the political track to catch up.

EU officials expect the coupling of the two eastern European countries to hold until all remaining clusters are opened. From that point, the situation is expected to shift quickly, provided Moldova keeps up its reform momentum.

"We have an ambitious target goal to be ready to close negotiations by early 2028," Gherasimov said.

World.title: Getting your mind ready for surgery is as important as physical preparation
World.content:
Failing to address patients’ mental health before serious surgery could hinder their recovery, particularly among older patients, according to a new study published on Wednesday in JAMA Network Open.

 

“The stress of surgery can worsen anxiety and depression symptoms and affect patients’ recovery and overall health,” the study’s first author Joanna Abraham said in a press release.

The authors argue that pre-surgical care should include not only physical preparation but also mental preparation from trained mental health professionals – something that current perioperative care usually misses.

“We recognize the importance of getting the body into shape before surgery, but preparing the mind and the brain is just as important,” said the study’s senior author Eric J. Lenze.

The way forward is to treat patients “holistically,” said Michael S. Avidan, uniting anesthesiology and psychiatry.

The power of a call

The study included 306 adults aged 60 and older who were scheduled for cardiac, oncologic or orthopaedic surgery. Patients were divided into two groups. One group got only self-help materials to read independently, while the other group talked with a trained mental health professional such as a social worker or mental health counsellor over eight to 12 phone sessions. The second group also received a personalised review by pharmacists and doctors to safely optimise doses of high-risk medications.

Three months after surgery, patients who received consultation from mental health professionals and medication reviews experienced a 2.2-to-2.5-point greater reduction in symptoms of depression and anxiety than those given educational materials alone, based on a 48-point scale.

Older adults undergoing cancer surgery experienced the strongest mental health improvements, scoring nearly five points lower than the control group.

Patients also reported positive experiences with the extra care, both from the wellness providers and the pharmacists who worked to eliminate unnecessary medications.

“What makes this care model so promising is that it’s practical to deliver,” said Abraham. “Patients and healthcare providers found the program manageable and easy to integrate into existing surgical workflows. Proactive mental health care doesn’t have to burden the hospital system.”

World.title: ‘Summer has shaken us’: Nepal’s flood disaster hits close to home in the shadow of melting Mont Blanc
World.content:
For centuries, French and Italian mountain communities have gazed upon the seemingly eternal glaciers and snow that gave Western Europe's highest peak its name: Mont Blanc, the white mountain.

 

But climate warming is dismantling the picture at alarming speed.

Europe's record heatwaves this summer savaged permafrost that for millennia has acted like glue on the Alpine landscape. Defrosting cliffs came apart, sending rock falls cascading from the heights. A famously dangerous gully that climbers have long braved on ascents to the summit, 4,805 metres up, became temporarily impassable.

“We weep for our mountain, the way it's changing. It hits us in the gut,” says Stéphane Bozon, a deputy mayor in Chamonix-Mont-Blanc, a French town at the foot of the giant that straddles France's border with Italy.

Tarpaulins cover the ice cave of the 'Mer de Glace' glacier to prevent it from melting, at the Montenvers station in Chamonix, France, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026. AP Photo/Laurent Cipriani

“From mid-July onward, we saw an increase in rock falls. We saw areas becoming difficult to access because of glacial retreat and snowmelt on the glaciers, with crevasses opening up and rock collapses making some areas difficult to reach or traverse,” he says.

Each degree of warming can have an outsized impact. On the Aiguille du Midi peak, which rises to an altitude of 3,842 metres in the Mont Blanc range, average temperatures for July have soared. From a chilly 1.6°C in 1994, the monthly average for this July was the warmest ever recorded, at 3.3°C, says Meteo France, the national weather service.

“The mountain really dried out, with temperatures unlike any I had ever experienced,” Bozon says.

The Himalayan flood disaster hits close to home in the Alps

In the wake of devastating floods in the Himalayas, news agency The Associated Press talked to researchers, climbers and residents coping with the risks and uncertainties of climate change on Mont Blanc.

The floods that swept through Nepal and China on 26 August were triggered after a collapse of bedrock and glacier ice sent debris and water surging through multiple Himalayan rivers. Initial assessments of many scientists are that climate change played a key role in creating conditions for the catastrophe.

As Earth’s global average temperature rises because of the burning of oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase.

In the Alps, glaciers once admired for their icy majesty are being eyed with trepidation as they shrink and lose stability.

People look at the 'Mer de Glace' glacier as tarpaulins cover the ice cave to prevent it from melting, at the Montenvers station in Chamonix, France, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026. AP Photo/Laurent Cipriani

Bozon, who is in charge of safety for Chamonix, says his town urgently needs to prepare for “serious scenarios” of chunks of glacier or mountain potentially falling onto inhabited areas.

“We have to move quite quickly because this summer has shaken us and year after year we’re being shaken by the glaciers’ retreat,” he says.

In Italy, researchers are also documenting dramatic damage wrought by heat on glaciers this year. In Lombardy, Alpine glaciers have lost more than 40% of their surface area since 1991, according to the region's glacier service.

“While it used to snow at high altitudes in the past, now it rains,” says Vanda Bonardo, head of the Italian branch of the International Commission for the Protection of the Alps, a nongovernmental organisation.

“So we’ve also seen the effects on the stability of the terrain,” she says.

Rock falls in the Mont Blanc area have surged

Permafrost that has held Alpine peaks in its icy grip for thousands of years acts as a cement, helping to hold their steep rock faces together. It took a beating from the succession of heatwaves.

“That doesn't mean that all the rock faces will collapse in the coming years or decades but quite a number of them are on the verge of becoming unstable and remain stable today only because of the presence of that ice,” says Ludovic Ravanel, a researcher at Savoie Mont Blanc University who specialises in climate change's impact on mountain snows, glaciers and frosts. "As the ice changes, we have seen a huge, huge number of rock falls and rock collapses this year."

A collapse is a major fall involving more than 100 cubic metres of rock – more than enough to fill a large shipping container. Ravanel expects this year's tally of collapses in the Mont Blanc massif “will probably reach around 400”. He says that is about 10 times more than two decades ago.

The last time things got close to this bad was the ’’catastrophic year″ of 2022, he says, with nearly 300 collapses.

“This has really been one of the defining features of the summer of 2026,” he says.

The Mont-Blanc massif mountains are seen from the Aiguille du Midi in Chamonix, France, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026. AP Photo/Laurent Cipriani

A Mont Blanc climbing guide juggles the risks

Chamonix-based mountain guide Stuart MacDonald says it shocks him to see how rapidly and extensively glaciers that hang from the flanks of the Mont Blanc massif are retreating.

When he guides people up the peaks, he points them to “where the glacier was last year and this is where it was 10 years ago. And that usually has quite an effect”.

Melting and the risk of rock falls made his job “pretty challenging” this summer and forced him to cancel plans to lead a group to Mont Blanc's summit last week.

“You hear it before you see it and then you’ll turn round and you’ll just see an enormous cascade of rocks coming down a slope and it can be quite terrifying,” MacDonald says.

“What’s most scary is that sometimes these rocks are falling on routes that we used to be climbing at this time of year,” he adds. “It can be depressing sometimes when you look at something that you maybe climbed in July or August in the past and you see that it’s absolutely impossible to do it now.”

World.title: The top 10 most walkable cities have been ranked – and seven are in Europe
World.content:
Many of us enjoy a city break, and the most seasoned travellers know that a successful trip is often down, in part, at least, to a destination being walkable.

 

Now Skyscanner has revealed the best up-and-coming cities for a break which aren’t the obvious choices – think Berlin or Dubrovnik.

Experts at the travel booking platform looked at flight data for destinations outside the United States which are walkable and easy to navigate.

A total of 14 factors for each city were evaluated, including the distances between the main attractions, the number of walking trails, average elevation, air quality and safety.

The result is a walkability index, which focuses on the walking distance between a place’s main attractions and the total steps and time taken to do it. The index also examines population density as well as the number of trails to explore in and around each city, and the amount of attractions in each place.

While Hiroshima and Nagasaki in Japan and Victoria in Canada were in the top 10, the rest of the spots were taken up by European cities.

The top 10 most walkable cities

How they ranked according to the Skyscanner data:

1. Córdoba, Spain

2. Nagasaki, Japan

3. Hiroshima, Japan

4. Reggio Calabria, Italy

5. Monte Carlo, Monaco

6. Tartu, Estonia

7. Bursa, Türkiye

8. Bolzano, Italy

9. Sarajevo, Bosnia & Herzegovina

10. Victoria, British Columbia, Canada

Europe’s most walkable cities

Córdoba, Spain

In the heart of Andalusia, Córdoba was once an important Roman city and, historically, a major Islamic centre.

Today, it’s arguably most famous for its striking mosque, La Mezquita, which can, of course, be seen on foot.

Be sure to check out the Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as well as the Palacio de Viana, La Judería, and the Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos.

According to Skyscanner, not only does it take just 26 minutes to walk around the main attractions, but there are also an impressive 29 walking trails to enjoy in and around the city.

Reggio Calabria, Italy

Reggio Calabria is often overlooked in favour of busier destinations in Italy, but this city in the south is ideal to explore on foot.

The coastal city, separated from Sicily via the Strait of Messina, offers stunning beaches as well as views across to Mount Etna.

As well as the impressive waterfront, visit the Rabarama statues along Via Marina and the Museo Nazionale Della Magna Grecia.

Best of all, all of the attractions can be seen on foot in just 25 minutes and 2,321 steps.

Millionaire’s playground Monte Carlo is surprisingly easy to explore on foot Braden Egli/Unsplash

Monte Carlo, Monaco

Although Monte Carlo goes hand-in-hand with fancy cars and super yachts, it’s actually a great place to explore on two feet.

Meander through the streets packed with designer shops – whether you’re strictly window shopping or otherwise – before taking in incredible views of the ocean from Rue des Remparts.

Head to the glamorous harbour as well as top attractions including the Oceanographic Museum of Monaco, Casino Square and the Private Cars Collection of HSH Prince of Monaco.

While Monte Carlo is certainly very walkable, as the city limits are less than one square kilometre, be warned that the hills here are pretty steep.

Tartu, Estonia

Despite being the second largest city in Estonia and a European Capital of Culture in 2024, Tartu is relatively unknown.

That’s despite a pretty old town, ruins and neighbourhoods made up of wooden houses.

The city, which is committed to sustainable practices and has the lowest air pollution of all destinations on the list, also boasts street art, plenty of parks and riverside walks.

Must-see attractions include the Estonian National Museum, the Town Hall Square and the Botanical Garden of the University of Tartu.

Bursa, Türkiye

This modern and industrial city in the northwest of Türkiye is home to the Royal Springs – renowned hot mineral waters, popular since Roman and Byzantine times.

Today, Bursa is a fusion of Ottoman heritage, as it was the first Ottoman capital. You’ll find buzzy bazaars and plenty of natural beauty, as well as the Tomb of Osman Gazi, Bursa Grand Mosque and Kozahan İpekçiler Bazaar.

Skyscanner data found that it will take a visitor about an hour to walk between the main attractions here.

Bolzano is known as the gateway to the Dolomites, but it’s worth exploring in its own right Fabrizio Coco/Unsplash

Bolzano, Italy

Known as the “gateway to the Dolomites”, Bolzano is often overlooked, with people simply passing through on their way to hike or ski.

The capital of the South Tyrol province, though, is well worth a visit if you’re a fan of city breaks.

Set in a valley surrounded by hilly vineyards, the city’s major attractions can be ticked off in about an hour on foot, and include Piazza Walther, Via dei Portici and the South Tyrol Archaeological Museum.

Bolzano also has a solid 505 walking trails in and around the city and is the safest city in the ranking.

Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina

The Bosnian capital isn’t only compact and walkable, but it also offers stunning scenery from its location on the Miljacka River and into the surrounding Dinaric Alps.

The city, filled with cobbled streets and eclectic architecture, is a great spot to learn about the country’s rich history on a walking tour. Follow that with a visit to the Museum of Crimes against Humanity and Genocide, and the War Childhood Museum.

Take the weight off in one of Sarajevo’s many cafes to try its famed coffee culture for yourself, before heading to the city hall, as well as the lively Baščaršija bazaar and the Latin Bridge.

World.title: New Apple CEO debuts latest iPhones and its first foldable Duo
World.content:
The company's new CEO, John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook on 1 September, introduced Apple's latest products at the company's Cupertino, California headquarters.

 

After cycling through other updates to the iPhone, the Apple Watch and AirPods, Ternus told the audience inside the Steve Jobs Theater that “actually there is one more thing," in a nod to the trademark phrase from Jobs that the company's legendary late founder himself borrowed from the 1970s detective show “Columbo.”

The foldable phone has the “largest display ever on an iPhone, yet fits into your pocket,” Ternus said.

The phone opens to a 7.6 inch display that is 80% larger than the newest iPhone 18 Pro. It will let people use an Apple Pencil on the phone, a capability previously reserved for iPad users. Duo, Ternus said, “will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone.”

The Duo lets users split the screen to use two different apps on the device, or two windows of the same website for things like comparison shopping. With a starting price of $1,999 (around €1,719), it is the most expensive iPhone yet.

The Duo “was always going to eclipse Apple’s other announcements at the event,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight. “The device adds a distinctive new design to the iPhone lineup and marks the company’s entry into the niche foldable smartphone category.”

Wood said that while there is certain to be demand for the Duo, which costs less than some analysts had anticipated, foldables still account for less than 5% of the overall smartphone market.

The iPhone Duo is displayed on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, on the Apple campus in Cupertino, Calif. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu) AP Photo

New iPhone 18 models

The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, Ternus said, bring improvements to the battery, camera, and performance. They will start at $1,199 and $1,299, respectively. Customers can preorder the phones starting on 12 September and they will be available on 18 September, although the Duo will be available on 23 October.

The new models feature a long battery life — 45 hours of video playback for the Pro Max — and faster charging. The camera offers what Apple called “cinematic effects” from regular video captured on the phone, as well as new options for manual controls and “smart focus tracking,” which lets users focus on a single moving subject, such as a kid during a soccer game.

Apple is also focusing on Siri's new AI capabilities with the new phones, emphasising privacy and security to stand apart from rivals who are further along in incorporating AI.

Many of Apple’s biggest rivals, such as Samsung, Motorola and Google, have already come out with foldable smartphones. But Apple is not one to rush on new technologies.

“The foldable launch is straight out of Apple’s playbook: Wait for the product to work out its kinks and for the market to offer glimpses of viability, then enter and shape the category,” said Forrester analyst Dipanjan Chatterjee. But, he added, the question will be whether it can expand demand for what's still a niche product category.

Compared with earlier generations, the iPhone 18 costs about $100 more (€86), due partly to a global memory chip shortage. The iPhone 17's price ranges from $799 (€687) to $1,999 (€1,719), depending on the model.

Earlier this year, Apple unveiled artificial intelligence advances, including upgrades to its Siri assistant, emphasizing a focus on privacy and day-to-day use as the company tries to catch up with rivals on AI.

Apple CEO John Ternus speaks during an announcement of new products on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, in Cupertino, Calif. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu) AP Photo

Ternus takes centre stage

The keynote address for Ternus was his opportunity to set the tone for his vision of Apple's future, Chatterjee said.

“John Ternus inherits perhaps the most successful consumer technology juggernaut in modern times. That is both a boon and a burden for him. Tim Cook’s perfected execution, scale, and monetization set a high bar, and Ternus must extend that run,” Chatterjee said. “But he must sustain that momentum while positioning Apple to disrupt itself in the near future, when the iPhone, or any smartphone for that matter, will cease to be the consumer’s primary conduit to the world.”

Wood noted that, with all the excitement around the Duo, the official arrival of Ternus as CEO “felt like less of a story” than he'd expected.

“This event marks a seamless transition from Tim Cook, and its timing to coincide with the iPhone Duo was undoubtedly planned,” Wood said. “However, despite the media frenzy about this new device, it is the broader strength of Apple’s hardware, software and services that will drive the company forward.”

World.title: Which European countries import the most crude oil?
World.content:
Brent crude topped $100 a barrel on Wednesday and held firm on Thursday morning after renewed attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz.

 

It has held above $70 since mid-February, almost seven months, and is up 65.7% since the end of 2025, when it closed the year at $60.85.

But this is no longer simply an energy market story.

More expensive crude raises the cost of diesel, petrol and jet fuel. Those increases then spread through transport networks, supply chains and eventually consumer prices.

For Europe, the timing could hardly be worse.

Eurozone inflation was already 3.3% in August, its highest since September 2023. Energy prices alone rose 14.3% over the year.

That is why the European Central Bank is expected to raise its deposit rate by a quarter of a point to 2.50% on Thursday. In the United States, futures put the odds of a Federal Reserve hike on 16 September at about 60%.

But which European countries are most exposed to the oil price shock?

Europe’s near-total dependence on foreign oil

Europe’s fundamental vulnerability to fossil fuels is easy to see.

The European Union imported 471.3 million tonnes of crude oil in 2024, while producing just 15.5 million tonnes domestically.

Its overall oil import dependency reached 96.6%, according to Eurostat.

In other words, almost every additional barrel consumed in the bloc must effectively come from abroad.

The United States, Kazakhstan and Norway were the three largest suppliers. Each accounted for between 12% and 15% of imports.

Libya followed at over 9%, Saudi Arabia at 6.8%, Nigeria and Iraq at 5.8% each.

Only around 7% of EU crude imports came from Gulf Cooperation Council countries in 2025, according to the Council of the European Union.

Europe is therefore less directly dependent on Gulf producers than many Asian economies. But oil trades in a global market.

A disruption in the Strait of Hormuz raises prices for US or Norwegian crude as well as Middle Eastern barrels.

Which European countries import the largest volumes?

By volume, the Netherlands imports more oil than any other European country by a wide margin.

Eurostat figures for 2024, the most recent full year available, show that it imported 138.3 million tonnes of oil and petroleum products.

Germany followed with 117.8 million tonnes, Spain with 85.8 million, France with 82.4 million, Italy with 73.3 million and Belgium with 56.7 million.

However, these figures require some context.

Rotterdam is one of the world’s largest energy hubs. Much of the crude entering Dutch ports is refined or transported onwards to other European countries.

The Netherlands exported 101.1 million tonnes of the 138.3 million it imported. Belgium also re-exported more than half of its imports.

Germany is the real major importer because of the size of its industrial economy, transport network and refining sector.

Spain, France and Italy also import substantial volumes to supply domestic consumption and large refineries.

Eurostat data show that Germany accounted for 20.1% of the EU’s final consumption of oil and petroleum products in 2024. France followed with 15.3%, while Italy and Spain each represented 11.1%.

Together, those four economies consumed almost 58% of the EU total.

Smaller economies may suffer the larger relative shock

Volumes tell you who buys most. They do not tell you which economies suffer the most.

A more useful measure of vulnerability compares net energy imports with the size and structure of the domestic economy.

Eurostat tracks the net trade balance in energy products as a share of GDP. Malta recorded the bloc’s largest deficit in 2025, equivalent to 5.4% of its economic output.

Bulgaria followed with a deficit of 3.5% of GDP, Croatia with 3.4%, Hungary with 2.9%, Belgium with 2.6%, Luxembourg with 2.5% and Cyprus with 2.4%.

The large economies were clustered closer to the middle. Italy’s energy trade deficit was equivalent to 1.9% of GDP, followed by Spain and Poland at 1.7%. Germany and France both recorded deficits of 1.5%.

The smallest deficits were recorded by Denmark at 0.1% of GDP, Sweden at 0.5% and the Netherlands at 0.6%.

Denmark benefits from domestic oil and gas production, while the Netherlands’ position reflects its role as a major refining and re-export hub.

Tourism-dependent countries are also heavily hit

Spain’s oil import dependency, which measures the share of consumption covered by net imports, reached 100.3% in 2024.

Portugal’s rate was 99.9%, while Ireland registered 101%.

All three economies rely on imported crude or refined products for almost their entire oil supply.

Malta imported 99.6% of its oil requirements in 2024. Cyprus imported 97.3%.

Their exposure is amplified by the importance of transport, aviation and tourism.

Almost two-thirds of the oil consumed in the EU goes towards transportation.

Road transport alone accounted for 47.7% of total consumption in 2024, according to the Council of the European Union.

Aviation represented another 9.2%, while maritime transport accounted for 8.4%.

That composition matters for southern Europe.

Rising jet-fuel prices increase costs for airlines serving Spain, Portugal, Greece, Cyprus and Malta.

Higher diesel prices affect hotels, restaurants and retailers through more expensive supply chains.

Tourism companies may initially absorb part of the increase. If oil remains above $100, however, higher costs are more likely to reach consumers through airfares and accommodation prices.

Denmark is the least dependent at 58.1%, followed by Romania at 77% and Hungary at 83.5%.

Italy sits at 89.8%, Germany at 96.9% and France at 99.8%.

World.title: Formula 1 sends Madrid holiday rents soaring: up to €20,000 near circuit
World.content:
Madrid is bracing for Formula 1's arrival in the city with a parallel contest to the sporting one: that of soaring accommodation prices. The Spanish Grand Prix, to be held from 11 to 13 September at the Madring circuit, has sent the cost of short-term rentals in areas close to the track, as well as in some of the most exclusive neighbourhoods in the city centre, soaring.

 

In recent weeks it was still possible to find homes to rent in Valdebebas, where the circuit is located, next to Ifema, for prices reaching as high as 20,000 euros for stays of barely a few days. In some cases, owners explicitly restricted availability to the period of the race.

"A 1-minute walk from the Madring circuit: experience the Formula 1 GP of Spain 2026 from the best-located luxury chalet in Madrid", read one of the listings that could still be found (source in Spanish) on the AirBNB platform last Tuesday, which was asking 11,400 euros for four days in "a house designed for VIP groups".

The increase is particularly striking when compared with usual prices in the area. Some of these properties are priced at several multiples of the cost of a standard monthly rent, which in this neighbourhood is usually around 2,500 euros a month, taking advantage of the intense demand concentrated into a single weekend.

Screenshot of one of the rental listings in the Valdebebas area published in recent days on the AirBNB platform. AirBNB

"There are homeowners, some of whom are even living in their properties, who are putting them up for rent", said Mario Serrano, founder and director of Inmobiliaria Valdebebas, in comments to 'Antena 3'. "Thanks to Formula 1, the spotlight has been put on the Valdebebas neighbourhood".

Up to 500 euros for a parking space

The pressure on accommodation is spilling over even into parking spaces. In Valdebebas, offers of up to 500 euros for a garage space for this coming weekend have been recorded.

The strong demand also reflects attendance forecasts. More than 120,000 tickets have already been sold and, according to organisers' estimates, more than 80,000 spectators will travel from outside the Madrid region, including some 45,000 from other countries.

The expected economic impact helps to explain the corporate interest the event has generated. A report by PwC, cited (source in Spanish) by the Grand Prix organisers themselves, puts the economic impact of the race on the region at 467 million euros and forecasts the creation of around 8,850 jobs.

Accommodation for teams, sponsors and VIP clients

Proximity to the circuit has become one of the clear selling points of the properties on offer. Many listings highlight the advantage of walking to the circuit, having views over the track or being able to avoid the expected transport problems that will arise during the Grand Prix.

According to estate agents consulted by local media, a large part of this demand comes from the teams and sponsors, as well as organisational staff and VIP clients, all of them profiles with far greater spending power than most of the spectators.

The phenomenon is not limited to private homes. Hotels have also raised their rates ahead of the arrival of the thousands of visitors expected to travel to Madrid for the race. An analysis by Simon-Kucher, cited by the 'Antena3' channel, puts the average price offered over the Grand Prix weekend at 1,071 euros per night, 147% more than the previous week.

The city centre, a meeting point for 'prime' visitors

Although the circuit is located around Ifema, that is, on the outskirts of the city centre, the luxury rental market is experiencing particularly strong pressure in the historic centre of the capital. Barnes, an estate agency specialising in high-end homes, estimates that 'prime' rentals have seen increases of up to 1,000% compared with a normal week, according to local media.

The districts of Salamanca, Chamberí, Chamartín and Los Jerónimos are among the areas where this effect is most evident. According to the agency, visitors with high spending power do not necessarily prioritise staying next to the circuit, but rather look for central locations and neighbourhoods regarded as upmarket.

Screenshot of one of the rental listings in the Chamartín district published in recent days on the AirBNB platform. AirBNB

"This unique place has its own style. Enjoy the Madrid Grand Prix from a privileged location and with maximum comfort", read an advert posted (source in Spanish) on AirBNB, offering an "entire accommodation" with five bedrooms, in the Chamartín district, for 17,100 euros, from Friday to Monday.

Slightly cheaper is the flat that, for those same dates, is being rented in the Salamanca district for 14,600 euros, which is advertised (source in Spanish) as "ideal for enjoying the Grand Prix with a high-level experience".

So the arrival of Formula 1 in Madrid has not only launched a new sporting competition in the Spanish capital, but also, at least for the coming days, has turned proximity to the circuit, the availability of a parking space or having large rooms in the historic centre into key elements in the other big race taking place in the city: that of those looking to squeeze the maximum return from their homes thanks to the Grand Prix.

World.title: Trump promises Americans $5,000 if Republicans win midterms
World.content:
The US president gave a wide-ranging speech at the Republican midterm convention. He defended the war in Iran, trade wars and tariffs, and the White House ballroom. He also called Democrats evil and immigrants animals.

US President Donald Trump made a pitch to voters on Wednesday: a $5,000 (€4,300) "dividend" for every American adult if the Republican Party keeps control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections.

"If the Republicans win ​the House of Representatives ​and ‌the United States Senate, both of them ... because of ‌our tremendous strength and success ‌economically, ​I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the ​United States of America for $5,000," Trump said at the ⁠Republican midterm ​convention on Wednesday.

"The only caveat we have is that the dividend must be spent in the United States of America," he added. "We don't want you going to Canada spending the money, we don't want you going to China or Germany."

The president did not say how he would finance the measure, nor how the government would track where citizens spend the funds. He had previously promised citizens $2,000 checks from tariff revenues that have so far not materialized.

What else did Trump talk about?

Trump made the announcement as the two-day event kicked off in Dallas, Texas.

In a wide-ranging speech, Trump talked up some of the biggest — and most divisive — aspects of his second term in office, including the crackdown on immigration, the war in Iran, tariffs and subsequent economic retaliation, the White House ballroom, and restrictions on transgender people.

The president told voters to "pretend” that he's on the ballot at the elections that will see new representatives and senators elected in November.

Trump joked about renaming a third body of water from the Strait of Hormuz to 'Trump Strait' Image: Jessica Koscielniak/REUTERS

His attempts to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario after America were met with rapturous applause. Later, he riffed on renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the "Trump Strait."

Who else was at the Republican convention?

Other speakers focused less on the Trump administration's track record and instead attacked Democrats as "evil," "communists" and "socialists."

Among those who spoke on Wednesday were Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a close Trump ally who is locked in a tough Senate race against rising Democratic challenger James Talarico, who represents a younger and more progressive wing of that party.

Another Republican senator, Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania, was introduced by his Democratic counterpart, John Fetterman, in an unusual move.

Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with Democratic Party positions in recent years, introduced the Republican as his "great friend" and pledged to work with Trump to protect the state's steel industry.

Senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, made the highly unusual move of giving a video message at the Republican convention Image: Kent Nishimura/AFP

Conservative activists were also in attendance.

The Associated Press spotted Stewart Rhodes, founder of the Oath Keepers extremist group. Rhodes had been sentenced to 18 years in prison for his role in the January 6, 2021, riot at the US Capitol, but later benefited from Trump's sweeping clemency after he returned to office.

Trump also praised Erika Kirk for being in attendance on the eve of the one-year anniversary of the killing of her husband, Charlie Kirk.

Vice President JD Vance received a brief shoutout near the end of the speech.

World.title: Philippines: Several killed, dozens missing after fire on ferry
World.content:
Footage released by the Coast Guard showed the vessel engulfed in flames as rescuers brought bodies ashore in body bags. The ship's manifest listed 134 passengers and crew.

At least five people were killed and 87 are missing after a ferry caught fire in the Philippine province of Palawan, the Coast Guard said on Thursday.

The incident aboard the MV June Aster occurred on Wednesday evening about 2.2 kilometers (1.3 miles) off the shore of the municipality of Coron, where it was headed after departing from Baseco ​in Manila.

Coast Guard officials said 42 people had been rescued, including 38 passengers and four crew members.

Footage released by the Coast Guard showed the vessel engulfed in flames, and bodies placed in body bags.

Volunteer fisherfolk assisting the survivors from the ferry that caught fire off Palawan Image: Philippine Coast Guard/AFP

The ship's manifest listed 134 people onboard, including 117 passengers and 17 crew members, according to the Philippine Coast Guard.

"Based on the data we have right now on rescued (42) and the casualties, we still have 87 people who are unaccounted for," Coast Guard Captain Noemi Cayabyab said on Thursday, adding that the figures could change as search and rescue operations continued.

World.title: Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
World.content:
Google has announced a plan to expand AI data centers and buy massive amounts of nuclear energy. Finland's security services have warned of there are risks, but the right-wing government says the deal will bring jobs.

US tech company Google on Wednesday announced that it would be investing €13 billion ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland as well as penning a massive deal to buy nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades.

This year, Google parent company Alphabet increased global investment to around $200 billion as it rushes to catch up in the AI race. Wednesday's announced deal is Google's biggest single investment in the EU to date.

Since repurposing a former paper mill in the coastal city of Hamina in 2009 and transforming it into a data center, Google has steadily increased its presence in the country.

The northern location offers two advantages, cold Arctic temperatures mean it needs less energy to cool energy hungry servers and the fact that Finland only has 6 million residents would seem to provide relief from the growing resistance that such projects are running up against in the US and elsewhere.

Google is not alone in looking to chilly Finland with its cheap nuclear, wind and hydroelectric energy supply to expand its business — Microsoft and TikTok parent ByteDance have also set up shop — with dozens of data centers being built in the country over the past few years.

Attracting data center investment has been a priority for Finland's right-wing Prime Minister Petteri Orpo as the nation confronts record unemployment and slow economic growth.

Why communities are fighting AI data centers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Google makes big claims about boosting Finnish GDP and creating jobs

In a statement, Google said the investment, scheduled to be doled out in 2027 and 2028, will include data centers, electrical grid improvement, and clean energy and battery projects for its chatbot, search and map services.

The company claims the investment will pump some €3.6 billion into Finland's GDP and create 37,000 jobs, with 7,000 being permanent and others coming during the construction phase.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo echoed Google's rosy outlook for his country's economy, emphasizing that it would spur further investment while downplaying fears that Google's project could drive up energy prices and gobble up resources."This investment is historical in Finland," said Orpo. "This makes us a front-runner in digitalization and AI."

Orpo said Google is, "committed to ensuring that electricity production in Finland ⁠remains sufficient and that prices remain under ​control."

The tax-avoiding US company said the deal was, "a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure."

"Now we are building more in Hamina, expanding that site on a remarkable level, and we are opening up data center operations in three new locations in the municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala," said Antti Jarvinen, the company's director of operations for Finland.

Resources under pressure To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Beyond skyrocketing energy consumption, Finland's data center boom presents a potential security risk

Wednesday's deal also includes a purchase agreement for 50% of energy output from one of Finland's two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years according to plant operator Fortum, which will team up with the tech giant to explore new nuclear and renewable projects in the country.

Fortum shares jumped 15.5% on news of the deal, pushing them to their highest level in over four years and making the company the biggest winner on European stock exchanges for the day.

"We call this BYOP — bring your own power," ‌said Google President and ​Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat, who noted, "This is Google's first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States."

Fortum said the deal would allow it to "continue operating the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant until the end of its operating licenses in 2050," adding that without it, the plant, which currently supplies about 10% of Finland's electricity, would not have been able to continue operations past 2030.

Overall, Finland's data center boom is expected to create a massive spike in energy consumption, with network operator Fingrid forecasting a 40% jump over the coming years.

Beyond the environmental and energy concerns raised by such deals, Finland's Security and Intelligence Service (SUPO) has also issued explicit warnings that foreign-owned data centers pose potential security risks for the Nordic nation.

SUPO is concerned that municipalities may be weighing the economic potential of data centers more heavily than the security risk associated with them, noting that despite data center investments being fundamentally good for Finland there may be concerns if their owners are linked to authoritarian countries like Russia or China.

SUPO says authoritarian states may, for instance, try to use Finland to circumvent restrictions and sanctions on technology exports. For example, for advanced chips currently banned from export to China.

World.title: Norway's PM: Zelenskyy's plane almost hit by drone
World.content:
A drone nearly struck a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo, according to Norway's prime minister. However, a Ukrainian source said the threat may have been overstated.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said on Wednesday that a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo for the funeral of Norway's recently deceased King Harald V was almost hit by a drone.

"His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in," Store told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK, adding that Zelenskyy had left Norway for Canada, where he would meet with leaders in Ottawa.

Store provided no further details about the incident, which reportedly happened on Tuesday, as Zelenskyy was en route from Moldova to Norway.

Moldova's government spokesperson said later on Wednesday that the flight was delayed when the country's airspace was closed over a drone alert. The spokesperson said in a statement that Zelenskyy's plane was able to depart after a Russian drone came down on Moldovan territory.

The Ukrainian president arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening. In the Norwegian capital, he held talks with Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide and Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg regarding military aid, including air-defense support, as well as civilian assistance.

On Wednesday, Zelenskyy then joined other foreign dignitaries at the funeral of King Harald.

At the funeral of the Norwegian King Harald V, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (center) was joined by other leaders Image: Dylan Martinez/REUTERS

Russian drone in Moldova

Meanwhile, neither Ukrainian authorities nor Zelenskyy himself have commented on the drone incident.

A claim that Zelenskyy was at risk was described as "exaggerated" by the source.

According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) — a US think tank — a Russian drone flew in Moldovan and Romanian airspace for about an hour on Tuesday.

The ISW said the defense ministries of Moldova and Romania both reported that a Shahed drone entered Moldovan airspace from Ukraine, flew over Romania, and then returned to Moldova, where it crashed.

However, it is unclear whether this was the same drone mentioned by Store and the Moldovan government spokesperson.

World.title: China: English to be removed as a graded core subject?
World.content:
A university professor is calling for English to no longer be taught as a graded core subject in Chinese schools. Opponents argue that, in a globalized world, knowing English is beneficial for the country and career.

From business and academia to social media and entertainment — English is considered the dominant global language. One in five people on Earth actively uses this lingua franca. In China, a mathematics professor specializing in vector algebra is now challenging this dominance in no uncertain terms. Tang Jiafeng believes that English should be abolished as a core subject in elementary schools, secondary schools and universities.

Tang is convinced that no other country in the world has placed as much importance on English as China has.

"Our children desperately begin learning English even before they have properly mastered their native language. Yet we are a civilization that dates back thousands of years. English is just a tool. It's enough to be able to use it. The tradition of revering and emulating Western cultures must come to an end," Tang says in social media.

China: Studying instead of Playing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

English as a required subject starting in third grade

English is considered difficult in China, since the Chinese language does not use an alphabetic script. It is a required subject starting in third grade. It is graded on par with Chinese and mathematics on the entrance exam for secondary schools, the central exam after 9th grade, and the high school graduation exam. A maximum of 150 points can be earned on the latter.

"How many resources and how much time do our children, parents and schools invest in a subject that is completely irrelevant to the majority of people in their future professional lives?" the mathematician asks, explaining his position.

He became well-known because many of his students achieved full scores on state math exams; in the class of 2011, six students from a single class did so.

Why English? 'AI translates'

Tang's opinion spread quickly online.

"Why cram for English when artificial intelligence can translate everything in seconds?" comments a user from Beijing.

Another suggestion from the southern province of Guangdong is to at least adjust the scoring — for example, to 120 points instead of 150 on the high school graduation exam.

Secondary schools in China end after 12th grade. These young people are headed to their final exam Image: HPIC/picture alliance

Many parents invest in private tutoring that focuses specifically on exam questions. In addition, all bachelor's students must pass the English exam before being admitted to master's programs. Tang suspects that this could cause many young talents in the natural sciences to fail, even though they have great potential to become top researchers.

No English proficiency, no competitiveness

There is no question that English is also important for STEM subjects. Research on future-oriented topics is typically published in English. There are fears circulating online that cutting back on English instruction could lead to a decline in China's competitiveness. A prominent advocate for English as a required subject is Hu Xijin, former editor-in-chief of the state-run "Global Times," who has previously drawn attention primarily for his nationalistic statements.

Hu emphasizes that foreign language skills are of great importance for every global citizen, "because we live primarily in the present," alluding to a debate over the ungraded history exam. "This present is shaped by globalization. China's opening up is not only state policy but also expands people's scope of action as well as the range of their diverse material and immaterial interests in life."

In Saudi Arabia, Mandarin is the second foreign language taught at schools ― after English Image: FAYEZ NURELDINE/AFP

Hu went on to say that connections to the outside world should not, therefore, be compared to intellectual ties to ancient history.

"Forcibly pitting them against each other — by asking whether foreign languages or traditional Chinese culture are more important — runs the risk of setting the wrong priorities and unnecessarily politicizing public discussions."

For him, an open engagement with the outside world is the top priority. English as a core subject also promotes equal opportunity, he noted, as it gives children in rural areas access to this important foreign language and thus to the world.

Why Mandarin Chinese courses are growing in African schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Little interest in language studies

Even Chinese universities specializing in foreign languages are feeling the pressure to adjust their educational goals and prepare incoming freshmen for future job markets. For example, fewer and fewer high school graduates are interested in German language studies, explains a university professor from Beijing who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity.

The new curriculum at Beijing Foreign Studies University has adopted a "foreign language plus major" model: English combined with law, information technology, or economics.

Similar cultural struggles already took place during the Self-Strengthening Movement in the late 19th century under the Qing Dynasty.

"Learn the superior skills from abroad so that you can later conquer the outside world," said Wei Yuan, a court scholar at the time.

Learning from abroad simply works better in the language used there. Even though it may be becoming apparent that, in some areas, other countries are more interested in learning from China— as is already the case today, for example in battery technology for the automotive industry, and humanoid robotics.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Ceuta: Documents show Spanish intelligence warned of crisis
World.content:
Spain declassified documents that showed warnings issued a day before more than 70,000 migrants rushed the Ceuta border fence. Meanwhile, the EU announced funds to strengthen the border and return migrants to Morocco.

Spain's national intelligence agency issued a warning about possible "mass entries" by migrants into Ceuta a day before more than 70,000 migrants stormed the border fences of the enclave in North Africa, according to documents declassified on Wednesday.

The Spanish government declassified a trove of more than 40 documents, including internal alerts, intelligence reports, charts and communications from multiple law enforcement and intelligence agencies.

One urgent memo sent by the National Intelligence Center to authorities in Ceuta on the day before the incident warned of "several calls to carry out entries into Ceuta."

"There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers," the declassified memo read, “just to give you an idea of its scale."

CENIF, a border division of the National Police, also published a warning about the social media groups a day before the incident.

"Internal communications have been detected in migrant groups in which they are trying to organize mass entries on the night of 29/07/2026," a document from CENIF read.

Sanchez downplays level of warning

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the documents prove his government had not been warned of the magnitude of the crisis that was about to unfold.

He said the National Intelligence Center only alerted authorities in Ceuta and not the military or Ministry of Defense.

"This is understandable because, with the information available at the time, no one could have foreseen the migration crisis that unfolded on the 30th and 31st," Sanchez said on social media. "No competent body did so. Neither in Spain nor in the EU."

Spain: Tensions in aftermath of Ceuta mass migrant crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU to fund Ceuta border enhancements

The European Union (EU) on Wednesday announced that it would grant Spain some €115 million ($130 million) in emergency financial aid to help bolster the bloc's external borders and return thousands of individuals who overwhelmed authorities in the country's North African exclave Ceuta in late July.

Spain initially requested the funding on August 24.

Brussels said the funds would help finance "measures to enhance border surveillance, border protection and security-related infrastructure" such as thermal cameras, floating buoy systems and underwater drones: "It will also serve to set up facilities for the screening of migrants, as well as to support returns of those who remain illegally in Ceuta."

"The situation in Ceuta has put pressure on our external borders," said European Commission Vice President Henna Virkkunen. "Our message remains clear: We are committed to combating illegal migration and ensuring the swift return of those who remain illegally in Ceuta."

What happened in Ceuta?

On July 30 and 31, images of migrants storming the borders of the exclave sent shockwaves across the EU and beyond as more than 72,000 individuals crossed into Spanish territory from Morocco.

Scores of migrants died in their attempt to reach EU territory, most by drowning.

Although most of those who breached Ceuta's borders have been returned, thousands remain, many of them unaccompanied minors living in dire conditions.

Unaccompanied minors at risk of sexual assault in Ceuta To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The incident caused a major rift among EU member states, most publicly between Spain's left-wing government and Italy's far-right leadership.

Although Sanchez has said that there is "no solid proof" that Morocco was to blame for the incident, Madrid's top criminal court on Monday opened an investigation into whether African authorities had facilitated the illegal rush.
