World.title: Almaty and Astana Maintain Economic Lead as Central Asia’s Cities Race to Catch Up
World.content:
ALMATY – Almaty and Astana are likely to retain their position as Central Asia’s leading economic centers, even as Tashkent and Bishkek record rapid growth and invest heavily in their future expansion. Kazakhstan’s two largest cities benefit from an economic scale, financial infrastructure and established business ecosystems that have been built up over decades, reported the Times of Central Asia.

Almaty has long combined Kazakhstan’s commercial and political functions and established itself as Central Asia’s leading business center. After Astana became the country’s capital, the two cities gradually developed more complementary roles. Almaty remained the region’s main business and financial hub, while Astana accumulated political, institutional and corporate weight.

Updated figures show Astana’s economy grew by about 10% in 2025, while Almaty recorded growth of about 5%. Together, the two cities generated nearly $107 billion in economic output last year.

Their position is supported by Kazakhstan’s broader economic weight. The country accounts for more than half of Central Asia’s GDP and nearly two-thirds of the region’s inward FDI stock, according to The Times of Central Asia’s Central Asia Balance Sheet. That larger economic base provides greater fiscal capacity for infrastructure and urban development, which in turn supports business activity.

Kazakhstan also has the region’s most developed capital markets. The Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE) in Almaty and the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) and Astana International Exchange (AIX) in Astana provide companies with access to equity and debt financing, institutional investors and financial infrastructure on a scale not currently available elsewhere in Central Asia.

Kazakhstan is also the only Central Asian country with an investment-grade sovereign rating. That status can reduce the country-risk premium and financing costs for companies and projects compared with lower-rated regional markets.

Tashkent and Bishkek are also growing rapidly

Tashkent is the most significant challenger to Kazakhstan’s two leading cities. Uzbekistan’s political and commercial capital had an economy of about $29 billion in 2025, nearly 40% the size of Almaty’s and about three-quarters that of Astana.

Its growth rate, however, has been considerably higher. Tashkent’s real GRP increased by 11.3% in 2025, according to preliminary national figures. Tashkent also benefits from Uzbekistan’s demographic scale. The country’s population is almost twice that of Kazakhstan, giving its capital access to a considerably larger domestic market and labor pool.

That advantage comes with its own demands. A larger and growing population requires continuous investment in employment, housing, transport and other infrastructure. If productivity and investment do not keep pace with demographic growth, population size can become a constraint rather than an economic advantage.

The difference in economic output per resident remains substantial. In 2025, GRP per capita stood at approximately $29,900 in Almaty and $23,700 in Astana, compared with about $9,300 in Tashkent. These figures measure economic output per resident rather than labor productivity, household income or living standards, but they nevertheless illustrate the difference in the economic scale of the cities.

Bishkek is growing from a considerably smaller base. Its economy was only about 30% the size of Tashkent’s in the reporting years used here, although the Kyrgyz capital recorded real GRP growth of 15.8% in 2024.

Its economic advantages are different from those of Tashkent. The Kyrgyz Republic’s 10% standard corporate profit-tax rate is below the standard rates in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The country’s predominantly hydropower-based electricity generation also provides a relatively low-carbon energy base, with further development potential.

At the same time, seasonal electricity shortages remain a constraint. Bishkek’s much smaller population and economy also mean a narrower domestic market and a smaller economic base from which to finance major infrastructure projects.

Can Tashkent catch up?

Tashkent’s ability to narrow the gap with Kazakhstan’s leading cities will depend on more than maintaining high growth rates. The city’s ambitious expansion will require enormous amounts of capital from public funds, domestic and foreign private investment and international borrowing.

Uzbekistan’s economy was about $147 billion in 2025, less than half the size of Kazakhstan’s $306 billion economy. Its sovereign credit remains below investment grade, while its capital markets are still less developed. Remittances also remained significant, accounting for 14.3% of GDP in 2025. Kazakhstan, by comparison, combines a larger economy with investment-grade sovereign credit and substantially greater financial and resource buffers.

These differences do not prevent Tashkent from growing rapidly. They do, however, mean that sustaining large-scale investment over several decades will require continued development of capital markets, labor-market reforms and stronger institutions capable of reducing investment risk and mobilizing capital. Tashkent is therefore narrowing the gap with Astana, but the current data do not indicate that it is on the verge of overtaking it.

The difference in recent growth rates is also smaller than it might initially appear. Tashkent recorded 11.3% real GRP growth in 2025, compared with 10.2% in Astana, giving it an advantage of only 1.1%.

Both cities are also expanding their physical and economic capacity. Construction of New Tashkent began in 2023. Its first phase is designed for 600,000 residents, while the eventual city is planned to accommodate up to 2 million people. By 2034, plans call for 200,000 apartments, together with business, education and transport infrastructure. Residential complexes, business facilities and university campuses are already under construction.

Astana is simultaneously adding substantial capacity of its own. Around 2.2 million square meters of housing were completed in January–July 2026, while new transport and utility infrastructure continues to be developed. The city’s master plan envisages a population of 2.275 million by 2035.

Almaty is a much higher hurdle

The challenge is substantially greater when Tashkent is compared with Almaty. Almaty’s economy is currently more than twice the size of Tashkent’s. Tashkent recorded 11.3% real GRP growth in 2025, compared with 4.9% in Almaty, giving Uzbekistan’s capital a considerably wider growth advantage over Almaty than over Astana. But again, the size of the existing gap matters.

Based on the 2025 economic sizes, Tashkent would need to maintain an average annual real-GRP growth advantage of about 1.75% over Almaty for 50 years simply to reach parity, assuming both economies continued to grow. There is little reason to assume that such a differential could be maintained indefinitely. Growth rates generally slow as economies become larger, while long-term OECD projections also point to slower growth in emerging markets as they converge toward higher-income economies.

Tashkent could therefore continue to grow faster than Almaty while still requiring several decades to close the existing gap.

Almaty, meanwhile, is not standing still. The city’s development programme and 2040 master plan envisage five key economic and urban centers intended to distribute business activity and development more broadly across the city. Revised proposals anticipate population growth to as much as 3.6 million by 2040, alongside additional housing and infrastructure.

Nearby Alatau City, although separately administered, is also being developed as part of the wider Almaty agglomeration. It could add employment, investment and economic activity to the metropolitan area, although its contribution is not included in the Almaty city GRP used in this comparison.

Can Bishkek overtake Tashkent?

Bishkek’s growth is impressive, but its much smaller economic base makes a near-term challenge to Tashkent unlikely. The Kyrgyz capital recorded real GRP growth of 15.8% in 2024. Yet its economy was only around 30% the size of Tashkent’s on the reporting years used here.

Even if Bishkek maintained relatively high growth for an extended period, it would need to sustain a significant advantage for many years before reaching a comparable economic scale. The city is nevertheless expanding. A 2024 administrative-territorial reform more than tripled Bishkek’s territory, from 12,900 to approximately 41,000 hectares, incorporating 24 surrounding settlements.

The city has since approved a development plan through 2030, with water networks and social infrastructure being developed in the newly incorporated areas. Its approved 2050 master plan prepares for a population approaching 2 million. Bishkek’s lower operating costs and hydropower base could help it attract investment in selected sectors. Its smaller domestic market and limited economic base, however, remain significant constraints on its ability to compete with the region’s larger centers.

Central Asia’s economic map is changing

The most likely outcome is not necessarily one city replacing another, but a more competitive and interconnected regional economy. Still, Almaty and Astana enter this competition with substantial accumulated advantages. Their combined economic output, financial infrastructure, corporate networks and access to Kazakhstan’s broader resource and investment base provide a strong foundation for continued regional leadership.

Tashkent can narrow the gap, particularly if it succeeds in sustaining productivity growth and mobilizing the capital required for its ambitious expansion. But current city-level data do not indicate that either Almaty or Astana is close to losing its position.

Central Asia’s economic geography is changing, but the region’s established leaders are expanding alongside the challengers. The competition is therefore less about one city simply overtaking another and more about whether the region’s major urban centers can convert growing economic scale into higher productivity, stronger connectivity and greater international competitiveness.

The article was originally published in the Times of Central Asia.

World.title: ‘Major cause for concern’: expert view on Armenian school students’ low level of knowledge
World.content:
Low knowledge levels among Armenian school students

School students in Armenia lag behind their peers in Georgia, Azerbaijan and Turkey in terms of their level of knowledge. The comparison focuses in particular on 15-year-old students.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) conducted its annual study as part of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). Experts assessed students’ knowledge of mathematics and science, as well as their ability to analyse what they read.

The study included 760,000 15-year-old students from 91 countries. The results showed that the overall state of education around the world leaves much to be desired. However, experts in Armenia are particularly concerned about the situation in their own country. The education problems have also alarmed people far beyond the field’s specialist community.

Economist Tigran Jrbashyan sees the study’s results as a major cause for concern.

“This is no longer a problem for the education ministry. It is a question of Armenia’s economic security and long-term competitiveness,” he stressed.

Jrbashyan published several posts on his Facebook page, calling on the government to take immediate action. He proposes introducing a special regime in the education sector over the coming years.

Подробнее о результатах исследования, а также комментарий экономиста Тиграна Джрбашяна.

Results for students in Armenia and leading countries

According to the study, some cities in China lead the rankings for educational achievement, followed by Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan. The UK and Estonia also rank among the top 10.

Armenia’s results lag behind those of every other country in the region. Armenian school students scored below the OECD average in all areas covered by the study.

The average share of Armenian school students reaching the benchmark was

28% in science (OECD average — 74%),

28% in mathematics (OECD average — 65%),

19% in reading and the ability to analyse written text (OECD average — 67%).

Less than 1% of Armenian students achieved the highest level in mathematics, while the figure was even lower in science.

“And virtually none of the students demonstrated reading skills that would indicate an ability to understand lengthy texts, work with abstract or contradictory concepts, and distinguish facts from opinions,” Radio Azatutyun reports.

Comment

According to Tigran Jrbashyan, an economist and head of Ameriabank’s management consulting service, the PISA study assesses not so much what 15-year-olds know as their ability to apply their knowledge in practice: understanding texts, analysing information and solving problems.

“Among our 15-year-olds, 28% reach at least the minimum, Level 2 proficiency in mathematics. The figure is also 28% in science. In reading, however, only 19% reach this level. In other words, four out of five of our 15-year-olds do not even reach the basic level of functional reading literacy,” he said.

Meanwhile, according to the PISA study, 39% of teenagers in Georgia reach the basic level of reading literacy, compared with 36% in Kazakhstan and 35% in Azerbaijan.

The economist argues that no matter how much Armenia talks about its achievements in artificial intelligence and high technology, all its planned initiatives will remain unrealised projects without human capital.

“If Armenia ranks third from the bottom in problem-solving skills among 15-year-olds, our ambitions in AI and high technology cannot be limited to investment, equipment and infrastructure alone,” he explained.

Jrbashyan notes that Armenia has built, renovated and modernised schools in recent years. He considers this an unquestionable investment in the quality of education. At the same time, he says the country needs to change how it assesses the effectiveness of education policy.

In particular, he proposes assessing

how students’ reading skills and their mathematical and scientific knowledge have changed as a result of these investments;

whether the share of students who fail to reach the basic level has decreased;

whether the share of high-performing students has increased.

The analyst insists that, given the current situation, the government needs to

take immediate action to determine at which stage of the education system, and for what reasons, students lose ground;

set measurable targets for 2028 and 2031 and consistently work towards achieving them.

“The cost of inaction in the context of PISA is not simply a low ranking. It means lost economic growth and the loss of Armenia’s competitiveness for decades to come,” he stressed.

The expert believes the PISA 2025 results show that the scale of Armenia’s education problem has outgrown the pace of the government’s response. As a result, reforms carried out at the usual pace are no longer enough:

“I would propose declaring education an emergency national priority and introducing a special management regime for three to five years.”

Jrbashyan stresses that an emergency regime should mean not only faster decision-making and more resources, but also much greater accountability for results.

Moreover, he sees a need for national mobilisation on the issue. He believes education policy should not measure its success only through the next PISA study:

“We need to create a national system of regular assessment that will allow us to see every year where we are making progress and where we are not, and adjust policy accordingly.”

Low knowledge levels among Armenian school students

World.title: Opposition says Georgian authorities are hiding demands from de facto South Ossetian authorities
World.content:
The opposition party Gakharia for Georgia claims that the de facto authorities of the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) are demanding the removal of a Georgian police checkpoint near the village of Chorchana and the handover of the territory to them. The Georgian authorities have not informed the public about the demands.

The party’s statement followed the latest meeting under the Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism (IPRM) in the village of Ergneti.

After the meeting, Yegor Kochiev, head of the delegation representing the de facto authorities in Tskhinvali, said no agreement had yet been reached with official Tbilisi over the Chorchana checkpoint. However, he said the issue had been discussed “very seriously”.

“The only acceptable option is to remove this checkpoint and subsequently withdraw it from the territory of South Ossetia,” Kochiev said.

What the Gakharia for Georgia party claims

“The Tskhinvali occupation regime has once again aggressively demanded the removal of the Georgian police checkpoint in the village of Chorchana and, accordingly, the transfer of these Georgian territories to the occupation forces,” representatives of the Gakharia for Georgia party said. The party was founded by Giorgi Gakharia, a former interior minister and former prime minister of Georgia.

According to the party, the Tskhinvali side is trying to portray the territory around Chorchana as its own land, while the ruling Georgian Dream party remains silent and has not told the public either about Tskhinvali’s demands or its own position.

Gakharia for Georgia also criticised the government over the ongoing criminal case against Giorgi Gakharia, which the party believes is directly linked to the establishment of the Georgian police checkpoint in Chorchana.

“Instead of defending the national interest, Georgian Dream is putting Georgia’s former interior minister on trial for setting up a Georgian police checkpoint in Chorchana and protecting Georgian land from creeping occupation,” the party said in a statement.

The party called on the authorities to immediately tell the public about their plans for Chorchana, saying that removing the checkpoint would amount to handing Georgian territory over to the occupation forces.

Background

The police checkpoint near the village of Chorchana was established in August 2019, when Giorgi Gakharia was Georgia’s interior minister. About five months earlier, a road had been built through the Chorchana forest leading to the future checkpoint.

Around the same time, the de facto authorities in the Tskhinvali region began placing borderisation markers in the area, including green banners and flags. In February 2019, the Tskhinvali side also began marking trees in the Chorchana forest.

Georgian Dream accuses Giorgi Gakharia of establishing the checkpoint without authorisation, which the government says led to an escalation of tensions in the area.

Gakharia told a parliamentary investigative commission that representatives of the occupation regime had been patrolling the Chorchana forest, detaining Georgian citizens and planning to expand the occupation line based on so-called 1992 maps. He said this posed a risk of losing around 1,800 hectares of the Chorchana forest.

After Georgian Dream declared the establishment of the Georgian police checkpoint near the village of Tsneli­si illegal, representatives of Tskhinvali and Russia called on Tbilisi to acknowledge the decision as a “mistake” and remove the checkpoint.

Checkpoint in Chorchana

World.title: Former Georgian prosecutor general says he served in Russia’s Arbat Battalion for nine months
World.content:
Former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze says that before forming his own unit to take part in the war against Ukraine, he served for nine months in Russia’s Arbat volunteer corps. Russia’s state-run TASS news agency reported his statement.

In Georgia, Otar Partskhaladze has been charged in absentia with organising a murder and placed on an international wanted list.

On 7 September, it became known, that former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who now lives in Russia and is known as Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze, would lead the international “St George” unit, formed to take part in the war against Ukraine.

Partskhaladze said that after Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine, he “could not stand aside” and decided to help Russian troops and civilians in Donbas and regions bordering Ukraine.

“After Supreme Commander-in-Chief Vladimir Putin invited me to the Victory Day parade on 9 May 2025, I made a firm decision and joined the Arbat volunteer corps, where I served for nine months. After completing my service with Arbat, my like-minded supporters and I decided to create the international volunteer ‘St George’ unit,” Partskhaladze said.

In an interview with TASS, Romanov-Partskhaladze also explained that the unit’s name refers to the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk, which he says played an important role in the history of the Georgian people. The treaty placed the eastern Georgian kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti under the protection of the Russian Empire.

According to him, the “St George” unit is recruiting volunteers who value the “shared history of Russia and Georgia” and their “centuries-old brotherhood”.

“Their main motivation is to defend the Christian faith, the traditional family, their culture and identity against the madness and pressure that the West is imposing today. For them, Russia is a bastion of normal, healthy human values, and they have made a firm decision to defend this bastion with weapons in their hands,” Romanov-Partskhaladze said.

Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze also told TASS that he was proud of the sanctions imposed on him by the United States, the European Union and the United Kingdom:

“I have always followed one main principle: justice, order and discipline. I faced unprecedented pressure because I stood up for the truth, took a firm patriotic position and refused to play by the West’s rules. The United States, the European Union and the United Kingdom have placed me on their sanctions lists twice. But I see these sanctions as a medal for standing up for the truth.”

What is known about Arbat

The Arbat volunteer corps was established in 2022 on the initiative of Armen Sargsyan, the head of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic’s boxing federation and a businessman linked to criminal circles. He is also known as “Gorlovsky”. Arbat initially fought as part of the well-known Abkhazian Pyatnashka brigade. In 2023, the unit came under Russia’s Defence Ministry.

Around 500 people serve in the battalion. Its ranks include assault troops, drone operators and electronic warfare specialists. The battalion’s representatives say former Wagner PMC mercenaries also serve in its ranks. According to Ukraine’s Security Service, the unit was largely recruited from prisoners in Russian jails.

Arbat has taken an active part in fighting in Donetsk region. In August 2024, after Ukrainian forces launched an offensive in Russia’s Kursk region, the battalion withdrew from the Ukrainian front and moved to the Kursk front.

In September 2024, Armenian authorities detained several people and said that Russia-backed members of Arbat had been planning an armed coup in Armenia.

On 3 February 2025, Arbat founder Armen Sargsyan was killed in an explosion near an upmarket residential complex in Moscow.

In February 2026, Arbat commander Hayk Gasparyan was killed in fighting. He had previously served a seven-year sentence in Russia for armed robbery and joined the battalion directly from prison.

Partskhaladze has so far published no photographs or video footage from the combat zone.

Who is Otar Partskhaladze?

Otar Partskhaladze became Georgia’s prosecutor general in November 2013, after the current ruling Georgian Dream party came to power. He held the position for just 47 days and resigned on 30 December.

His resignation followed opposition claims that Partskhaladze had been convicted in Germany in the early 2000s for stealing trainers.

After leaving the prosecutor general’s office, Partskhaladze went into business. He later obtained Russian citizenship and changed his surname to Partskhaladze-Romanov.

In September 2023, the United States imposed sanctions on Partskhaladze. According to the US State Department, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) worked with Partskhaladze to influence Georgian society and politics in favour of Russia. The State Department says Partskhaladze worked with FSB officer Alexander Onishchenko.

In October 2023, then-Georgian President Salome Zourabichvili stripped Partskhaladze of his Georgian citizenship.

In 2025, the United Kingdom also imposed sanctions on Partskhaladze for supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Partskhaladze is currently facing criminal charges in Georgia. In December 2025, the Georgian Interior Ministry named him as the organiser of the murder of businessman Levan Dzhangveladze. According to the ministry, Partskhaladze led an organised criminal group and ordered the murder of Dzhangveladze.

Partskhaladze has been charged in absentia and placed on an international wanted list.

Former Georgian prosecutor general on serving in Arbat

World.title: Georgian parliament speaker says Brussels policy towards country ‘at dead end’
World.content:
Georgian parliament speaker on EU policy

“Yesterday’s statement by the European Union’s spokesperson once again confirms that Brussels’ policy towards Georgia has reached a dead end,” Georgian parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili said on social media.

Papuashvili later also commented on the situation of prisoners of conscience, describing them as “prisoners of Brussels’ lack of conscience” and accusing Brussels of having encouraged them to take to the barricades.

On 8 September, addressing a session of the UN Human Rights Council, the EU’s deputy permanent representative to the UN, Michele Cervone d’Urso, said the EU was deeply concerned about the “politically motivated use” of the judiciary and the adoption of repressive measures against civil society organisations in Georgia. A report by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights says Georgia must protect fundamental freedoms and repeal or revise all laws that undermine human rights.

According to Papuashvili, the EU representative’s statement at the UN is concerning because it repeats what he described as “worn-out lies” about “arbitrary detentions” and “repression”.

“It is thought-provoking that statements by European Union officials once again completely contradict not only the facts, but also the values and principles recognised by the EU itself,” Papuashvili wrote.

He alleged that violent protests against the Georgian authorities had been partly funded by the European Union and that an attempt to overthrow the government had been made on 4 October 2025 after the EU gave it the “green light”.

“However, the Georgian people and the Georgian government properly defended the country, its freedom, sovereignty and interests. Today, it is clear to everyone that the foreign-funded revolutionary process of 2024 has failed,” the speaker wrote.

Papuashvili also said narratives about “election fraud” and the “crackdown on peaceful protests” had been “disproved by time and reality”.

“The violent crimes that were committed have been investigated, sentences have been handed down, everything has been documented and recorded and, moreover, acknowledged by the perpetrators themselves.

Once again, facts have prevailed over perceptions. A lie does not become the truth simply because Brussels persistently repeats it, nor does a criminal become a victim simply because some European Union official wants it that way.”

The speaker compared Brussels to “a soldier who does not know that the war is over and continues to plan military operations”.

Papuashvili said that if EU officials wanted to normalise relations with Georgia, they should end what he called their “aggressive rhetoric” towards the country, stop “providing information support for the failed revolutionary scenario” and show respect for Georgia’s sovereignty and the Georgian people’s “democratic choice“.

World.title: Sanctions against IDS Ukraine: Georgian stake could become ‘casualty’ of nationalisation of Ukrainian company
World.content:
Ukrainian authorities are seeking to take control of IDS Ukraine, one of the country’s largest mineral water producers. Russian businessmen under sanctions own almost half of the company, while 34.83% belongs to the family of the late Georgian businessman Badri Patarkatsishvili.

The process launched by Kyiv could also affect this stake, even though the Patarkatsishvili family is not under sanctions.

According to The Guardian, Ukraine’s Asset Recovery and Management Agency (ARMA) is seeking to transfer IDS Ukraine’s assets to an independent manager. At the same time, shareholders are challenging the partial or full nationalisation of the company in Ukraine’s High Anti-Corruption Court.

IDS Ukraine produces several well-known mineral water brands in Ukraine, including Morshynska, Myrhorodska and Alaska. The company estimates the value of its assets at around 8 billion hryvnias, equivalent to roughly $180 million.

Sanctioned Russian businessmen and Badri Patarkatsishvili

The direct owner of IDS Ukraine is Cyprus-registered International Distribution Systems Limited. The company is part of IDS Borjomi International, which also includes Borjomi producer IDS Borjomi.

The group’s ultimate ownership structure is as follows: 49.99% belongs to sanctioned Russian businessmen, 34.83% to the Patarkatsishvili family, 7.73% to the Georgian government, and the remaining 7.45% to other shareholders.

According to IDS Ukraine, Mikhail Fridman, co-owner of Alfa Group and one of Russia’s wealthiest businessmen, holds an indirect 18.23% stake in the company.

Fridman is under Western and Ukrainian sanctions. The grounds for the sanctions cite his ties to the Russian authorities and President Vladimir Putin.

IDS Ukraine says Fridman has had no influence over the company’s management or decision-making since the sanctions were imposed.

What ARMA is seeking

ARMA head Yaroslava Maksymenko says the agency has repeatedly had to overcome legal and bureaucratic obstacles in its efforts to transfer IDS Ukraine to an independent manager.

According to Ukrainian media reports, Ukrkapital, a company owned by Serhii Belashov, the owner of Ukrainian Capital Bank, won a three-stage auction to select the manager.

Maksymenko says the company’s current management creates a risk of money laundering and extracting value from its assets.

The Guardian stresses that there is no official finding that such a crime has taken place.

According to the ARMA head, the Patarkatsishvili family’s investment vehicle, New World Value Fund Limited, made unfounded allegations that agency employees had engaged in potentially illegal actions. Maksymenko described the claims as “disinformation”.

The Patarkatsishvili family, meanwhile, believes that seizing the property of shareholders who are not under sanctions is unacceptable.

A family representative said that if Ukraine fails to protect their property rights and the asset is nevertheless seized, they will take the case to international courts.

The family also stresses that it has supported Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion and considers the approach taken against it unfair.

The company denies the allegations

IDS Ukraine rejects the concerns raised by ARMA.

A company representative said IDS Ukraine operates in strict compliance with Ukrainian law, including tax and financial regulations.

IDS Ukraine says no Ukrainian state agency, including the tax authorities, has found evidence of money laundering, illegal transfers of funds or other similar financial violations at the company.

The company also says it is unaware of any investigation based on such allegations.

According to IDS Ukraine, it has not stopped operating for a single day since the war began. It has continued supplying water to people across Ukraine despite missile and drone attacks.

The cyberattack question

Amid the dispute, ARMA made another allegation. The agency said its systems came under a cyberattack during one of its attempts to find an independent manager for IDS Ukraine.

However, it is not known who was behind the attack. According to The Guardian, the Patarkatsishvili family has not faced any suspicion related to the cyberattack.

IDS Ukraine believes ARMA’s statements could create the impression that the attack was linked to the company itself.

“This information is simply false and, in fact, completely irrelevant,” a company representative told The Guardian.

The Patarkatsishvili family’s assets

Badri Patarkatsishvili, who died in London in 2008 at the age of 52, made his fortune in Russia. He later acquired a number of major assets in Georgia, including the Imedi television company.

In 2002, he acquired Borjomi, after which the business expanded into the Ukrainian market.

In 2007, Patarkatsishvili became one of the most prominent opponents of former Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili and took part in an early presidential election. According to the Central Election Commission, he won 7.1% of the vote and came third.

After Patarkatsishvili’s death, his fortune, estimated at around £6 billion (about $8.13 billion), passed to his wife Inna Gudavadze and daughters Liana and Iya Patarkatsishvili, according to The Guardian.

The Patarkatsishvili family later sold some of its Georgian assets, including Imedi.

In 2013, the family sold its controlling stake in IDS Borjomi, including IDS Ukraine, to Alfa Group.

Liana Patarkatsishvili now works in the British theatre industry and heads the production company Sage & Jester. According to The Guardian, her company produced the immersive play Storehouse in 2025, which explored the theme of disinformation.

Badri Patarkatsishvili, 2005. Photo: STR New/Reuters

How did the Georgian government become an IDS shareholder?

The Georgian government became part of IDS’s ownership structure in 2022.

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Western sanctions against Russian businessmen linked to Alfa Group created problems for IDS Borjomi. The company suspended operations at both of its Borjomi mineral water bottling plants on 29 April 2022.

In June that year, the Georgian government received a 7.73% stake in IDS Borjomi International free of charge.

As a result of the deal, the controlling shareholder lost control of the company. Its representation on the board of directors fell from eight members to two, while a government representative became board chairman.

The Borjomi plants resumed operations after the deal.

Representatives of the Georgian government and the Ministry of Economy have not commented on the dispute surrounding IDS Ukraine.

Sanctions against IDS Ukraine

World.title: Conflict analyst’s view on clash between Georgia’s former and current prime ministers
World.content:
According to conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili, members of Georgia’s ruling team have more sympathy for former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili than for the current prime minister, Irakli Kobakhidze. Zakareishvili links the activity of the jailed Garibashvili and his recent letters to this sense of his own political strength.

Zakareishvili believes Garibashvili may have come to believe that Kobakhidze could lose the next election. Kobakhidze, meanwhile, may have realised that even a former prime minister in prison has more political influence than he does.

However, the conflict analyst believes Garibashvili should set out his position more clearly in his letters.

Former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili was sentenced to five years in prison in January 2026 after being convicted of laundering a particularly large amount of illicit income. He pleaded guilty and reached a plea agreement with the prosecution. On August 24, he was charged with a second offence — accepting a particularly large bribe. Gharibashvili has pleaded not guilty to the new charges. On September 1, Irakli Gharibashvili issued another letter from prison, calling on government officials to answer questions about what he described as suspicious circumstances surrounding the death of former human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze. A day later, Gharibashvili was questioned in prison in connection with the statement. According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the former prime minister was unable to provide investigators with any new substantive information.

Paata Zakareishvili: “Irakli Garibashvili’s letters should contain more facts, and everything should be made more specific, with names given.

When he spoke about Lazare Jorbenadze, he clearly said that Jorbenadze had been murdered, not that he had taken his own life.

This means Garibashvili knows something and wants to see the case through. But if he cannot prove it, this issue will be discredited.

However, his latest letters increasingly resemble toasts. It seems he has enjoyed the impact his letters have had. For example, Mamuka Mdinaradze left politics, the minister of regional development. It did not happen because of the letters, though. Mdinaradze simply failed to silence Garibashvili or rein him in.

I am deeply convinced that Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze decided to destroy the Garibashvili ‘clan’ before the 2028 parliamentary elections. Then it suddenly became clear that Garibashvili was not alone and that politically killing him would not be so easy.

Garibashvili received a signal that he was more popular within the ruling Georgian Dream party than Kobakhidze. He sensed his strength and now wants to harness it. He realised that Kobakhidze could lose the upcoming election.

Garibashvili followed the decision of ruling party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili and went to prison. Yet it suddenly turned out that this was not enough for Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Garibashvili feels that Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze are afraid of him.

We should also remember that Georgian Dream Secretary General Kakha Kaladze has remained in the shadows, watching everything, including developments in Ukraine. He is watching and sees that Irakli Kobakhidze is very weak, and that Garibashvili could take the entire team with him before the election.

Kobakhidze has discovered that even Garibashvili, sitting in prison, is stronger than him. Garibashvili has a great many supporters in the regions. As a political figure, he is weak, but he has built a very strong, old-school system of corruption based on the principle: ‘I eat, and I let you eat too.’

Irakli Kobakhidze has been ‘sidelined’ and has no allies. So what could happen today — his resignation — will happen later, probably by 2028. Unless Bidzina Ivanishvili calls an early election.”

Garibashvili and Kobakhidze

World.title: Progress or decline: what study found about the quality of school education in Georgia
World.content:
In 2025, Georgian 15-year-old school students performed better in mathematics, reading and science than they did in 2022. However, there has been no broad or sustained progress over the past decade. In fact, Georgian school students now struggle more with reading comprehension than they did in 2015.

These are the findings of PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment), the largest international study of the quality of school education, conducted by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

OECD (English: OECD) is an international economic organisation that brings together developed countries with high-income economies and established democracies. The organisation is often referred to as a “club of rich or developed countries”.

Despite the positive trend, Georgia remains significantly below the OECD average in all three core areas. Reading is particularly concerning, with 61% of students failing to reach even the basic level.

Georgia’s results

According to the 2025 PISA study, Georgia’s average scores were:

Science — 422 points;

Mathematics — 416 points;

Reading — 384 points;

Problem-solving using computational methods — 413 points.

In 2022, Georgia scored 384 points in science, 374 in reading and 390 in mathematics. The country therefore improved in all three areas in 2025.

The biggest change came in science, with an increase of 38 points. Reading rose by 10 points, while mathematics increased by 26 points.

However, 2022 was a low point for comparison. It was the first study conducted after the pandemic, when education systems were still dealing with its consequences.

The report’s authors also link the decline between 2018 and 2022 to a change in the testing format, alongside the pandemic. Georgia moved from paper-based tests to an electronic format.

Comparing the results with 2022 therefore mainly shows a partial recovery from the losses caused by the pandemic. It cannot, however, serve as a sufficient measure of the education system’s long-term success.

he 10-year results are less impressive

Compared with 2015, Georgia improved its science score by 10 points. Its mathematics score rose by 8 points. In both areas, the country achieved its best result of the past decade.

However, its reading score fell by 17 points. Georgia’s average score stood at 401 points in 2015, but fell to 384 points in 2025.

This means that Georgia’s result in one of the three core areas is worse than it was ten years ago. This is particularly significant because reading skills provide the foundation for learning other subjects.

The short-term improvement therefore does not amount to a systemic breakthrough. Georgia has recovered some of the ground it lost after the pandemic. But it has failed to achieve consistent progress across all three areas over the past decade.

The gap between Georgia and the OECD remains wide

In PISA 2025, the OECD average was 482 points in science. The average mathematics score was 463 points, while reading stood at 461 points.

Georgia trails the OECD average by:

60 points in science;

47 points in mathematics;

77 points in reading.

Georgia comes closest to the OECD average in mathematics. Even there, however, the gap remains significant.

With 422 points in science, Georgia ranks at the same level as Serbia, Romania and Mongolia. The same group also includes Costa Rica, Moldova, Bulgaria, Kazakhstan and Malaysia.

Georgia scored 384 points in reading. Thailand, Vietnam, Peru, Argentina and Kazakhstan recorded statistically similar results.

In mathematics, Georgia trails neighbouring Azerbaijan, which scored 422 points..

What the basic level means

A country’s average score tells only part of the story. A more important question is how many students have the minimum skills they need for everyday life.

In PISA, Level 2 is considered the basic level. At this level, students should be able to apply their knowledge in simple, practical situations.

In Georgia, 55% of students reach the basic level in science. The OECD average is 74%.

In mathematics, 47% of Georgian school students reach the basic level. The average across OECD countries is 65%.

Reading is the most problematic area. Only 39% of Georgian students can identify the main idea and find information in a moderately long text. The OECD average is 69%.

This means that 61% of Georgia’s 15-year-old students do not reach even the basic level in reading.

A shortage of high-performing students

Georgia’s rise in the average score was mainly driven by a decline in the share of low-performing students. The share of high-performing students, however, has not increased significantly.

In science, only 1% of Georgian school students reach the highest performance levels. The OECD average is 7%.

In mathematics, around 2% of students reach the highest levels. The average across OECD countries is 8%.

In reading, virtually no Georgian students reach the highest performance levels. The OECD average is 6%.

The system has therefore managed to help some of its weakest students catch up. However, it still does not create an environment where high-performing students can fully develop their potential.

First place in just one indicator

After the study was published, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said that the country had ranked first among 91 countries.

“In terms of improving performance in science, Georgia ranked first among the 91 countries around the world that took part in the study,” the prime minister said at a government meeting.

The statement refers not to Georgian school students’ overall level of knowledge, but to the change in their science score between 2022 and 2025. Georgia’s score rose by 38 points during this period, the largest increase among all participating countries.

But Georgia does not rank first in the overall results. Its average science score is 422, compared with the OECD average of 482.

The study also stresses that it is impossible to determine countries’ exact rankings. PISA relies on a sample of students, so average scores have a margin of statistical error.

The second achievement highlighted by the Georgian authorities concerns the decline in the number of low-performing students. Georgia did indeed rank among the top three countries on this indicator. Between 2022 and 2025, the share of such students fell by 19.6 percentage points. That is significant progress. However, the share of high-performing students increased by just 0.6 percentage points over the same period.

How the authorities interpret the study’s results

Representatives of the ruling Georgian Dream party and pro-government media have focused mainly on three indicators: the rise in scores compared with 2022, first place for the rate of improvement in science, and the decline in the share of low-performing students.

These figures do appear in the report. The problem lies in presenting them without context.

The authorities’ version barely mentions that Georgia started this improvement from a very low baseline. The large gap with the OECD averages and the decade-long decline in reading also receive little attention.

Kobakhidze noted that “the best results in mathematics and science have been achieved over the past decade”. He also said that “despite the global decline in performance, Georgia continues to show a steady trend of improvement”.

The first statement is correct, although incomplete. Georgia’s best results in science and mathematics remain significantly below the international average.

The second statement raises questions. Georgia’s results did not improve steadily from one PISA cycle to the next. Scores fell in all three areas between 2018 and 2022, while the 2025 reading score remains below the 2015 level.

The authorities presented the public with the most favourable part of the study. However, the full picture shows both some achievements and long-term problems within the education system.

The urban-rural gap has narrowed, but not disappeared

The prime minister also highlighted the narrowing gap between urban and rural schools.

The report confirms this trend. The narrower gap in science and mathematics resulted from improved performance among students in rural areas and settlements.

In reading, however, the gap narrowed for another reason as well: students in the capital performed worse.

This is an important distinction. A reduction in inequality does not always mean that performance has improved across all groups. Sometimes the gap narrows because the stronger group becomes weaker.

In 2025, students in Tbilisi scored an average of 441 points in science. Students in other cities scored 417, while those in villages and settlements scored 405.

In reading, Tbilisi’s score was 401 points. Other cities scored 384, while villages and settlements scored 363.

In mathematics, Tbilisi scored 434 points. The score for other cities was 410, while schools in villages and settlements scored 403.

Private, state and Azerbaijani-language schools

The report shows inequality between private and state schools just as clearly as the gap between urban and rural schools.

Private-school students scored 465 points in science, compared with 418 points for students in state schools. In reading, the corresponding scores were 419 and 381, while in mathematics they were 464 and 412.

The mathematics score for private schools is almost equal to the OECD average. State schools, however, remain significantly below it.

Azerbaijani-language schools perform particularly poorly:

Science — 338 points;

Reading — 307 points;

Mathematics — 341 points.

The corresponding scores for Georgian-language schools are 426, 387 and 420 points.

This gap points to deep inequality within the education system. However, the difference between the languages of instruction did not feature at all in the prime minister’s statement.

Girls outperform boys in reading and science

In Georgia, girls outperform boys in reading and science. The gap is particularly wide in reading.

In science, girls scored an average of 430 points, compared with 415 for boys. In reading, girls scored 399 points, while boys scored 364.

In mathematics, girls scored 417 points, compared with 416 for boys. This difference is not statistically significant.

According to the report, the gender gap in reading narrowed after 2015, but widened again in the latest cycle.

A new challenge in the digital world

PISA 2025 introduced a new area of assessment: “Learning in the Digital World”. One of its components was problem-solving using computational methods.

This component assesses computer modelling and programming skills. The assessment also covers conducting experiments and creating digital products.

Georgia scored 413 points in this area, compared with an OECD average of 500.

This is Georgia’s largest gap among the four areas assessed in the study. Statistically, the country is on a par with Jordan.

Poor reading performance and a lack of digital skills are interconnected problems. Both require students to understand and process information and solve problems independently.

What is PISA?

PISA assesses the knowledge and practical skills of 15-year-olds. The study does not simply test whether students remember the school curriculum. It measures how well they can apply their knowledge to real-life situations.

The 2025 assessment was the ninth cycle of PISA. The study was previously conducted every three years. From 2025 onwards, the interval between cycles has increased to four years.

Georgia first joined PISA in 2010 as part of the PISA 2009+ programme. Subsequent assessments took place in Georgia in 2015, 2018, 2022 and 2025.

A total of 6,855 students from 265 schools in Georgia took part in the latest assessment. Parents, school principals and 1,350 science teachers also completed questionnaires.

PISA 2025 study on Georgia

World.title: What Georgian, Russian and Tskhinvali sides discussed at 134th IPRM meeting
World.content:
The 134th meeting of the Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism (IPRM) was held in the village of Ergneti, in Georgia‘s Gori municipality.

The sides discussed developments along the occupation line in the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) since the previous meeting, as well as the current security situation.

The IPRM is a forum for addressing urgent security and humanitarian issues in the Georgian-Ossetian and Georgian-Abkhaz conflict zones. Its main objectives include securing the release of detainees, preventing incidents and addressing everyday problems faced by people living along the occupation line. Representatives of Georgia, Russia and the Tskhinvali region/Abkhazia take part in the meetings, facilitated by the OSCE and the EU Monitoring Mission.

According to Georgia’s State Security Service (SSG), the meeting included a detailed discussion of key incidents recorded in the occupied region and along the occupation line. Particular attention was paid to restrictions on freedom of movement at the so-called crossing points.

Irakli Antadze, deputy head of the SSG’s Analytical Department, said the Georgian side had demanded the release of all those it says are being illegally detained.

“We called for a humanitarian approach to ensure that all those illegally detained can return to their families. Our international partners also supported us on this. At this stage, I cannot say anything about specific results, as consultations are continuing,” Antadze said.

Irakli Antadze

According to Antadze, the sides also discussed new cases of so-called “borderisation” recorded in the Tskhinvali region since the previous meeting.

“Our positions were once again diametrically opposed, and we were unable to find common ground on this issue,” Antadze said.

At the meeting, Georgian officials again condemned what they described as illegal “borderisation” and highlighted what they said were continuing violations of fundamental human rights in the occupied Tskhinvali region.

The Georgian side also raised again the killing of Georgian citizen Tamaz Ginturi, demanding accountability and justice for the member or members of what it described as the Russian occupation forces responsible for his death.

The Georgian side also strongly demanded the immediate release of all those it says are being illegally detained.

The next IPRM meeting is scheduled for 22 October 2026.

World.title: Uzbekistan, IsDB advance major investment projects across key sectors
World.content:
Photo: the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 10. Uzbekistan and the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) discussed advancing priority investment projects in water, agriculture, transport infrastructure, energy, education and healthcare.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, following a meeting between Minister Laziz Kudratov and Hammad Zafar Hundal, the newly appointed head of the IsDB Regional Hub in Almaty.

According to the Ministry, in the course of the meeting, Kudratov congratulated Hundal on his appointment and wished him success in his new role.

The meeting focused on the implementation of priority projects and further development of cooperation between Uzbekistan and the IsDB. The discussions covered several sectors identified as important areas for joint investment and development.

Particular attention was given to projects related to water and agriculture, transport infrastructure, energy, education and healthcare.

“The parties reaffirmed their readiness to further expand cooperation, promote new investment initiatives and implement joint projects,” Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade said.

The meeting also provided an opportunity to discuss the next stage of cooperation between the Uzbek government and the development bank, including potential new investment initiatives alongside projects already being advanced.

The IsDB has been a development partner for Uzbekistan across infrastructure and social and economic sectors, while the latest talks highlight the focus on projects with practical development outcomes.

The sides expressed readiness to maintain close engagement and continue working on new initiatives aimed at strengthening the partnership.

The meeting comes as Uzbekistan continues to attract financing and investment for infrastructure, agriculture, energy and social-sector projects, while working with international development institutions to support economic development and modernization.

Furthermore, the sides agreed to continue cooperation on expanding engagement, developing new investment initiatives and implementing joint projects across the identified priority sectors.

World.title: Kazakh enterprises set to join new EAEU cooperation projects
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 10. Kazakh enterprises will participate in new cooperation projects within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).

This was announced in a statement by the press service of the Kazakh government.

"The decisions were made at a regular online meeting of the Council of the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC), with Kazakhstan represented by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin," the statement noted.

According to the information, one of the new cooperation projects involves the construction of a plant in Moscow Region to produce AKRUS paints and coatings. The facility is expected to produce coatings with higher resistance to corrosion and fire compared with existing analogues. The project is designed for five years and is scheduled to start this year.

The project participants will include Belarusian Research and Production Enterprise Orion-VK, Kazakhstan’s Asyl Construction LLP, which will supply part of the materials and technological equipment, and Russia’s AKZ Pokrytiya LLC.

Another new cooperation project involves the construction of a new mixing line at the Samara Gypsum Plant. The project is expected to increase annual production of dry construction and special-purpose mixtures by 75,500 tons. Kazakhstan’s Elita LLP will participate in the project by providing engineering and construction services, while Belarus will be represented by Remeza CJSC.

The projected economic effect for Kazakhstan’s budget from tax revenues generated by the project is estimated at around 180 million tenge (about $396,637).

Additionally, the government noted that in 2025, a cooperation project to produce agricultural machinery in Akmola Region was approved.

According to the Kazakh government, cooperation projects within the EAEU receive preferential financing through subsidized interest rates on loans provided for project implementation.

“The projects are designed to promote technological development and the creation of new production models, as well as expand trade and economic ties among the countries of the economic union,” the government said.

The Council also approved amendments to a number of documents concerning the agricultural sector, including changes to the methodology for field testing of crop varieties.

The sides also agreed to amend the Unified Quarantine Phytosanitary Requirements for regulated products and facilities at the customs border and within the territories of EAEU member states.

The amendments concern phytosanitary measures related to pepino mosaic virus, which affects tomatoes, peppers and eggplants. The requirement for the absence of the virus in such products will be removed provided that an adequate level of quarantine phytosanitary safety is ensured by the country.

The Council also decided to amend the list of regulated products subject to quarantine phytosanitary control at the customs border and within the territories of EAEU member states.

In particular, a phytosanitary certificate will no longer be mandatory for wooden packaging and securing materials if they bear the marking stipulated by the Unified Requirements.

The amendments are aimed at creating more favorable conditions for the production and trade of the relevant products across the EAEU.

The Council also approved amendments to the Customs Union technical regulation “On the Safety of Toys.” The amendments establish mandatory requirements for toys intended for children under 14 and are aimed at protecting consumers from misleading product information and preventing the circulation of toys that do not meet established safety standards.

The sides also discussed and adopted decisions on a number of other procedural matters concerning various sectors and the activities of the Commission

World.title: Fourth day of Baku Climate Action Week to address climate and energy issues
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 10. The fourth day of Baku Climate Action Week will feature three roundtable discussions focusing on climate action, the preservation of cultural heritage and biodiversity, as well as sustainable energy transition, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

The first roundtable will be dedicated to the topic of “Impact Dialogue: Subnational Entities.” The discussion will focus on the role of local and regional institutions in climate action, implementation of climate commitments, and opportunities for cooperation in sustainable development.

Another roundtable will address the preservation of cultural heritage and biodiversity in Turkic civilization. The event titled “Cultural Heritage and Biodiversity Conservation in the Turkic Civilization: From Shared Traditions to Joint Action” will focus on protecting shared cultural heritage, preserving traditions, safeguarding biodiversity and expanding cooperation in these areas.

The third key session of the day will focus on the role of sustainable energy centers in promoting climate resilience, innovation and energy transition.

Within the framework of the regional dialogue titled “Regional Dialogue on the Role of Sustainable Energy Centres in Promoting Climate Resilience, Innovation and Energy Transitions,” participants will discuss opportunities to accelerate the energy transition and strengthen regional cooperation.

Partner organizations will also hold events as part of Baku Climate Action Week. A roundtable titled “Green and Digital Social Services Model: DOST Experience” will explore green and digital approaches in social service delivery, innovations in the sector and the experience of Azerbaijan’s DOST centers.

In addition, the “Green Ball” tree-planting campaign is planned to take place.

Baku Climate Action Week is being held from September 7 through 11. The event brings together discussions on climate action, energy transition, climate finance, sustainable cities, water resources, agriculture, digital technologies and other related areas.

World.title: Kazakhstan, China advance $1.2B wind power project in Pavlodar
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy and the management of China’s State Power Investment Corporation (SPIC) discussed the progress of a project to construct a 1 GW wind power plant in Pavlodar Region.

This was reported by the Ministry of Energy of Kazakhstan.

“During the working meeting, the sides discussed the current status of the project, as well as further steps for its implementation. The project is being implemented by SPIC jointly with Pavlodar Green Energy LLP in the area of Ekibastuz,” the ministry said.

According to the Ministry, the sides also discussed promising areas of energy cooperation and opportunities for implementing new joint projects.

Following the talks, the sides confirmed their interest in further cooperation on investment initiatives in Kazakhstan’s energy sector.

The project envisages the construction of a wind power plant with an energy storage system with a capacity of 300 MW/600 MWh. The volume of foreign direct investment in the project amounts to $1.2 billion. The wind power plant is scheduled to be commissioned in 2029.

Moreover, the project is expected to increase electricity generation from renewable energy sources and contribute to the stability of the regional power system.

According to the Ministry of Energy, electricity generation from renewable energy facilities in Kazakhstan amounted to 2.3 billion kWh in the first quarter of 2026, up 15% compared with the same period of 2025. Renewable energy generation is projected to reach 8.8 billion kWh in 2026.

Ten new renewable energy facilities are planned to be commissioned this year, including four wind power plants, five solar power plants and one hydropower plant. Their combined capacity will amount to 245 MW.

The share of renewable energy in Kazakhstan’s total electricity generation reached 7% in 2025. Kazakhstan plans to increase this share to 15% by 2030.

World.title: Azerbaijani oil scales up in price
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 10. The CIF price of Azerbaijan's Azeri Light crude at Italy's Augusta port increased by $5.14, or 4.75%, from the previous level to $113.32 per barrel, a source in the oil market told Trend.

FOB price of Azeri Light crude at Ceyhan port in Türkiye went up by $4.88, or 4.65%, to $109.87 per barrel.

The price of Urals crude grew by $3.65, or 4.45%, from the previous level to $85.60 per barrel.

Meanwhile, the price of North Sea “Dated Brent” crude rose by $5.58, or 5.13%, to $114.26 per barrel.

Azerbaijan's 2026 state budget is based on an average oil price assumption of $65 per barrel.

According to Trading Economics, oil prices remained above $96 per barrel on Thursday, trading near their highest level since May. The increase was attributed to growing concerns over potential disruptions to energy supplies from the Middle East amid escalating tensions between the United States and Iran.

“Iran has announced that it is prepared for a broader confrontation, said it would resist the U.S. naval blockade and warned that it would intensify attacks if U.S. strikes on Iranian territory continue.

U.S. President Donald Trump predicted that the conflict would end after the November midterm elections and said a significant decline in gasoline prices was unlikely before then. The remarks indicated that the likelihood of tensions easing in the near term remains limited.

After nearly a month of relative calm, the confrontation intensified again over the past week, with both sides increasing their attacks. The conflict expanded further after Iran-backed Houthis attacked several energy facilities in Saudi Arabia. Some facilities were temporarily shut down following the attacks,” the report notes.
