World.title: Women and complex-care patients losing out under Medicare, review says
World.content:
Patients who need longer GP appointments, particularly women with complex health needs, are being short-changed by inadequate Medicare rebates that should be increased, a major government review has found.

The draft report from the federal government's independent Medicare advisory committee found the system is rewarding short GP appointments more generously than those over 20 minutes, financially penalising doctors for providing longer consultations with patients when clinically appropriate.

Royal Australian College of GPs (RACGP) president Michael Wright said it had been a "flaw" of Medicare that incentivised GPs to churn through patients.

"What we've seen over the last 20 years is care is getting more complex, GPs are on average spending more time with patients, but they're being penalised by Medicare for doing that," he said.

The average cost of a long appointment — which is more than 20 minutes but less than 40 minutes — is $132, according to the latest government figures.

Michael Wright says GPs are spending more time with patients as care becomes more complex. (ABC News)

This means patients are typically about $52 out of pocket, but because prices vary significantly, the gap fee can be as much as $100.

However, the Medicare rebate does not double just because the appointment time does — generally the rebate per minute decreases as the appointment gets longer.

The Medicare Benefits Schedule (MBS) Review Advisory Committee report suggested this was inequitable.

"Patients aren't getting a fair go when it comes to longer consultations," Danielle McMullen, president of the Australian Medical Association (AMA) said.

"Those longer visits have a poorer rebate and we really need to rebalance the scales there."

The review suggests increasing the rebates for appointments lasting longer than 20 mins. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Major medical bodies have long argued the current system is not fit for purpose as patients are presenting with increasingly complex needs.

The review said increasing the rebates for appointments lasting longer than 20 minutes was an option that could be implemented the fastest.

But it did not say how much the rebates should be increased by, with Dr Wright noting the "devil is in the detail".

The RACGP has previously said increasing the rebate for appointments between 20 and 59 minutes by 40 per cent would cost the federal government up to $1 billion a year.

The review proposes rebate increases for level C, D and E appointments: Level A: less than six minutes — brief consultation

Level B: Six to 19 minutes — standard consultation (most common)

Level C: 20 to 39 minutes — long consultation

Level D: 40 to 59 minutes — extended consultation

Level E: 60+ minutes — prolonged consultation

Abolishing acupuncture and antenatal Medicare items

Female patients and GPs are particularly disadvantaged under the current system, according to the report, because they are more likely to use or provide longer consultations.

Dr McMullen said complex issues such as reproductive care or menopause management took time, and she had personally experienced the gender pay gap in practices where male doctors saw more patients per hour.

Danielle McMullen says women are particularly disadvantaged under the current system. (ABC News: Charlie Mclean)

"That has an impact on the sustainability of the business as well, which is a factor when we're trying to improve flexibility in our workforce and get more doctors to be GPs," she said.

The report also found bulk-billing incentives further exacerbated the issue, as GPs currently received the same flat-rate incentive for both short and long appointments.

The federal government last year expanded the bulk-billing incentive to all Australians, as part of a plan costing $8.5 billion over four years.

Anthony Albanese unveiled Labor's Medicare funding policy last year. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

But the review proposed changing the incentive from a flat-rate to one tied to the length of the consultation.

It also recommended abolishing standalone items for GPs who provide services such as acupuncture and antenatal care, arguing clinicians should be able to provide holistic care and bill according to the length of the consult, rather than the condition.

Evidence has shown acupuncture can help with conditions such as chronic pain, and some patients choose to receive it from their GP as they can be bulk-billed or address other health concerns in the same appointment.

Will a new bulk billing pledge mean you'll see your GP for free? Federal Labor and the Coalition both want to expand the bulk-billing incentive to all Australians, to make nine out of 10 GP visits free by the end of the decade.

Dr McMullen said she was not sure if patients would be better off under the new proposal.

"If this becomes a cost-cutting exercise then that's a problem … we want to see more detail about how they will balance that with appropriate rebates for time-tiered consultations," she said.

The review also recommended simplifying the rules around after-hours care by defining it as any service after 6pm on a weekday and abolishing the many Medicare items for after-hours care, instead replacing them with a loading fee.

"Obviously practices need to pay their staff more from that time to keep the doors open and we do think this will go a long way to help more practices be open later into the evening," Dr McMullen said.

The report is now open for consultation.

A health department spokesperson said the final version was due to be handed to the government by the end of the year.

"The MRAC is an independent committee which makes recommendations to government, which are then subject to consideration. Any changes to the MBS then need to be considered in a budget context," they said.

World.title: Police failed to test bloody knife linked to missing woman, inquiry told
World.content:
The family of missing woman Janine Vaughan has criticised the police investigation into her disappearance while giving evidence to a parliamentary inquiry.

The inquiry into unsolved murders and long-term missing persons' cases has held its third hearing in Sydney, where the Vaughan family's grief was laid bare.

Ms Vaughan was 31 when she was last seen getting into a red car outside a nightclub in the central west New South Wales town of Bathurst in December 2001.

A 2009 coronial inquest determined she was likely killed by an unknown person, but her body was never found and her cause of death remains unknown.

Adam Vaughan says he has struggled with the lack of closure around what happened to Janine. (Supplied)

Her brother Adam Vaughan and sister Kylie Spelde gave evidence to the inquiry today, describing waiting 25 years for answers as "torture".

"The frustration of not knowing is devastating … her killer has never been brought to justice," Mr Vaughan said.

" Losing a sibling in this way is not something you ever come to terms with. "

The inquiry heard the family had serious concerns around how aspects of the investigation into Janine's disappearance were managed.

"What makes the grief even harder to carry is the knowledge that this was not just a tragedy, it was also a failure," Mr Vaughan said.

" The early investigation into Janine's disappearance was marked by serious shortcomings. "

Kylie Spelde and Adam Vaughan gave evidence to the parliamentary inquiry into missing persons. (ABC News)

The inquiry heard key pieces of evidence, including a knife found with blood and hair on it, were not forensically tested.

"It's just not acceptable," Ms Spelde said.

The family said they also did not feel police had adequately communicated with them about where the investigation was up to.

"We understand that the homicide unit cannot allow us to roam freely through all of its evidence related to Janine's case, but … we believe families should receive regular updates," Mr Vaughan told the inquiry.

CCTV analysis

Mr Vaughan also told the inquiry the family had consistently requested access to the original VHS tape with CCTV footage showing Janine getting into the red car outside the Bathurst nightclub, the last time she was seen alive.

"Technology is improving all the time and just because footage has been reviewed 5 or 10 years ago with what was then cutting-edge technology, doesn't mean that advances in technology may reveal a different result."

The family have engaged US-based forensic expert Bryan Neumeister to help them examine the footage.

Mr Neumeister also addressed the inquiry, telling it he believed if the original VHS tape was examined using new film restoration technology, it could help identify key details like the make and model of the car Janine got into.

"With an old … recording like that, if it's ingested properly … you can get up to about 60 times the pixel resolution.

"That doesn't mean you're going to get more pixels that weren't there. It's just the clarity and the way it's encoded gives you a better look at it," he said.

Janine Vaughan went missing after moving from Muswellbrook to Bathurst. (Supplied: Vaughan family)

'Understaffed' homicide unit

Former senior crown prosecutor Mark Tedeschi AM KC told the inquiry he believed the NSW Police Unsolved Homicide Unit was struggling with a lack of resources.

"The impression that I got is that they're very dedicated, they want to do the best they can, but at least at that time they were understaffed and they had to allocate priorities and it was very difficult," he said.

The daughter of missing woman Marion Barter told the inquiry earlier this year that the unit has "no capacity" and called for more resources.

For Mr Vaughan, the search for answers will continue.

"There is a unique pain watching life continue without Janine," he told the inquiry.

"It's a form of ongoing torture that has been carried by our family for 25 years."

World.title: 'We're doing this': Labor goes for gas reservation over tax
World.content:
Australia would require gas companies to reserve up to a fifth of their exports to supply the domestic market under a new scheme proposed by the federal government.

The amount reserved each year would be calibrated to keep Australia modestly oversupplied with gas, rather than Labor's original plan to automatically require exporters to provide the full 20 per cent.

Energy and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen said the scheme would put "downward pressure" on domestic gas prices, denying the draft proposal unveiled on Thursday had been watered down.

Mr Bowen said the scheme was about ensuring supply for Australian industry and households rather than setting a price "target".

"However obviously, engineering a modest oversupply … is very much designed for downward pressure on prices," he said.

Labor initially proposed requiring liquefied natural gas (LNG) exporters reserve 20 per cent of their exports, but the draft makes that a ceiling rather than a fixed requirement.

Chris Bowen has denied the scheme is a backdown from the government's earlier policy. (ABC News: Megan Hughes)

Asked if this amounted to a "backdown", Mr Bowen said the government did not "see it that way at all".

"We see it as sensible calibration," he said.

" The 20 per cent figure is still the absolute core of the policy, but there is no point reserving gas that Australians don't need. "

Mr Bowen said it was "no secret" the major buyers of Australian LNG, including Malaysia and South Korea, wanted "reassurance" their existing contracts would be honoured.

He said the reserve was calibrated to guarantee Australia a "modest oversupply" of gas without threatening those contracts.

Labor promises cheaper gas, more jobs

The Australian Energy Regulator would set exporters' obligations each year to provide enough gas to meet 110 per cent of forecast domestic demand, capped at 20 per cent of exports.

The government has estimated exporters could provide up to 200 additional petajoules of gas a year, "more than enough" avoid forecast shortfalls of up to 140 petajoules.

Under the scheme, gas companies would be required to apply for a license to export gas, which would only be approved if they met their obligations to supply the domestic market.

The licensing process would start in January next year, while the domestic supply obligation would take effect in mid-2028.

Exporters would be required to actually supply their domestic allocation, rather than merely offer it for sale.

Industry Minister Tim Ayres said the reservation was an "enduring structural reform" that would deliver more secure jobs in Australia's industrial regions and also allow future investment.

Tim Ayres says the gas reservation was an "enduring structural reform". (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"We are a global energy and resources superpower," he said.

"A gas reservation ensures that Australia is playing to our strengths — cheaper energy means more manufacturing, means more secure jobs in our regions and our suburbs."

Exemption looms for Western Australia

The national gas reservation scheme would treat Western Australia and the east coast as separate markets, because they are not connected by pipeline.

WA currently has a 15 per cent state-based reservation scheme, though is forecast to face serious gas shortfalls in the 2030s unless additional supply is secured.

Resources Minister Madeleine King said the Commonwealth scheme would allow the minister to reduce the domestic supply obligation in a market that was already adequately supplied.

Madeleine King says the scheme would allow the minister to change obligations to meet the needs of different markets. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"For example, if the Western market was found to be well supplied, it would be possible for the discretion to be applied to reduce that obligation to zero," she said.

Ms King said Western Australia's reservation scheme was "well established" and ensuring the state was "well provided for" with gas for households and industry.

"As to their shortfalls, they are aware of … what they have to do to make sure there is more gas to meet that," she said.

Ms King said no decision had been made in relation to exempting WA from its obligations.

Labor accused of watering down gas scheme

Greens resources spokeswoman Steph Hodgins-May argued the government had "watered down" the reserve to "appease the gas industry".

"A reservation scheme won't raise a cent for Australian households," she said.

"And Labor is designing it in close consultation with the very gas industry that has spent years fighting any policy that asks them to pay their fair share."

Senator Hodgins-May said the government should instead pursue a tax on gas exports.

"Labor should drop this pathetic capitulation to the gas industry and work with us to finally make sure Australians get a fair return from our gas," she said.

Steph Hodgins-May argued the government had watered down the scheme. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Asked if he would rule out any extra tax on gas, Mr Bowen said the reservation was "much more impactful".

"We're not doing [a tax], what we're doing is this," he said.

Gas industry argues oversupply will 'destroy' investment

In a statement, the Coalition said it would "scrutinise" the government's proposal, and was ready to "work constructively" to pass the laws.

All gas crisis roads 'lead to Santos' Cracks are appearing in the facade of the gas industry's solidarity and all fingers are pointing towards one player.

The Opposition has argued there are "key criteria" that must be met, including more gas for Australians, more investment, honouring existing contracts and lowering prices through supply rather than price controls.

The east coast LNG exporters have different exposure to the domestic market, with Santos-led Gladstone LNG historically buying Australian gas to help meet its export contracts rather than contributing to local supply.

Santos chief executive Kevin Gallagher said yesterday the project would no longer contract third-party gas, while arguing Australia did not have a gas shortage but "just needs to get more gas out of the ground".

Kevin Gallagher argued Australia did not have a gas shortage. (ABC News: Felicity James)

Australian Energy Producers chief executive Samantha McCulloch said Labor had made a number of "sensible" changes to the proposed design of the reservation, including calibrating it more closely to domestic market needs.

But she said the 110 per cent oversupply of the east coast gas market would "destroy investment signals" and "crowd out" smaller domestic-focused producers.

"The 'must sell' requirement exacerbates these risks," she said.

"Producers should not be forced to sell gas below cost or on non-commercial terms."

World.title: Don't Look Back In Anger proves surprisingly moving Oasis reunion tour doco
World.content:
Oasis were Britpop's biggest band. But their world-conquering fame grew in tandem with hostile in-fighting between frontman Liam Gallagher and guitarist-songwriter Noel Gallagher, which boiled over backstage at a 2009 Paris concert, breaking up the band.

Fifteen years later, a reunion tour provided an opportunity to "fix the narrative," as Noel Gallagher puts it in Don't Look Back In Anger, a documentary on Oasis's 2025 live comeback.

Far from a run-of-the-mill concert film or puff piece, it's a surprisingly moving portrait of reconciliation and the celebratory power of music.

Scripted by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight and directed by Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern, it's the perfect souvenir for tour attendees but also the clearest illustration why Oasis means so much to so many.

Loading Instagram content

The film begins with a montage, from the band's '90s heyday to their fateful Paris split, and voices wondering, Noel included, whether the volatile siblings could survive a rehearsal without incident, let alone a global trek.

Spoiler: They did. But the movie shines in depicting the tense lead-up.

We're ushered into rehearsals where Noel prepares the band before his younger brother's arrival, all the while expressing the stakes and his grave doubts: "I cannot see it. Me, on-stage with Liam."

Prospects don't get better when the frontman shows up, scowling his way through songs and departing unceremoniously, as casually as he appeared.

It's awkward, stressful viewing, underscoring the male bravado that tore Oasis apart. But the bad mojo swiftly lifts at their first show in Cardiff when the nervous anticipation shared backstage and by the 60,000-strong audience, morphs into triumph as the band stroll onstage.

Liam grabs Noel's hand and raises it aloft: An impromptu, showbiz gesture of harmony that Noel himself scrutinises, but a ritual he embraces as the tour rolls onward.

The Gallagher brothers arrive at the first Oasis reunion concert on July 4, 2025, in Cardiff. (AP: Scott A Garfitt/Invision)

What's the story? Fan glory

Don't Look Back In Anger then barrels forwards into a victorious concert movie capturing Oasis successfully re-applying for the job of "World's Biggest Band".

They receive a hero's welcome in their hometown, Manchester, and similarly rapturous receptions in Dublin, Seoul, Sao Paolo, Tokyo, Buenos Aires and New York.

The expertly shot live footage is "biblical" (to borrow a band-favourite phrase), capturing both the outsized swagger and vigour of their enduring hits but also intimate, deeply human moments from within the throng.

Australian fans await Oasis at their first Melbourne Show on October 31, 2025. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Mobs of aging, bucket-hat sporting men openly weeping? Certainly. Shirtless, shouting lads? Loads! But also, reams of footage of young, diverse crowds having the night of their lives.

Beaming, hugging, weeping, absorbing the "religious experience", as Noel labels it, of a miraculous occasion many thought would never happen.

The doco puts a human face on the Oasis phenomenon, stitching fan stories that show how these songs reach unlikely places and often help folks feeling at their lowest.

A victim of the 2017 Manchester bombing overcoming survivors' guilt; a Brazilian outsider finding community; South Korean haenyeo free-divers singing ' Acquiesce ' as self-motivation.

How Oasis made Britpop blockbuster (What's The Story) Morning Glory Over 30 years ago, Oasis were about to release an enduring British rock classic. Here's how they did it.

This sentimental streak is at odds with a group famous for macho posturing and making vulgar, tabloid-grabbing put-downs a national UK sport.

The siblings' foul-mouthed irreverence remains hilariously entertaining. Witness Liam's sweary wisdom: "If you're going to be a c***, be a funny c***".

But age and nostalgia for their own legacy has softened the Gallaghers.

Unprepared for the "intense outpouring of joy and tears", Noel confesses to turning his back at shows to hide his emotions. "Fathers and sons, that always gets me."

Speaking of the Gallaghers' own children, spitting images of their dads, they are shown singing along side-of-stage as it's revealed the cousins first met on tour and are now "best friends".

It speaks to the film being more victory lap than warts-and-all. Its two-hour running time finds zero space to explore staging a blockbuster production or interrogate the dynamic ticket pricing controversy that excluded working-class fans. Nor the cancer diagnosis that temporarily sidelined guitarist Paul "Bonehead" Arthurs, credited as "the sound of Oasis".

These details are cast off as distractions to the movie's heartwarming focus, and the story it excels in telling: the healing impact of Oasis, particularly on its estranged siblings.

The Gallaghers with Steven Knight (far left), Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace (far right) at the Venice International Film Festival. (Disney/Getty Images: Giulia Parmigiani)

Live Forever

There's no detailed autopsy on how time healed all wounds. Instead, we learn that Noel and Liam reconciled in the most emotionally stunted, fittingly Manchunian way: "All forgiven without saying a word."

The tour "fixed a lot of things," not least Oasis's bank accounts. But it'd take a stony heart to not to be moved by the sight of Noel and Liam sharing smiles, hugs and laughs.

It's truly touching when the camera reveals the Gallaghers are side by side, conducting their first joint interview in more than 20 years.

"It's not a power struggle anymore," says Noel, offering warm, authentic insights on his brother.

He sagely notes how the opening lines of debut single Supersonic ("I need to be myself / I can't be no-one else") became Liam's "way of life". Absence has clearly made him fonder of his rockstar credo.

Loading Instagram content

"If I did that, I'd look an utter c***," he remarks of Liam's signature move: balancing a tambourine on his head. "Somehow, when he does that, it's the greatest thing I've ever seen!"

Why we still love Wonderwall A quarter century after its release, why does Wonderwall still speak to so many people?

It's a delight seeing Noel chuckle as Liam describes the benefits of being an aging rocker who stands still, unlike Mick Jagger, doomed to forever perform "this Jumping Jack Flash nonsense".

In a serious moment, Liam discloses swearing off cigarettes, booze, and harder stuff for the tour's duration because "these songs, they need to be treated with the utmost respect".

This new-found professionalism shows how, in his own sweary way, Liam grasps the importance of being custodian to a legacy bigger than stadium singalongs.

"It's bigger than Noel and me. It don't belong to us. We're part of it but it belongs to all of us," he says.

In an era where AI-generated content floods our fractured feeds, Don't Look Back In Anger is a welcome, regularly poignant reminder of the power of a human-powered, monocultural moment. You don't get that with Blur.

It's an uplifting dose of euphoria that you'll want to relive again. If rumours of another Oasis tour prove true, we just might.

Don't Look Back In Anger is in cinemas now and will stream on Disney Plus after its theatrical run.

World.title: 'Uproar' unleashed after OpenAI says it solved major maths mystery
World.content:
Scientists at OpenAI say its new artificial intelligence (AI) model found a mathematical proof to one of the Millennium Problems — significant and complex mathematical problems with a US$1 million reward.

But what could have been a public relations win for the company has morphed into a reputational blow.

Australian scientist Tristan Buckmaster posted a long statement saying he had been working closely with Levent Alpöge, who works at OpenAI competitor Anthropic, to also solve the problem.

And they were using a very similar, and quite niche, proof method.

While Professor Buckmaster did not claim his work was plagiarised, his version of events did not paint OpenAI in a positive light.

Here's a breakdown of the controversy and why, even though the subject matter is complex, it boils down to simple questions about trust, ethics and the role of AI.

Don't worry, you don't need to be a mathematician to follow the saga.

What is the Navier-Stokes problem?

The mathematical problem is one of six remaining unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.

According to Zsuzsanna Dancso, a mathematician at the University of Sydney, the problems stretch across mathematics disciplines.

"They are universally acknowledged as some of the most important or hardest problems in mathematics," Dr Dancso said.

"What makes them special is that there's a prize for solving one of them."

OpenAI shared this graphic of local incompressible motion shared, but did not disclose if it was AI-generated. (Supplied: OpenAI)

Navier-Stokes equations describe the motion of fluids, and overall are well understood by scientists, according to Melissa Lee, a mathematician at Monash University.

"They are incredibly important in lots of applications such as aerodynamics for planes, and the study of blood flow," Dr Lee said.

"In practice, engineers and scientists calculate approximate solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations for their applications every day.

"But it's unknown if the fluids always act in a same way.

"This is called the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem.

"The problem has taken a long time and a lot of work to study because fluid flow can be extremely complicated."

What is the controversy?

OpenAI announced its proof to the Navier-Stokes problem on Tuesday morning, US time.

The company said it used 10,000 AI agents, AI assistants that can go about tasks on their own, to complete the proof in about 88 hours.

At the same time, Professor Buckmaster, an Australian mathematician at New York University, said that he and Dr Alpöge had completed several closely related problems with the help of AI, including those from OpenAI.

Tristan Buckmaster is a mathematics professor at New York University. (Supplied: New York University)

Professor Buckmaster said he and Dr Alpöge used an idea based off the work of Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez Zoroa as a starting point.

They used several AI models to push their program to completion, pushing it to what's known in the field of fluid dynamics as the Euler equations.

This was a major stepping stone for tackling the Navier-Stokes problem.

And it was quite a niche approach.

"Almost nobody else I know of was working on it," Professor Buckmaster said.

"It is not the direction one arrives at in a few days by giving a model the problem statement."

Making 'real progress'

Work on this was slow but, after about a year, Professor Buckmaster said the pair made "real progress" on August 15 and verified it by August 22.

"Since this point, we have been working around the clock to understand this proof and turn it into something readable," Professor Buckmaster said.

In its announcement, OpenAI said it started training an unnamed model about a week later.

"Since August 28 we have been training a new internal model that has exhibited unprecedented performance in our benchmarks, including mathematics," OpenAI said in a statement.

Rumours swirl

"On Tuesday, September 1, we heard rumours that two Millennium Prize problems had been resolved," OpenAI said.

"Inspired by these rumours and by the step change in performance of our internal model, we launched an effort to evaluate it on all open Millennium Prize problems and a few other high-impact problems."

Professor Buckmaster and Dr Alpöge had heard these rumours too.

"Levent had received tips that information about our progress had been passed to OpenAI," Professor Buckmaster said.

So on September 3, he said he emailed someone from OpenAI.

Sunday afternoon calls

Three days later, on a Sunday afternoon, Professor Buckmaster had two calls with Sebastien Bubeck from OpenAI and another unnamed OpenAI mathematician.

"I asked whether the model had been trained on, or had access to, our sessions in Codex, into which we had been putting all our drafts for the whole of this project," Professor Buckmaster said.

"I was told the model did not look up user data.

"I asked again, about training, and I did not get an answer."

Professor Buckmaster said he was presented with two options:

Option one: The pair posts their Euler result and OpenAI post its Navier-Stokes result the next day, saying the pair deserved the prize

The pair posts their Euler result and OpenAI post its Navier-Stokes result the next day, saying the pair deserved the prize Option two: After posting Euler, Professor Buckmaster alone write a paper presenting the Navier-Stokes result, acknowledging that an internal OpenAI model had resolved it — leaving Alpöge off because he works for Anthropic

'Why would you ruin your career?'

Professor Buckmaster said he declined both offers and said he'd go public if OpenAI proceeded with those proposed options.

"The reply was, 'Why would you ruin your career?' I replied that I am an academic, and asked why he thought going public would ruin my career," he said in his statement.

"The reply was, 'If you don't want me to be nice, then I don't have to be nice.'"

He finished his statement by saying he wanted to make a few things clear about the situation.

"I do not know what their model did, or how," he said.

"I do not know whether our data was used.

"I am not accusing anyone of anything."

How did OpenAI respond?

OpenAI's Dr Bubeck first posted on X, condemning the "false and inflammatory allegations" and promising to say more the next day.

In two lengthy follow-up posts, Dr Bubeck said he had wanted to coordinate releases with the pair and "came in with the best possible intentions".

He said he never asked for Dr Alpöge to be removed from authorship of his own work.

He said he had suggested Professor Buckmaster be the lead author on a rewrite of OpenAI's proof and felt it would be "inappropriate" for an Anthropic employee to author OpenAI's work.

Here's how he described the call with Professor Buckmaster:

"I was confused why one would turn an incredible source for celebration (of their achievements!) into such bickering, which is when I said that I did not understand why one would risk their career [over unfounded accusations]. "Genuinely, at that moment, I was trying to care for him and do a last ditch attempt to get a chance to give them all the credits that they deserve. "I deeply apologise for this extremely poor choice of words, it is the opposite of what I was trying to convey. (I should say that I retracted them on the spot by the way.)"

'Our proofs differ significantly'

He said OpenAI did not see any of Professor Buckmaster and Dr Alpöge's work until they released it publicly.

"One can in hindsight see that our proofs differ significantly and even the precise results proved are different in the Euler case," Dr Bubeck said.

Then OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman chimed in, saying he would have "greatly preferred coordination".

Sam Altman weighed in on the saga on X. (Reuters: Shelby Tauber)

"We did not rush to publish even though the other team wasn't communicating with us," Mr Altman posted on X.

"The team threatened us with unfounded accusations of plagiarism."

In its announcement, OpenAI said none of its researchers or agents saw the pair's data before it was publicly released and "no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem".

"While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models."

And then came the memes

As you'd expect, with news this big and a drama unfolding on X, there was a lot of commentary about it on social media.

Here's just a few of the many takes on the saga people have been posting on X:

An 'uproar' in mathematical community

According to Dr Dancso, OpenAI went against the spirit of mathematics.

"In mathematics, but also in science in general, there are two very basic ethical principles — one is we acknowledge our sources, and two is we acknowledge our collaborators," she said.

"If we collaboratively solve the problem, then we publish it together.

"And if we use someone else's work, then we reference it and acknowledge that person's work.

"I think OpenAI fails on both counts."

Why should I care?

"The situation raises legitimate questions about privacy and trust, especially in the current age where mathematicians and researchers more generally are exploring the integration of AI tools into their work," Dr Lee said.

"Researchers need to know very clearly what happens to unpublished work they enter into AI systems, which is perhaps something that has not been considered carefully enough in certain quarters.

She said it boiled down to trust between researchers and AI companies.

"Companies such as OpenAI already know that trust in this context is a big deal, and many education and enterprise workspaces claim that data given there is not used to train AI models," Dr Lee said.

"However, I think such assertions will gain greater scrutiny over the coming weeks and months.

"If scientists are going to use AI tools while developing new and unpublished ideas, they want to be confident that those ideas will remain protected and will not somehow feed into a competing research effort by the relevant AI company.

"This also raises broader questions about who gets credit when AI plays a major role in a discovery, and what responsibilities AI companies have towards researchers using their systems."

World.title: Commissioner 'deeply worried' by sexual violence trajectory
World.content:
The domestic, family and sexual violence commissioner says she is "deeply worried" about the trajectory of rates of sexual violence in Australia following the release of her annual report, which has called for national attention on the issue.

Micaela Cronin's report found Australians were experiencing unacceptable levels of harm within the family law and justice systems and through rising levels of sexual violence.

Sexual violence in Australia reached its highest level in 33 years in 2024.

Ms Cronin said the rate had dropped by less than 1 per cent in the past year and more action was needed to address the issue.

"I am deeply worried about the trajectories that we're on, particularly with sexual violence, and you're right, it is absolutely increasing between young people," she told the ABC.

"So we absolutely have to face up to what isn't working and identify what is working.

"We've got a real problem, and we've seen that in the national conversation in the last few weeks."

The issue came into national focus last month after two young boys were charged with rape in NSW.

DV commissioner frustrated recommendations gathering dust She's examined thousands of recommendations made by more than 25 different inquiries providing practical solutions to stop and respond to violence against women

A leading violence against women scholar at Monash University, Kate Fitz-Gibbon, called the figures "frightening" and said it was a reminder to governments they had to do more to protect women and children.

"I think it's certainly a call to action … some progress has been made, but there is significantly more action needed," she told ABC.

The commissioner's report recommends sexual violence should have targeted and sustained national attention, but it does not outline what programs or policies are necessary.

The report also recommends governments at all levels invest more in violence prevention services, arguing opportunities to "intervene earlier, support recovery and reduce future demand" were often missed.

While Micaela Cronin hopes the new action plan will secure better funding, she is frustrated that governments have not adopted her earlier recommendations. (Image: Patrick Rocca/ABC News)

Ms Cronin said early intervention was part of the broader solution to reduce gendered base violence.

"Australia has largely invested in systems designed to respond once violence reaches crisis point … These services are essential, but on their own they will not reduce the prevalence or impact of gender-based violence," she wrote in her report.

Do you know more about this story? Get in touch via Signal (claudialong.01) or email long.claudia@abc.net.au

Ms Fitz-Gibbon said early intervention needed to be "multi-pronged", and schools should be given more support to identify at-risk children earlier.

"We've been calling for greater attention within schools to connecting children and young people up to safety earlier to try and interrupt those trajectories of harm," she told the ABC.

"School staff are not equipped; they have not been trained to provide an early intervention response for children and young people."

Change needed within family law and justice systems

Ms Cronin singled out the legal system as an area that needed change to better protect survivors of domestic violence and sexual violence.

She acknowledged there had been significant reform in family law, but said more work was needed.

New guide released for preventing child abuse Leading family violence advocates call for children to be directly involved in designing policy to prevent child abuse.

"We are still seeing the family law courts being a site for weaponisation, so people using the court to continue to drag out relationships and harm," she told the ABC.

"There are real concerns about decisions that are being made that are putting children in harm's way."

Her concerns about the legal system more broadly have been echoed by executive director of advocacy group With You We Can, Sarah Rosenberg, who herself navigated the justice system after a sexual violence incident.

Sarah Rosenberg has experienced how the justice system treats survivors of sexual violence. (Supplied)

"Very few victim survivors report; of those who do, very few cases progress to a charge [and] these aren't individual choices, this is attrition by design," she said.

Ms Rosenberg, whose organisation assists victim survivors to navigate the complex and daunting justice system, said if governments were serious about ending violence they needed to listen to the experts.

"The Australian Law Reform Commission has told governments exactly what to do, give victims their own lawyers … Eighteen months on, not a single jurisdiction has fully legislated or implemented that," she said.

Targets for First Nations women and children going backwards

The report also collated data that showed the overall number of women killed by an intimate partner trended downwards since the late 1980's

However, rates of violence against First Nations women and children have increased.

Between 2019 and 2022, the rate of Indigenous children hospitalised after family violence incidents fell but has since shot up to 45 children per 100,000 — its highest level since data has been collected.

Rates of intimate partner homicide of First Nations women increased in each of the two years since a baseline was established in the commissioner's first report, reaching four victims per 100,000 people in the 2024-2025 data.

However, the commissioner warned it was too early to identify trends against the baseline.

The number of women killed by a partner has trended downwards since the late 1980's. (Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commissioner)

The trend for First Nations women is the reverse of the broader community, with the number of those killed by a partner going up. (Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commissioner)

Ms Cronin said the experience of First Nations women and children within existing support systems was "very distressing".

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek tabled the commissioner's third report to parliament on Wednesday and said while progress had been made, she conceded not enough work had been done.

Tanya Plibersek says she has an "incredible sense of urgency" when it comes to ending violence against women and children. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"I have an incredible sense of urgency for more change," she told the ABC.

Family violence review calls for harsher alcohol and gambling laws An expert panel examining how to best prevent violence against women and children has called on alcohol, gambling and porn companies to be more proactive in tackling the crisis.

Ms Plibersek also shared her own experience of assault, while also acknowledging that there are plenty of "wonderful men".

"I'm a cabinet minister, I'm in a pretty powerful position, when I walk to my car at night in a dark car park, I still get my keys out at night in case someone attacks me," she said.

"I've been assaulted walking home in Canberra at night."

The federal government is working on the second action plan for the decade-long National Plan to End Violence against Women and Children.

The specific road map for how the broad aims of the national plan can be realised over the next five years is expected to be released in the first half of 2027.

World.title: Sydney businessman jailed for foreign interference in Australian first
World.content:
Sydney businessman Alexander Csergo has been sentenced to three-and-a-half years in prison for reckless foreign interference, but will be eligible for parole as early as next month due to the time he has already spent in custody.

The long-running case about reports Csergo compiled for two suspected Chinese spies while he was working in Shanghai represents the first time an Australian has been sentenced for the charge.

A District Court jury found the 58-year-old guilty in March, after hearing weeks of evidence about Csergo's communication and meetings with two people he knew as "Ken" and "Evelyn" between 2021 and 2023, when he returned to Sydney.

Csergo prepared reports, upon request and in return for payment, about topics including lithium mining, the change in the German government, defence, the Quad alliance and AUKUS.

The prosecution told jurors he believed they worked for a Chinese intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security (MSS), and was reckless as to whether his conduct would support foreign intelligence activities.

But Csergo's lawyers argued he handed over worthless information from open-source material along with fictitious interviews, and there was no evidence he ever revealed any national security secrets.

Csergo originally pleaded not guilty to reckless foreign interference. (ABC News)

Judge Craig Smith found that the offending effectively took place between May or June 2022 until December 2022.

He said Csergo's subjective awareness of his situation shifted around May 2022, in the context of being asked to prepare a defence report that was "materially different" to his previous work.

In WeChat messages to Csergo, specific topics of interest were identified including "China spy", "anything about China in ASIO", and strategy, targets, tactics, methods and technology.

Csergo warned Ken that they needed to be "careful" and said "we don't want to find ourselves being questioned by any governments".

He also said that one of his contacts had "strongly warned" him against what Ken had requested.

'Degree of sophistication' in offending

The judge found beyond reasonable doubt that Csergo was relevantly reckless from May or June 2022 and part of his conduct was deceptive, satisfying all four elements of the charge.

He said there was "clearly a persistence in his conduct" as he "extensively researched, downloaded and prepared materials", and that there was a level of deception to the conduct.

Judge Smith said he did not consider Csergo's conduct to have been "overly sophisticated in the criminal sense", but there was a "degree of sophistication".

He handed Csergo a backdated sentence of three years and six months, with a non-parole period of one year and ten months.

"The substantial effect of the sentence … is you would be eligible for consideration for release to parole on 24 October 2026," the judge told Csergo, who appeared on a video link in the Downing Centre.

He took into account that Csergo had spent more than 600 days in custody prior to sentence, including a period between when he was arrested and then granted bail, and when he was taken into custody shortly after the jury's verdict.

Csergo's mother was seen entering the court the morning of the sentencing. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The judge accepted Csergo had no criminal history and was a person of good character.

He said the evidence showed he was an intelligent, highly-motivated and loyal person with strong support from his mother, brother and friends.

It demonstrated that he was "otherwise a decent man" who had committed a serious offence, the judge found.

Attempted contact with ex-prime minister

The judge also found that the nature of Csergo's time in custody was a "significant matter" and said the evidence showed he has suffered a particularly hard and isolating time in prison which exacerbated mental health issues.

He said existing mental health issues, including heightened anxiety during COVID lockdowns, created a "degree of vulnerability" in Csergo when he was initially contacted on LinkedIn by someone seeking part-time consultancy services.

The court heard that at one point, Csergo attempted to contact former prime minister Kevin Rudd through an online contact form, but never interviewed Dr Rudd.

When he returned to Australia, Csergo had with him a so-called "shopping list" of subjects Ken and Evelyn were interested in, which the crown had highlighted as being important to the prosecution case.

But the judge did not accept the businessman intended to act upon the list.

"There is no evidence he did anything in relation to the shopping list, although there is evidence of his continuing communication with Ken while he was in Australia."

World.title: Instagram boss warns users will be 'overwhelmed' without algorithm
World.content:
As the Australian parliament considers new rules for opting out of the social media algorithm, the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, has warned most users do not enjoy what they find on the other side.

The federal government unveiled a proposal this week to force platforms to give users the choice, via push notifications, to opt out of the algorithm that curates their feed and instead view posts chronologically.

It is part of a long-awaited Digital Duty of Care framework, designed to shift responsibility onto big tech to proactively reduce harms, or face $100 million fines.

Government proposes social media algorithm choice Labor wants to make social media platforms proactively reduce foreseeable harms while giving users control over whether algorithms shape their feeds.

Mr Mosseri weighed in to the debate indirectly, during a rare Australian press briefing today, intended to promote the platform's new short-form series Algo Confessions, as well as the Your Algorithm feature, which theoretically allows users to see and even edit their algorithm.

A Meta spokesman told reporters on the call that the Instagram chief would not be commenting on the government's proposal, but Mr Mosseri volunteered his view on chronological feeds.

Citing the company's experience in other countries, he said "the average user experience gets much worse".

"If you go to a chronological feed, it ends up getting overwhelmed with content from companies, brands, and publishers," he said.

" Creators get drowned out, and then your friends get drowned out even more. "

The reason, he said, was that the best way to achieve reach in a chronological feed was to post more often, and businesses could afford to post more often than ordinary people.

While he did not provide figures, he said engagement ultimately fell by as much as 50 per cent.

"You miss a lot more content … and you spend a lot less time on the platform," he said.

Adam Mosseri says most people are not satisfied after opting out of the algorithm. (ABC Radio Canberra: Hannah Walmsley)

For the people shaping these laws, causing users to spend less time on the platform is one of the main goals, but Mr Mosseri said crucially, user satisfaction also suffered.

"We ask people every day how satisfied they are with the experience," he said.

"Both at the aggregate [experience], 'Are you satisfied?' and at the specific post, 'Was this worth your time?', those numbers fall off a cliff.

"So, there's this interesting tension between what an individual might want and what happens when you actually explode that to the entire community."

Mr Mosseri said he assumed the "passionate few" who really wanted to opt out of the algorithm were happy with the choice, but those users were in the minority.

Australians can opt out of their algorithm now, but few realise it

What few users realise is that a chronological feed is already available on Instagram globally, including in Australia.

On Instagram, users can tap on the logo to access a drop-down menu, which offers a "following" setting.

If selected, the user's feed transforms into a stream of posts from followed accounts in reverse chronological order, minus the algorithmic recommendations.

But unlike in the Netherlands, the feed reverts to using the algorithm when you close and re-open the app.

Mr Mosseri agrees the option to change to a chronological feed could be made more known to users. (Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz)

Mr Mosseri said, although he did not have figures, that uptake in Australia had been low.

"An educated guess would be in the low single-digit percentages," he said.

He said users probably did not know about the option, but "that's not on purpose".

"I'm not trying to hide it…. I think we can make it more prominent," he said.

"Instagram is too complicated, if you ask me.

"There's a lot of things to squeeze into the page … so we've been trying not to just add more buttons for everything.

"There's definitely room to improve the discoverability of that."

The federal government's My Feed, My Way bill comes less than a year after a court decision brought about similar rules in the Netherlands.

Mr Mosseri does not believe the platform is addictive. (Unsplash: Katka Pavlickova)

Since 2023, the European Union has had laws in effect for 27 member states requiring large platforms such as Instagram to give users the option of a chronological feed.

Under those rules, the choice must also be made accessible to users, rather than being buried in settings controls, where many users might never find it.

But in October 2025, a Dutch court went a step further, ordering platforms provide chronological feeds as a default.

This morning, Mr Mosseri said in the absence of defaults, uptake would probably remain low.

"Anything that isn't the default just doesn't get used the majority of the time, which is why defaults are so important," he said.

The federal government's push on chronological feeds was not originally slated as a centrepiece of the Digital Duty of Care, but the idea gained prominence after Meta's landmark $23 billion US court settlement last month, in which the company also agreed to allow US teens to choose a chronological feed.

The suit, brought by 29 US states, was premised on the accusation that Instagram's parent company had intentionally designed its platforms to addict young people.

Meta's 'big tobacco moment' might not flow to Australia Meta's landmark court settlement is being hailed by some as social media's "big tobacco moment", but there is no guarantee Australians will benefit from the safety measures it has agreed to.

Mr Mosseri said he did not believe Instagram was addictive, although that might be "controversial to say".

"I do think we often, in English anyway, conflate the way we colloquially use the word addicted, like, 'I'm addicted to this show and I'm binge-watching it,'… [as opposed to] clinical addiction," he said.

"I just think those things are different."

Mr Mosseri acknowledged that social media users were increasingly frustrated by the "black box" nature of the algorithms that decide what they see.

"What we are trying to figure out now is how do we bring back more agency, bring back more transparency, bring back more control?" He said.

He said ultimately, Instagram wants people to enjoy the app, and that the company needed to take "a long view" when it came to how much time people using it.

"We try to optimise for things like… satisfaction, preference, which I think [it's] hard to imagine benefit from people compulsively using the platform."

World.title: With witty dialogue and good comic timing, this new play finds plenty to laugh at in Canberra
World.content:
Opera House Drama Theatre, September 9, until October 17.

Politics is a harsh business. As brutal as a set dominated by cold marble columns – the pillars of democracy – where a lone woman vacuums as the audience enters.

Canberra’s Parliament House has hardly been a welcoming workplace for women, as countless news stories in recent years have made clear. Why, you might wonder, would you want to work there?

Johnny Nasser, Franca Lafosse and Susie Youssef as their characters at work in parliament house. Prudence Upton

Playwright Emily Steel has taken a light-hearted approach with a satire that focuses on three women drawn to Canberra’s limelight: first-time government MP Ruth (Susie Youssef), her jaded chief-of-staff Anna (Emily Taheny) and naive junior staffer Kelly (Franca Lafosse).

Ruth is determined to make a splash with healthcare reform. Anna wants to hold together her stressful job and her unravelling home life. Starry-eyed Kelly just wants approval. She is so incompetent and lacking in initiative that it’s hard to see why she was hired.

Laurence Boxhall and Emily Taheny. Prudence Upton

Yet she proves pivotal. When she spends a night with the science minister, Kelly unleashes a Pandora’s box of ambition, compromises, betrayals and all-round Machiavellian behaviour.

These shenanigans become so labyrinthine in the second half that one can get lost in the maze. But it’s clear that no one emerges unscathed.

The strength of the play is that there are no black-and-white characters. All are flawed, which allows scope for ambiguity and nuance about their actions.

It’s not only male attitudes to female colleagues that are in the spotlight. Female solidarity has gone AWOL. Ruth accuses Anna of not being up to the job if she won’t sacrifice her family for it. And Anna accuses Ruth of throwing Kelly under a bus to get the science minister’s backing for the health bill.

Indira Naidoo plays the prime minister in the story, which relies on witty back-and-forths for its humour. Prudence Upton

Despite an early sight gag involving bad hair, the play relies for its comedy not on slapstick but on witty dialogue and good comic timing.

Taheny as the overburdened Anna has the lion’s share of these lines, which she delivers to incisive effect. She is the core of the play, the woman who has soldiered on even as she’s watched her dreams die. Lafosse is a spirited Kelly. Despite her implausible character, she manages to evoke sympathy as the scales fall from her starry eyes.

Youssef’s backbencher Ruth is part idealistic campaigner, part prima donna, with the dial on opening night leaning towards the latter. Indira Naidoo doubles as prime minister and a cleaner, who provides a witty analysis of what changes after an election. Johnny Nasser as the science minister gives a rounded performance of a man in crisis.

Director Shannon Rush directs with unflagging energy and draws out the comedy. Early scenes could dial back the frenetic pitch to allow pace to build. Ailsa Paterson’s set evokes the impersonal feel of parliament house, the chamber and a serviced apartment, aided by Nigel Levings’ stark lighting. Composer Andrew Howard utilises a driving percussive beat, like troops marching to war.

This is a breezy, behind-the-scenes look at the workings of political power. While it offers few fresh insights, it reinforces the adage that if you want a friend in politics, get a dog.

World.title: Meet the $235m NFL superstar with one quad bigger than the other
World.content:
SportNFLMelbourne major events Meet the $235m NFL superstar with one quad bigger than the other Roy Ward September 10, 2026 — 3:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From head to toe, Nick Bosa catches your eye on the football field. The San Francisco defensive end has been a star dating back to his US college days at Ohio State and his rippling arm muscles and powerful legs capture plenty of attention, whether at training, on game days or even modelling underwear, as he did in 2023. San Francisco 49ers defensive lineman Nick Bosa runs on Wednesday. AP Photo But it’s Bosa’s quads that have earned him extra attention this week as he prepares to return to the field after recovering from a knee reconstruction last October. His right quad has suffered some muscle atrophy during his recovery and is now noticeably smaller than his left. That difference has lessened somewhat since he returned to full training, but it’s still stark for the $235 million star who is contracted with the Niners until the end of the 2028 season.



San Francisco linesman Nick Bosa stretches at AAMI Park on Wednesday. Luke Hemer “I don’t remember [the size difference], but it was drastic after surgery,” Bosa told The Athletic this week. “It’s going to take a couple of years to get that last couple of centimetres.” Niners coaches have made it clear this week that Bosa, 28, will be playing at the MCG on Friday morning, and he moved well during the portion of training that was open to the media on Tuesday and Wednesday. Niners defensive coordinator Raheem Morris has no issues sending his superstar into the centre of battle this week.



“Nick Bosa is really easy. You watch this guy do it over a span, a long time in his career, [and he’s] been able to do it at different levels,” Morris said on Wednesday. “[It’s] a different question than what we just talked about with Romello [Height, another Niners defensive end], where we haven’t seen him do it yet. “Bosa knows his body as well as anybody. “He’ll be prepared and ready to go as well as anybody, whether it’s from a conversation in point, from meetings, from what he needs to get ready for his body. [I have a] very high confidence level in where he’s going to be.” Skims ambassadors: NBA star Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, NFL lineman Nick Bosa and Brazilian soccer player Neymar Jr model underwear in 2023.



Quad muscle atrophy is particularly common for those who’ve suffered ACL ruptures, given the need for the leg to be immobilised in the weeks after surgery. In sports where athletes do more running or constant aerobic activity, like Australian rules or basketball, athletes typically regain a good amount of their muscle by the time they return to action. But sometimes photos emerge of how players look in their return to training. Bayern Munich and Canada soccer star Alphonso Davies was shown running five months after his knee reconstruction last year.



His right quad was wafer thin while his left was noticeably larger, which caused a stir, given fans of both the European powerhouse and his national team were desperate for him to return to full fitness. Physiotherapist Konstantinos Ikonomou highlighted the issues around quad atrophy in a Linkedin article referencing Davies’ issues last year, explaining that most rapid muscle loss happened in the two weeks after surgery but could continue for weeks or even months after. “This isn’t unusual. Quadriceps atrophy is one of the most stubborn challenges after ACL reconstruction – even in elite athletes with world-class rehab teams,” Ikonomou wrote. A number of NFL stars, such as Detroit defensive ace Aidan Hutchinson and Washington wide receiver Stefon Diggs, have featured in training videos on social media that have highlighted the same issue.

World.title: Nike is collapsing. Yes it went woke, but that’s not why it’s going broke
World.content:
NationalActive wear Opinion Nike is collapsing. Yes it went woke, but that’s not why it’s going broke Stephen Brook Special correspondent, The Age Updated September 10, 2026 — 3:50pm , first published 3:47pm

Updated September 10, 2026 — 3:50pm ,first published 3:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This week there’s been era-defining upheaval in the capitalist cultural zeitgeist: sportswear icon and behemoth Nike has suffered such a loss in market value it’s set to crash out of the top 100 companies on the US stockmarket. To which I say – good. The corporate megalodon has lost more than $US200 billion ($277 billion) in value since its record high of 2021 – a share price rout of nearly 80 per cent that one investment newsletter dubbed “a collapse for the history books”. It was worth about $US280 billion, it is now less than $US60 billion. A pair of Air Jordan 1s, from 1985, which were worn by Michael Jordan. AP Some people have eagerly sheeted the disaster home to the company’s controversial embrace of plus size, trans and woke values. This is false. But I am celebrating. My animosity to the brand was hardened by Nike’s decades of ruthless, macho alpha corporate culture – famously paying the designer of its iconic Swoosh logo just $US35; the allegations of Asian sweatshops; child labour; tax avoidance, “technology doping” at the Tokyo Olympics (guidelines were changed after Nike’s Vaporfly shoe was found to boost performance). Oh, and the company infuriated The Beatles by using John Lennon’s anthem Revolution in an ad campaign against the surviving band members’ wishes.



But I am really celebrating because I have harboured an intense dislike of Nike ever since schoolyard taste arbiters told junior me that Nike and its win-at-all-costs ethos was to be lauded, embraced and, above all, purchased. Frankly, Just Do It and 1980s American cultural imperialism never inspired me. Besides, what’s wrong with Dunlop Volleys? I am proud to this day that I have never made any Nike purchases. Naomi Osaka steps out at the Australian Open wearing an outfit inspired by jellyfish with a touch of butterfly. It was designed by the player, couturier Robert Wun and Nike. Getty Images To be fair, it is incredible that when Nike was formed in the 1960s, jogging as a leisure pursuit did not exist. Running was for serious track and field athletes only. Co-founder Bill Bowerman brought jogging to the States from New Zealand, of all places, and helped cement jogging (and Nike) in the global fitness boom. When Forrest Gump ran across America and through 1970s history in the film, he ran in a pair of Nike red, white and blue Cortez. The film Air starring Ben Affleck tells the story of how the firm hired nascent basketball star Michael Jordan in 1984 – Jordan preferred Adidas and Converse – and changed sports marketing, cementing the popularity of sneakers globally.



Nike’s founding fathers - Phil Knight, a former University of Oregon runner (right) and Bill Bowerman, his college coach (left) in 1999. AP However, the excellent business podcast Acquired’s special episode on Nike details how the company masculine arrogance meant it missed the 1980s aerobics boom, which Reebok sales topped. Cultural warriors point to the downfall beginning in 2018, when the company launched ads featuring former quarterback Colin Kaepernick, who had kneeled during the US anthem. This was bold and visionary – and got up a lot of people’s noses. Nike stock fell but sales rose and the campaign dominated the discourse for weeks. Nike Mind 001 and 002 performance shoe. But just six months earlier, Nike had been engulfed in a massive MeToo scandal, when female employees complained about harassment and sexism after years of inaction. It forced a massive executive exodus. A year later, Nike’s elite running group the Nike Oregon Project fell apart after separate doping and abuse scandals.



While some said the price collapse was a result of woke ad campaigns using trans-identifying influencers who were born biological males to sell women’s apparel, angering women campaigning to protect women’s sport, the stock fall had more to do with over-reliance on online distribution over retail sales, Trump tariffs affecting imports from its Asian factories, and a big drop-off in the Chinese market. After Nike pulled back on retail sales, newer brands such as New Balance, Arc’teryx and HOKA took up the shelf space. So did On Running, backed by former tennis star Roger Federer, who invested in the brand after dumping Nike when it threatened to cut his endorsement deal. Adidas might be considered cooler, it is still half Nike’s size. And while the shareholders don’t like Nike, huge swaths of the public still do. On Friday the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers take to the Melbourne Cricket Ground for the first National Football League competition match played in Australia, they will do so in Nike supplied uniforms, (for which the apparel brand pays a reported $US200 million each year for the privilege). As the company’s bosses look hopefully towards a reset and revival, it’s worth considering that only a brand of Nike’s size and strength could do a deal like that. And as it looks to the future, it still has about 500 million people use its mobile apps for shopping, fitness and running club. I am just not one of them. Stephen Brook is The Age’s special correspondent. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘We are on borrowed time’: Rudd’s dire warning Australia is becoming ‘second rate’
World.content:
PoliticsFederalChina relations ‘We are on borrowed time’: Rudd’s dire warning Australia is becoming ‘second rate’ Matthew Knott Updated September 10, 2026 — 3:50pm ,first published September 10, 2026 — 7:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia risks becoming a second-rate country unless it urgently changes its national mindset, Kevin Rudd has declared as he challenges Anthony Albanese and business leaders to pursue a more ambitious policy agenda including sweeping government intervention in the economy. The former prime minister’s dramatic appeal against complacency came as he declared there was a one-in-three chance Chinese President Xi Jinping will try to seize the self-governing island of Taiwan as soon as 2028, a move that could trigger a devastating war with the United States and Australia. Rudd told the National Press Club in Canberra that Australians need to embrace a “radical change in our national mindset” to confront “mega-changes” that are unprecedented in modern history, including rapid advances in artificial intelligence and China’s rise to superpower status. Former Labor prime minister Kevin Rudd. Alex Ellinghausen “We are now on borrowed time,” Rudd said in one of his most substantial interventions in the national debate since leaving parliament in 2013.



“Incrementalism will no longer work for Australia. Urgency must be our national watchword if we are to navigate our future as an independent, prosperous and resilient nation.” The alternative, he said, is “to slide into becoming a second-rate country”. While Rudd began his speech by declaring his remarks were not targeted at the federal government, and were directed at Australians in all leadership roles, he called for a sweeping expansion of federal industry policy across a swathe of emerging technologies. Challenging the “self-appointed Knights Templar of economic orthodoxy” in the federal Treasury, Rudd said Japan, South Korea, Singapore and China had achieved impressive economic growth while championing national priorities such as manufacturing. Albanese should appoint seven “industry tsars” with strong private sector experience to drive policy development and implementation in areas such as artificial intelligence, biotechnology, clean energy, critical minerals and defence, he argued.



“Each industry plan would have a tailored set of tax, regulatory policy and permitting incentives – Commonwealth, state and local,” Rudd said. Related Article Updated

AI ‘Create jobs, not replace them’: PM flags crackdown on data centres and AI copyright Lamenting the loss of the local car-making industry under the Abbott government, Rudd called for the Australian automotive sector to be revived, with a focus on 3D printing and electric vehicles, to “repair this fatal vulnerability in our national security”. While praising the “intelligent framework” on AI that Albanese unveiled in July, Rudd urged the government to settle its policy quickly to ensure Australia is not left behind. “Other countries are tailoring their own policies right now to take our place,” he said.



“We need to move with urgency to maximise the upsides and develop our own Australian AI, built on our own data, rather than making ourselves dependent on others.” Related Article Opinion

Kevin Rudd What next for Rudd? He’s steeling himself for his grandest ambition Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Rudd did not let business off the hook, calling for a “venture capital industry that will get off its arse” and invest in start-ups, especially in biotechnology. The world-renowned China expert, who left his post as Australia’s ambassador to the United States in March, also called for the defence relationship with Japan to be upgraded and the government to be prepared to spend more on defence than under the current trajectory. In a speech on Wednesday night, Rudd said there was an “increased possibility” of Xi attempting to invade Taiwan as early as 2028.



“And when I say an increased possibility, I don’t mean from 5 per cent to 10 per cent. I mean an increased possibility, which I argue is around about one in three, and I don’t use that lightly,” he said. Rudd said the US, Australia and other allies needed to work to deter China from taking military action, including by forging ahead with the AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine pact. Loading The head of the Asia Society has previously raised the possibility of a 2028 Chinese invasion of Taiwan, including in a recent New York Times podcast interview with Ezra Klein, but did not put a percentage on the likelihood of the scenario. The re-election of current Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te – whom Rudd described as “pro-independence” – could prompt Xi to take action by claiming an anti-secession law passed by China in 2005 had been breached, he said.



The US will also be in a presidential election year in 2028, possibly distracting it from events in China and Taiwan. Related Article AUKUS AUKUS makes Australia a nuclear target, top experts warn “Put those factors together, we just need to be mindful of an increasing level of risk, but still in the possibility stakes, not the probability stakes,” said Rudd, who turned his doctoral thesis on Xi Jinping’s political philosophy into a recent book. “When people ask what then shall be done about this, my response is pretty simple. What’s worked since 1949 is deterrence, deterrence, and deterrence. And for those who find this some sort of ancient Cold War rhetoric, it’s not.” It is crucial for the US to sustain its military capabilities and sense of political will that it will act to defend Taiwan, Rudd said.



“Deterrence, properly constructed and properly perceived, is the best guarantee for sustaining the peace,” he said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: From LinkedIn approach to prison: Australian expat jailed for being China spy asset
World.content:
NationalCourts From LinkedIn approach to prison: Australian expat jailed for being China spy asset Tom Wark September 10, 2026 — 3:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A seemingly innocuous message on a social media platform has snowballed into a man being jailed for foreign interference. Alexander Csergo, 58, was jailed for three years and six months on Thursday after being found guilty by a jury in March of helping Chinese spies. Alexander Csergo arrives at court in March. He has been jailed for three years and six months for helping Chinese spies. Sitthixay Ditthavong With time served, he will be eligible for parole in October. Between May and December 2022, the business owner knew he was assisting Chinese operatives known only as Ken and Evelyn when he prepared fake, plagiarised reports about Australia’s defence arrangements, District Court Judge Craig Smith said on Thursday.



His relationship with the spies began after the Australian IT consultant was approached on LinkedIn in November 2021 by a woman claiming to be from a Chinese think tank. Csergo, living and working in China at the time, should have known Ken and Evelyn were working for China’s Ministry of State Security, the jury found. Csergo’s mother, Cathy, attends Downing Centre Court on Thursday. Wolter Peeters But Judge Smith said it was not proven that Csergo was reckless about the prospect of helping the foreign power from the moment he read the message. “Spotting Chinese intelligence operatives on that program requires training on what to look for,” the judge said.



Related Article Courts Australian expat was Chinese spy asset, jury finds Csergo used open-source information to compile reports on a variety of topics including lithium mining, German politics, defence and security. He was specifically asked to dig up private information about Australia’s involvement in the Quad security group and the AUKUS deal, Judge Smith said. He falsely claimed he had interviewed a number of individuals, including former prime minister and Mandarin speaker Kevin Rudd. The reports were handed to Ken or Evelyn in person – sometimes at restaurants and cafes devoid of other people – in exchange for envelopes containing the equivalent of thousands of dollars in cash.



While the information was worthless, the jury accepted prosecution submissions that the relationship with Csergo and his contacts was valuable. “I do not consider what he did can be described as overly sophisticated,” Smith said. “But there was certainly a degree of sophistication around the extensive nature of what he did.” Alexander Csergo was arrested by the AFP at his Bondi home. Ken also handed the 58-year-old a “shopping list” of sensitive topics to research when he returned to Australia in early 2023.



However, the judge said there was no evidence Csergo carried out any espionage relating to the list. Ultimately, Smith ruled it was important to deter the wider community from being wooed into compromising Australia’s national security. Sentencing Csergo to time served would not appropriately reflect the seriousness of the offence to Australia’s interests, he found.
