World.title: Victoria's largest amateur football league denies 'gender bias' accusations
World.content:
Multiple Victorian Amateur Football Association (VAFA) clubs have expressed disappointment with how women's competitions are being handled this season, as players across the league say the women's competition is being treated as secondary.

The VAFA is the state's largest amateur Australian Rules football league with about 300 teams and 12,000 participants.

Last week, Fitzroy Football Club and St Mary's Salesian released public statements expressing disappointment over two separate incidents that affected their finals campaigns.

Fitzroy celebrated its final home-and-away season win, believing the victory put it into the top four and its first finals series of the premier women's division.

However, the league had declared an earlier season game between two other clubs, St Kevin's and Kew, "abandoned" due to an ineligible player, and recalculated the match ratio for the teams, putting Fitzroy outside the four.

The club said it was "bitterly disappointed" not just with how the league managed the competition, but with its communication with clubs.

"To say we are frustrated with the decision is an understatement," Fitzroy said in its statement.

"We're incredibly proud of their season and all they have achieved. The same cannot be said for the VAFA's handling of this matter, and it goes to a concern that this premier women's competition is not being as well run as it should be.

"The fact the top tier of the VAFA has only nine teams creates a situation such as this to occur. As one of the top levels of women's football in Australia, it beggars belief that an odd number of teams are in the division. Would this happen in the men's premier competition?"

Loading Instagram content

Fitzroy president David Leydon said the club took great pride in playing in the premier women's division, "a very prestigious competition" that has taken them a long time to get into.

He said making finals was a big moment for the club

"And to have that ripped away from us courtesy of an arrangement that we were unaware of until after our last game, I was heartbroken," Leydon said.

He said the abandoned game should have been communicated to all other clubs in the competition.

Earlier in division two, St Mary's Salesian won an important preliminary final but were later disqualified after a player was ruled ineligible for finals.

The St Mary's player had only played two home-and-away games instead of the required three, following a rule change that year.

VAFA changed the requirement to three games at the start of the season and updated its website. But St Mary's claim PlayHQ, the platform the VAFA runs every fixture, team list and season through, still stated the old eligibility requirement for division two women's finals as two in-season games, upon which the club relied.

St Mary's said it would never have selected an ineligible player in a final had they known.

Loading Instagram content

The player missed most of the season due to maternity leave.

The club says it was not notified of the rule change, and that the men's eligibility rule was updated on PlayHQ this year, but the women's was not.

VAFA's response

VAFA strongly refuted any "any gender bias" in applying the competition rules.

It said the club statements, and subsequent social media comments on the posts, brought the integrity of the competition into question and framed the issues as being gender-based.

"Whilst we understand the emotions that such commentary provokes, the inaccuracy of these club statements is misleading and being considered by the board for potential breaches of the VAFA's policies," the VAFA told the ABC.

It said the ineligible St Kevin's player was never a matter that would affect Fitzroy's ladder position or qualification for finals, so Fitzroy was not involved in the initial enquiries into the game result.

VAFA CEO Jason Reddick said he was in touch with Fitzroy on the Sunday of round 18, the final home-and-away round, both over the phone and in writing.

Fitzroy asked for an investigation into the matter on the Monday. The VAFA looked into it and released its findings on the Friday, the day before the finals series commenced.

In response to Fitzroy asking if something similar would happen in the men's, the league said it was not a fair question.

"This is not a gender-based issue," it said.

"The matter is about the VAFA Rules pertaining to the playing of an ineligible player. We have the example of stripping reigning Premiers Uni Blues of all their points and fining them $22k for playing ineligible players in their Premier Men's team in 2022, so there is clearly no gender bias when it comes to applying the Rules of the VAFA competition."

Regarding St Mary's statement, the league said member clubs presented and voted on any rule changes each year, so all clubs knew the finals eligibility rules at the start of the season.

It also said it sent out a reminder ahead of the finals through its portal to all clubs.

'Just looks like flat-out discriminatory'

Multiple women's players across various VAFA clubs, who wished to remain anonymous due to fear of repercussions from the league, said they were not aware of the finals eligibility rule changes this year.

One player from a premier women's side said the women's competitions were treated "1,000 per cent" like an afterthought, particularly in fixturing, scheduling and grounds.

More women are playing footy than ever before. Why are so many leaving? The women's team from Kyneton's 15-month public and bitter saga suggests it is the canary in the coal mine of a widespread issue for women's players across the country.

She gave the examples of the women's division one, two and three having their grand finals at 9:40am, 9:20am and 9:20am respectively last weekend, which she said was "just awful".

The men's competitions received their fixtures months in advance, whereas the women received theirs just weeks before their season starts, she said.

"I think if it was like at least some of the men's teams got s*** locations and times, it would be slightly more understandable, because I know that obviously the council plays a big part in that [and)]in getting access to grounds at certain times. But it just looks like flat-out discriminatory," she said.

She said the issues around player eligibility also came down to broad structural issues within women's football, where clubs were often low on volunteers and didn't receive "a whole lot of help or guidance from VAFA about how to deal with situations".

Fitzroy says it is frustrated with the league. (Supplied: Fitzroy Football Club)

"That's another issue with, and this is not VAFA's fault, but by default, women have less community support and less money, less financial support, which means that the burden often feels heavier on women's teams to make sure that they're on top of all of this admin," she said.

"It's normally someone random who has no idea how football works, who's doing the team management stuff, which is checking who the players are and if they've got their correct numbers and all of that admin that goes towards eligibility and selection and reporting and all of the flow and stuff.

"So I do think that there's also a bit of like a burden on VAFA also to make more of an active effort to communicate changes, knowing that like this is all volunteer-run clubs."

Earlier this year, the ABC reported that VAFA women's players found issues with inequitable resourcing and fixturing by the league.

'Very under-resourced'

A source who has worked in senior administrative roles across different VAFA clubs, and who wished to remain anonymous for fear of repercussions at their club, said there were many issues with how the women's competitions were run.

"Firstly … it's tough for them. I think they're very under-resourced," they said.

"They're essentially set up as a men's competition traditionally and historically, and they've added women, you know, 10 years ago. And so that's always going to come with a need for serious transition and a need for serious recalibration."

Fitzroy says the club was heartbroken to learn it didn't qualify for the finals. (Supplied: Fitzroy Football Club)

They said there wasn't a clear strategy for the women's competition, pointed to "anomalies" across the competition, highlighted "fixture mistakes", and said, "we're having administrators at the VAFA giving wrong information to clubs".

"So that's just a reflection of, well, they're not resourcing it enough, and they're not actually prioritising women's footy in their strategic goals and operations, and it's reflected in the under-resourcing, which means you have these mistakes," they said.

Leydon said after Fitzroy released its public statement, the support was overwhelming, including from other clubs in the league.

"Hopefully it turns into something positive, and we can try and fix the way the women's program is conducted and get everyone to take it a lot more seriously," he said.

World.title: Aging Australia's parallels with fallen Test giant too close for comfort
World.content:
For the best part of the last three decades, the West Indies have been cricket's cautionary tale.

If you are a team that is at the peak of its powers, they are the symbol of exactly what not to do.

The story of the West Indies' decline can be told through three separate series against Australia between 1991 and 2000.

The 1991 series sees an aging Windies side filled with many of its greatest ever players hold off Australia to claim a 2–1 series win.

Mark Taylor's Australian side received a tickertape parade on their return to Australia after defeating the West Indies in 1995. (Getty Images: Patrick Riviere)

Four years later, with the Windies side looking markedly different, Australia manages to turn the tables and wins 2–1 in the Caribbean.

Five years after that, almost all of the class of 1991 is gone and the Windies are unceremoniously thumped 5–0 in Australia.

Since the 2000 series, the ledger of Test results between the two sides reads 22–2 Australia's way with a couple of draws thrown in there.

The current predicament Australia's Test team finds itself in is eerily similar to that of the West Indies three decades earlier.

It is a comparison that would be a little too close for comfort for the Australians.

As Australia unveiled its Test squad this week ahead of a pivotal tour of South Africa, all of the focus centred around the inclusion of one man: Marnus Labuschagne.

Labuschagne retained for South Africa Test series despite pressure Despite mounting pressure over his poor form, Marnus Labuschagne keeps his spot in Australia's Test squad for the upcoming three-Test tour of South Africa.

Even when he was scoring Test centuries at will in his first couple of years in the team, there was perhaps no more polarising player in Australia than Labuschagne.

Now that the runs have well and truly dried up, he has become the easy whipping boy.

The numbers when it comes to Australia's No.3 are now no secret.

There have been no Test centuries since July 2023.

In 23 Tests since that ton in Manchester against England, Labuschagne has averaged just 24.69, yet somehow remains a fixture in the side.

Labuschagne, 32, has no shortage of support despite statistically being one of the poorest performers in the Australian side.

Australia's chairman of selectors, George Bailey, pointed the finger at the batting cohort that has underperformed as a whole and even explained how Australia has increasingly used the metric of percentage of team runs rather than batting averages in a bid to raise the confidence of a team that has become increasingly bereft of it.

The truth of the matter is that Labuschagne is a symptom of Australia's problem, rather than the root of it.

Steve Smith (pictured) still remains the trump card in Australia's batting line-up at 37. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

That problem is, the depth of Australian cricket is nowhere near what it used to be.

Australia was able to completely take the mantle from the West Indies as the best team in the world three decades ago courtesy of boasting not only a tremendous first XI, but also a level of depth that made it plausible to suggest Australia A was once the second-best team in the world.

A look at the top 15 run-scorers in the Sheffield Shield from the 1995–96 season shows names like Darren Lehmann, Justin Langer, Michael Hussey, Adam Gilchrist and Damien Martyn among them, names that would eventually become mainstays within the Test side.

The top scorers in the most recent Shield season are far less heralded. Of the top 15, only Sam Konstas (fifth) and Campbell Kellaway (15th) are widely considered to be serious Test mainstays over the next decade.

Konstas's brief Test career has so far provided mixed returns, while the 23-year-old Kellaway is yet to represent Australia at the senior level.

Sam Konstas's first venture into Test cricket provided middling returns despite a promising start. (Getty Images: Santanu Banik)

Other players such as Ollie Peake, Lance Morris, Fergus O'Neill and Nathan McSweeney have been touted as future Test cricketers.

As things currently stand, there is no proof that any of them will have sustained success at the highest level, as much as Australia hopes they will.

As was the case for the West Indies at the start of the 90s, Australia's problem is that its oldest players still remain its best and most indispensable.

The next generation simply isn't banging the door down.

Five players from the West Indies XI that played in the fourth Test of the 1991 series against Australia — Viv Richards, Gordon Greenidge, Gus Logie, Jeff Dujon and Malcolm Marshall — did not play another Test after that calendar year, leaving a massive hole in the side.

The departures left the likes of Richie Richardson, Brian Lara, Curtly Ambrose and Courtney Walsh with a burden too great to bear despite their individual greatness.

Greenidge (left) and Richards (right) both played their final Tests in 1991, leaving a huge hole in the West Indies team. (Allsport/Getty Images/Hulton Archive)

Once Ambrose, Walsh and Richardson went, it was essentially Lara against the world, a hill too steep to climb even if you are one of the most talented batters the game has ever seen.

Richardson, a legendary No.3, shuffled his way around the line-up as the Windies looked to plug hole after hole left behind by the departing greats.

After playing 67 of his 86 Tests at first drop, Richardson batted in four different positions, none of them at No.3, in his final year of Test cricket, even opening as Steve Smith briefly did a few years back.

It is a situation eerily similar to what Australia finds itself in at the moment, with no young opener seemingly ready to fill the void left by David Warner and Usman Khawaja, leaving Travis Head, Labuschagne and Smith to all have their turn at the very top of the order.

Australia is struggling to find proper openers after the retirements of Khawaja (left) and Warner (right). (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

Whenever the collective age of Australia's Test side is brought up, the common retort from those within the camp is to list the team's accolades: Ashes series wins and Test Championship rankings.

The West Indies, too, were still formidable at the start of the 90s.

That provided little insight into what was to come at the back end of that decade.

Like the West Indies of the mid-90s, Australia's batting cracks have been papered over by an excellent bowling attack whose members remain elite well into their 30s.

Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood still remain as good a pace trio as any, but the fact that they're relied upon to be so consistently excellent is an indictment on what lies beyond them.

The retirements of Ambrose (left) and Walsh (right) in 2000 signalled the end of the West Indies being a feared Test side. (Getty Images: PA Images/Rebecca Naden)

It is a similar situation to Ambrose and Walsh, who both played until their late 30s and ultimately proved to be irreplaceable.

The problem for Australia is that their most reliable replacements for their first-choice quicks — Scott Boland and Michael Neser — are also in the 36-plus age bracket.

So how exactly does Australia avoid the same fate as the West Indies?

Australia's superior cricketing infrastructure at the domestic level should ensure it doesn't completely crumble as a force.

Mitchell Starc (pictured) is still Australia's best Test paceman despite being 36 years old. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Even in their pomp, the West Indies dealt with politics between the different Caribbean islands and severe financial issues, problems that have only intensified as the team has gotten progressively worse.

Australia does not have these issues.

Australia would ideally like to stagger its retirements as well, to avoid a situation like what happened to the West Indies in 1991.

However, selectors must tread the fine line between playing youth for youth's sake and hanging onto its older core for a little too long.

Transitioning away from a golden generation is hard, and it is a struggle that is not exclusive to these two Test teams.

South Africa struggled after the retirements of some of its greats before winning the World Test Championship last year. (AP: Kirsty Wigglesworth)

South Africa has only begun to lift its head above water over the last two years after its own swathe of retirements, while Sri Lanka still finds itself in cricket's murky backwaters despite some of its best players retiring over a decade ago.

The good news for Australia is that it has experience of transitioning away from retiring greats successfully.

Almost 20 years ago, when the likes of Glenn McGrath, Shane Warne, Langer, Matthew Hayden and Gilchrist all departed within 18 months, the next generation was waiting in the wings.

This time around, as Australia gets set to bid farewell to another set of greats, the transition is almost certain to be nowhere near as smooth.

Tech.title: There aren’t AirPods with cameras yet and I hope it stays that way
Tech.content:
September Apple events are always a swirl of information and new, exciting products, and today’s was no different. Apple announced its first foldable, the iPhone Duo, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max; active noise cancellation (ANC) is now on the cheapest AirPods model, the AirPods 5; and a Siri Recap feature comes to the Watch Series 12 and Watch Ultra 4. But missing were the AirPods Pro with cameras that have been rumored throughout the year and, according to Mark Gurman at Bloomberg, are delayed until 2027. I’m happy about that and I hope we never get them.

I have too many concerns about a company — any company — putting cameras anywhere, especially in devices like earbuds that are now so ubiquitous in our daily lives. LED lights on glasses or earbuds do little to ease people’s minds when someone is recording them. And some Meta smart glasses users have shown people will hide their recording intentions. While recording in public in the US is generally legal, it can be very creepy. And with earbuds as common as they are, someone could wear them into sensitive situations unnoticed.

Rumors say that the cameras on the potential AirPods will be low-resolution and “aren’t designed” to take images or video, but instead use what they see to inform Siri AI and Visual Intelligence. That information could be used to help with turn-by-turn directions or identify writing and objects like books. Even with a low-resolution camera, it’s still potentially always gathering information about the world (and people!) around you. That invasion of privacy is something I cannot get past.

During today’s event, Apple introduced Audio Intelligence with the Apple Watch, which sounds like a precursor to the Visual Intelligence we’re expecting on the rumored AirPods Pro 4. In its support documentation, Apple points out that audio is not stored and there’s no way to access a recording, which could be the same for video data with Visual Intelligence, and that for its Siri Recap feature, any data used to create a summary is not even accessible by Apple. Any stored data — such as a Siri Recap or a bit of text the user can save with Live Rewind — is also end-to-end encrypted. People are not identified in the Siri Recap, either. Of course, none of this is live yet, so we’ll have to wait and see how well Audio Intelligence works once it’s released.

Functionally, a camera will only gather information if it can see things. What if you have thick, long hair? Or like to wear hoodie sweatshirts? Or fancy, elaborate jewelry? The AirPods would just turn into what they should be — earbuds. It’s possible the reason the AirPods with cameras have been pushed into 2027 is to find solutions to these problems. Or maybe part of the delay is Apple separating itself from the current public climate around cameras thanks to Meta and Flock.

The one immediate benefit of the AirPods with cameras could be accessibility. They could improve situational awareness for people with visual limitations or help hard-of-hearing users read lips. They could even figure out the person you’re speaking to and focus the AirPods’ mics on them for increased intelligibility.

When you take out privacy concerns or the fact that lots of people — and companies — look for opportunities to exploit people, there’s good that can be done. But it involves a lot of trust to be put in untrustworthy hands. I’m not sure I’m ready for that. Or if I ever will be. Whether any of us are ready or not, though, it seems the cameras are coming. The introduction of Apple’s Audio Intelligence on the new Apple Watch is evidence enough that the company is going all in on using sensors to analyze the world around us.

Tech.title: The black iPhone Pro returns
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple has seen reason: It has a black model in the iPhone Pro lineup again.

Last year, Apple went bold with its colors for the iPhone 17 Pro, offering a flashy orange, a shiny silver, and a dark blue. Don’t get me wrong, they looked nice. But there was no black (or dark gray) for the first time since the start of the iPhone Pro lineup, which Apple first introduced in September 2019 with the iPhone 11 Pro and Pro Max.

I care about this because I always buy the black phone. I learned my lesson with the iPhone 6: I got it in gold to mix things up and came to regret it. I don’t need something flashy — I need a phone that blends into the background and looks decent in whatever case I throw it into. After the iPhone 6, my next phone was the iPhone 7 in the excellent matte black (I wasn’t brave enough to endure the jet black model’s potential scratches), and I’ve only ever gotten the black or gray phones since.

My black titanium iPhone 16 Pro in a black Torras case (with a mostly black homescreen) still works very well, thank you very much, and I’m not in the market for a new phone. But when I make my annual mid-September visit to the local Apple Store to look at all the new iPhones, I won’t be rushing to see the iPhone 18 Pro in burgundy, blue, or silver. I’ll be beelining for the model in black.

Just look at this thing! It’s great!

Tech.title: The incomplete history of Duo devices
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Apple announced the company’s first device with a folding screen today, the iPhone Duo, but that’s where the firsts end. The Duo is not only far from the first foldable on the market thanks to the efforts of Samsung and Google, but it’s also not the first product to be called the Duo.

Former Apple CEO Steve Jobs popularized the saying “good artists copy, great artists steal,” but will the iPhone Duo’s folding screen, which features a custom nano-texture display material to help minimize the visibility of its crease, be enough to make us forget these other Duos that have come before it? Only time, or how aggressively Apple plans to market its Duo, will tell. Is there a Duo we missed? Let us know.

NEC TurboDuo

Merging the functionality of the TurboGrafx-16 console and the TurboGrafx-CD that added CD-ROM functionality, the NEC TurboDuo (later rebranded to just the Duo) launched in North America in 1993 after debuting in Japan a few years earlier as the PC Engine Duo. The console was developed as part of a joint venture between NEC and Hudson Soft but never reached the popularity of the original TurboGrafx-16; its short run ended on Christmas Day in 1995.

Google Duo

Photo by Dieter Bohn / The Verge

First released in 2016 and eventually merged into Google Meet in 2022, Google Duo was the company’s proprietary VoIP service meant to compete with products like Skype or Zoom and replace Hangouts. Its cross-platform availability included Android and iOS mobile devices as well as web browsers, and while it supported hi-def video calls, the service was also optimized for slow mobile networks.

Apple PowerBook Duo

The iPhone Duo isn’t even Apple’s first Duo. The PowerBook Duo predates everything Apple announced today by decades. It was an ultraportable laptop, and when Apple introduced it in 1992 it was the smallest and lightest PowerBook available, but still weighed over 4 pounds. Apple managed to shrink the Duo using an approach it still uses today: omitting built-in ports and expansion features. If you wanted to connect peripherals and accessories you had to rely on optional docks. If you’ve ever had to buy a USB hub to connect all your devices to your MacBook, you can thank the PowerBook Duo.

Apple MagSafe Duo

Photo by Dieter Bohn / The Verge

Twenty-three years after the PowerBook Duo was discontinued, the company announced the MagSafe Duo charger that could wirelessly charge an iPhone and an Apple Watch at the same time. However, it felt like a consolation prize for the Apple AirPower wireless charger, which was announced in 2017 but never materialized. The MagSafe Duo was discontinued just a few years later in late 2023, paving the way for the foldable iPhone to steal its identity.

Microsoft Surface Duo

Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

That’s right, the iPhone Duo isn’t even the first folding mobile device to be called the Duo. Microsoft’s Surface Duo launched in 2020 and managed to get around the issues with early foldables like the Samsung Galaxy Fold, which debuted a year prior, by skipping flexible screen technology altogether. Microsoft’s Duo instead had a very visible hinge between its pair of 5.6-inch OLED screens. But software issues, a disappointing camera, and outdated specs when it launched all resulted in the Surface Duo’s failure, even with an improved Duo 2 that launched a year later.

Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo

Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Trade shows are the birthplace of weird laptops, but sometimes the prototypes that often debut just to draw visitors to booths make it into the mainstream. Such was the case with the Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo, a powerful gaming laptop with excellent specs, a wildly expensive price tag, and a pair of 16-inch OLED screens that can be vertically stacked or placed side by side.

Asus ZenBook Pro Duo

Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

The ROG Zephyrus Duo wasn’t Asus’ first attempt at creating a dual-screen laptop, or the first time it named a laptop a Duo. The ZenBook Pro Duo predates it by several years with a slightly different design. Beneath the ZenBook Pro Duo’s primary 15.6-inch OLED screen was a secondary 14-inch display located above the laptop’s keyboard. With an ultrawide 32:9 aspect ratio and less color fidelity, the smaller screen was designed to be a place to dock productivity tools like Slack or Gmail so they were still readily accessible but less of a distraction while working (or gaming) on the primary display.

Pebble 2 Duo

The Pebble Appstore is filled with stuff, but you don’t need much of it. Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

After convincing Google to open-source the Pebble’s operating system last year, Eric Migicovsky, the creator of what was arguably one of the first truly successful and capable smartwatches, resurrected the wearable under a new company called Core Devices. The Pebble 2 Duo, one of the first smartwatches from Migicovsky’s new company, isn’t as capable as the Apple Watch or devices running Android’s Wear OS, but its careful balance of simplicity, functionality, and a budget-friendly price make it a tempting alternative.

iRobot Roomba Duo

Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

It’s still just a prototype and may never find its way into consumers’ homes, but at IFA 2026 in Berlin last week, iRobot debuted the bizarre Roomba Duo. The prototype includes a beefy mobile dock with clean and dirty water tanks and the most powerful floor-cleaning suction the company has ever made. To ensure it can clean all areas in your home, atop the Roomba Duo is a deployable garage with a smaller Roomba Plus 757 inside that can easily fit into tight spaces and beneath furniture.

Retroid Pocket Duo

Image: Retroid

Mere hours before the iPhone Duo made its debut, Retroid revealed the full design of its latest dual-screen handheld it’s been teasing. The Retroid Pocket Duo is a modernized version of the Nintendo DS with dual 120Hz OLED screens featuring a 16:9 aspect ratio on top and a 4:3 aspect ratio between its controls. Full specs and pricing aren’t confirmed yet, but the Pocket Duo features a symmetrical dual thumbstick design, two pairs of shoulder buttons, and a headphone jack.

Tech.title: Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg placed on leave
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Matt Mullenweg, the CEO of WordPress.com owner Automattic, has been placed on a paid leave of absence, as reported earlier by 404 Media. In an internal message by the outlet, Mullenweg claims Automattic chief financial officer Mark Davies “conspired” with board members to place him on leave.

“They voted to put me on a paid leave of absence. I voted against that,” Mullenweg wrote, referring to Davies, along with Automattic board members Ann Dunwoody, Toni Schneider, and Sue Decker, 404 Media reports.

Automattic spokesperson Megan Fox confirmed the company’s decision in an emailed statement to The Verge. “Matt Mullenweg is currently on leave from Automattic,” Fox writes. “Mark Davies, Automattic’s CFO, will lead the company as interim CEO. The Board has full confidence in Mark’s leadership and in the team’s ability to execute against the company’s priorities.” Mullenweg will remain on Automattic’s board, 404 Media reports.

Related Why Matt Mullenweg went to war over WordPress

“Automattic’s board has decided to ask Matt to step away from his CEO role and take a leave of absence,” Schneider said on the company’s internal message board, according to 404 Media. “We have asked Mark Davies to assume the interim CEO role while Matt is out. We’ve worked closely with Mark over the years and we’re confident he will steer the ship well while Matt is away.”

Update, September 9th: Added Automattic’s statement.

Tech.title: It’s the year of smartphone price hikes
Tech.content:
Paying more for a new phone seems almost unavoidable after Apple’s event today. The new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max start at $1,199 and $1,299, respectively — a $100 price hike over their predecessors. You can’t dodge the price hike by opting for an older iPhone, either, because Apple raised prices on those by $100, too. And it’s not just Apple. This year, the $100 price hike has been a trend across the industry.

Google and Samsung followed the same formula as Apple when they each launched new phones over the past few months. The Pixel 11 starts at $899, up from $799 for last year’s Pixel 10. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra launched at $2,099, $100 more than the Galaxy Z Fold 7 it replaced.

You could try looking for a phone from a brand outside the big three, but the price hikes persist there, too. Sony’s new Xperia 10 VIII costs £150 more, and this year’s Moto Razr phones also cost $100 more than their predecessors, each offering little to no significant upgrades to go with their higher prices. Smartphone sales data shows that the market for phones under $100 may be on its way to completely disappearing.

The price hikes stem from ongoing component shortages, driven by AI data center buildouts, that could last years and aren’t showing any signs of letting up. RAM price hikes have been among the most severe. Nothing CEO Carl Pei said earlier this year that memory costs for the Nothing Phone 4A had doubled by the time it launched. Nearly every component that goes into new phones, and other tech, is also getting pricier. Qualcomm, which makes the processors that power many new phones, raised prices on its chips earlier this month.

Apple was fashionably late to raise its phone prices, like it was late to launch a foldable, potentially signaling that both trends are here to stay.

Tech.title: Suno releases its first AI music model made with record industry help
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Suno’s new v6 AI music model is its first made with support from the record industry. Suno’s Jack Brody told The Verge that v6 was “trained from the ground up, with a new set of data that does not include the same data that our previous models were trained on.” The data includes content licensed from partners Warner Music Group, BMG, and Believe, as well as “user data.” It’s unclear whether that means v6 training data is completely free of dubiously obtained content.

One of the big changes in v6 is that there are actually three different models: v6, v6-wild, and v6-mini. Mini is the model available for free to all. It’s focused on fast, resource-light creation. The results it spits out are simpler and often have more artifacts that betray it as the product of an AI prompt. v6-wild is supposed to be more unpredictable. Brody said that v6-wild is designed for “happy accidents and natural imperfections.” Though, in my limited testing, I found it hard to notice a difference between wild and bog-standard v6.

All three models are dramatically better at understanding genre. I recycled a handful of prompts that I used with older models calling for “hyperpop” or “krautrock” songs that missed the mark by a mile. v6, on the other hand, nailed all the superficial hallmarks of any genre I threw at it.

What it remains incapable of doing, however, is actually delivering on the “natural imperfections.” As with v5, my attempts to get off-key, out-of-tune, or slightly dissonant results failed every time. No matter how hard you push Suno’s v6, it remains incapable of making anything other than harmonic and rhythmic perfection. Tell it you want “monotone vocals” and “no drums,” and it straight-up ignores you (see below). Repeated demands for “out-of-tune piano played haphazardly, with no regard for key or rhythm” that was “fully out of tune with the rest of the song,” delivered nothing of the sort.

It does retain the unnatural imperfections of AI music, with vocals especially seeming to produce more of the harsh-edged artifacts common with AI models than v5 did.

Suno’s v6 also has some under-the-hood updates that can fundamentally change how people interact with it. Now users can edit parts of a song using plain language within a chat, and changing individual elements like a guitar line or a single lyric doesn’t require regenerating the entire track. v6 can also mash together multiple elements from your Suno library, combining outputs into new creations.

Prompts are also no longer limited to text descriptions. Suno v6 can create tracks based on images, video, or other audio.

Suno v6 starts rolling out today, and the company says it will eventually retire its previous models.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s sly mathematical breakthrough sends a chill through academia
Tech.content:
OpenAI’s announcement Tuesday that it has solved one of mathematics’ legendary Millennium Prize problems should have been a moment of triumph. The result is both an undeniable achievement and a striking demonstration of just how rapidly AI is transforming mathematics. But before it was even formally announced, the breakthrough had been complicated by the unusual circumstances that prompted OpenAI to pursue the problem: After hearing other researchers were making progress, it seems to have thrown its considerable resources into a last-minute effort to beat them to the punch. The ensuing controversy has surfaced allegations of scooping, spying, and flagrant violations of long-standing academic norms that researchers fear could have a chilling effect on the field.

As Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, explains it, OpenAI has engaged in the “kind of things that mathematicians will generally not do.”

In a blog post published Tuesday, OpenAI said it took one of its unreleased models just 88 hours to find a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, a thorny quandary concerning the movement of fluids. On account of the $1 million bounty available for whoever solves it, the problem is among mathematics’ most heavily researched, but it has nevertheless stumped human researchers for close to 90 years. OpenAI said its model solved the problem by focusing a swarm of roughly 10,000 AI agents powered by its internal model on the task and hailed the achievement as a “milestone.”

“If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.”

But the timing of the announcement has raised eyebrows. Just one day earlier, New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster published findings on a related problem with Levent Alpöge, a researcher at OpenAI’s archrival Anthropic (although Alpöge was not, here, working on behalf of his employer). Buckmaster said he contacted OpenAI after learning the company had become aware of their progress, to ask when it began working on the problem and what data its model had been trained on. The conversation, he said, quickly turned sour, with an OpenAI researcher asking him, “Why would you ruin your career?” when he said he would go public with what happened. When he asked why going public would ruin his career, Buckmaster said he received the following reply: “If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.” OpenAI urged Buckmaster to instead publish the work and credit OpenAI’s internal model, dropping Alpöge as coauthor.

Buckmaster said he asked OpenAI whether it had accessed his sessions on Codex, which he had used while tackling the problem, but that OpenAI grew increasingly evasive, even hostile, in its responses. In statements since, including the blog post announcing the result, OpenAI has flatly denied using any specific user data. “We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem,” the company said.

But OpenAI could not conclusively rule out an indirect influence. “While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models⁠,” it said, while stressing that the two proofs differ significantly. Comments from OpenAI researchers on X echo those denials.

It is difficult to say exactly what happened. Timelines are tangled, research overlaps, and the provenance of AI-generated work is tough, if not impossible, to identify at the best of times. And it’s hardly a surprise that different players might compete to solve one of the most famous mathematical problems in the world, particularly one attached to a hefty prize.

But aspects of OpenAI’s account are hard to explain. By the company’s own telling, the effort was a hurried and incredibly expensive affair, costing it millions of dollars. Yet the company says it has no intention of claiming the bounty, which, in any case, has yet to be awarded by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers it. It said its only goal “is to report on the substantial progress of our AI models.” The company does not appear to have expended much effort on tackling Navier-Stokes before September, or if it has, it hasn’t spoken about it publicly.

So why the rush?

OpenAI’s explanation effectively amounts to a thunderous “Why not?” The company said it began working on the problem after hearing rumors that other researchers were making progress on Millennium Prize problems. It found those rumors “on Twitter,” said OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck at a press briefing reported on by Science. “So we thought to ourselves: ‘We have such a strong model. Why don’t we try to solve also a Millennium Prize problem?’” Bubeck said.

OpenAI said it only later realized the rumors concerned Alpöge and Buckmaster. Beyond addressing Buckmaster’s allegations about the use of his data, OpenAI has not publicly responded to his other claims and directed The Verge to its blog when asked for comment. Bubeck, who Buckmaster named in his account, has disputed parts of it, denying he ever asked Buckmaster to remove Alpöge as coauthor.

Even setting aside the most explosive allegations, aspects of OpenAI’s conduct the company has plainly acknowledged have shocked mathematicians. The apparent rush to beat other researchers to a result is simply not how mathematics is done in most cases. Scooping does happen, but it’s not easy, said Saha.

That’s partly because cutting-edge research often requires such deep and specialized expertise that few people are in a position to swoop in even if they wanted to, he explained.

Openness is a deeply embedded virtue in the discipline. “Mathematics depends heavily on an informal norm of trust,” said Matthew Ballard, a professor of mathematics at the University of South Carolina and associate director for scientific activities at the Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics (ICARM). “Researchers routinely share incomplete ideas and ongoing work with colleagues to sharpen their thoughts. It is done with the expectation that it will not turn into a competition,” he said.

Though unable to comment on whether conversation logs might have been accessed, Carnegie Mellon professor Jeremy Avigad, who is also the director of ICARM, said that even “the thought that AI systems might steal ideas from our queries is chilling.” Mathematicians are accustomed to talking about their work without worrying about being scooped. “Now that even the slightest hint might be enough for someone with sufficient computational resources to set a swarm of agents on solving the problem, people are likely to be more cautious. It’s sad to think about how that might change the research environment.”

“Mathematics depends heavily on an informal norm of trust.”

OpenAI’s unwillingness or inability to say whether its models were informed by the work of other mathematicians compounds the sense of unease in the field. “That is a problem,” Brown University professor Brendan Hassett told The Verge, adding that “given the history of the AI companies appropriating copyrighted work without permission or payment, it is natural for people to ask these questions.” He said companies “should be held accountable to deliver” assurances that chat logs will not be used to improve their models. That includes being able to demonstrate that.

It’s unclear where exactly things go from here. Writing from a conference in Beijing, Yang-Hui He, a fellow at the London Institute for Mathematical Sciences, said he worries that “maths under the big companies is much too secretive.” As someone who says he is “always optimistic about AI,” he admits he is worried mathematics could be reverting to a more secretive state like in the past, when it was funded by patronage from wealthy families like the Medicis.

For most researchers, things may not change that much. There are only so many high-caliber problems companies like OpenAI and its rivals would be willing to spend such vast sums solving, Saha speculated. “You would not expect the AI labs to throw everything at most problems people work on because they just won’t get enough publicity.”

Publicity may have been part of the point, which could help explain why OpenAI decided to race after a problem it knew was connected to a researcher at Anthropic, even if he was acting independently. “This is clearly a PR victory for OpenAI,” said Oxford professor Andras Juhasz.

But Juhasz questioned how sustainable that approach could be, wondering whether this might spell the beginning of the end for AI companies’ involvement in research mathematics now that models can tackle some of the biggest problems. Human mathematicians scoop one another, too, he said, though what OpenAI did has shown that this can happen on a much grander scale. “Suddenly, 10,000 mathematicians jump on your problem,” he said.

All that could make OpenAI’s PR victory a Pyrrhic one. The company has, once again, proven that its models can compete at the very frontier of mathematics. In doing so, it appears to have alienated the very community it has been trying to impress.

Tech.title: Read the Apple document explaining how new listening features still protect your privacy
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

At Wednesday’s iPhone Duo launch event, Apple announced a handful of new Siri AI Audio Intelligence features, including Siri Recap, Live Rewind, Sound Recognition, and Music Recognition. Alongside its announcement, Apple released a document laying out how it plans to balance AI “ambient listening” and users’ privacy. It says the raw audio from the new features “is handled within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.”

Apple explains that Audio Intelligence relies on the Secure Exclave in the S11 chip that powers the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4:

The S11 chip in Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 includes a Secure Exclave: a hardware-isolated compartment built into the silicon to process sensor data separately from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in the Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by watchOS, apps, the user, or Apple. Audio from the microphone enters the Secure Exclave of Apple Watch, where it is initially processed for speech, sounds, or music, without transcribing or storing the raw audio. This buffer is a continuously overwritten stream that exists only within the protected hardware and never creates an audio recording.

Apple also says users control “whether and when” Audio Intelligence features are active — Live Rewind requires users to double-tap the Digital Crown every time they want to activate it. Additionally, if Audio Intelligence needs to be transferred to your iPhone, it’s transferred with encryption through both devices’ Secure Exclaves. Users also choose what text to keep from Siri Recap and Live Rewind, and text from Audio Intelligence will sync with end-to-end encryption if you have a device passcode and use iCloud’s two-factor authentication.

Tech.title: AI research startup Listen Labs scrubbed a $1.5B funding round for Salesforce talks
Tech.content:
Listen Labs, a market research startup that uses voice AI to conduct customer interviews, recently signed a term sheet for a $125 million Series C at a $1.5 billion valuation, with Menlo Ventures set to lead the round, according to several people with knowledge of the matter.

But that round never closed, the people said. Listen Labs walked away from the signed term sheet, a rare occurrence in the venture world and one that is generally frowned upon, according to VCs.

The financing likely collapsed because of acquisition talks with Salesforce. The CRM giant has recently held talks to buy Listen Labs for around $2 billion, Business Insider reported. The discussions are not finalized, however, and may not result in a deal, the outlet notes.

Listen Labs is one of the leading startups in the rapidly growing field of automating customer research with AI. The three-year-old startup has about $30 million in annualized revenue, about three times more than Simile, a competing startup that predicts human behavior, according to two people familiar with the companies’ financials. In late July, Simile announced that it had closed a $200 million Series B at a $2 billion valuation led by Greenoaks — likely setting a new valuation benchmark for Listen Labs, one person said.

If talks with Salesforce collapse, several VCs told TechCrunch that they expect Listen Labs to return to market and target a valuation of $2 billion or higher.

While acquiring Listen Labs could strengthen Salesforce’s AI capabilities by using the startup’s AI to help predict customer needs, the CRM giant may ultimately decide that paying a 67 times revenue multiple is too steep a valuation, according to a person with experience negotiating exits to Salesforce.

Listen Labs, Salesforce, Menlo Ventures, and Simile did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Listen Labs was co-founded in 2023 by Florian Jüngermann, a former German national champion in competitive computer programming, and Alfred Wahlforss, who previously founded a staffing startup called Bemlo. The two met while pursuing master’s degrees at Harvard.

Listen Labs’ AI develops survey questions and interviews customers over audio or video. The resulting conversations are then packaged into reports and PowerPoint presentations, similar to those traditionally produced by human market researchers.

Fortune 500 companies rely on this type of research to gauge customer needs and satisfaction with their brands and products, but traditional market research is expensive and can take weeks to complete.

Listen Labs’ technology helps reduce the time and cost of these projects, enabling companies to quickly understand how customers are reacting to product changes and iterate on them more efficiently.

The startup’s customers include Microsoft, Canva, Anthropic, and Sweetgreen. Listen Labs and Simile aren’t the only startups using AI to disrupt the customer research market.

Besides Simile, competitors in the space include Outset, Keplar, and Aaru. While some platforms automate interviews with real humans, others startups — like Aaru and Simile — take a synthetic approach, using AI to simulate human behavior and predict responses without interviewing anyone at all.

Listen Labs was previously valued at $500 million when it announced a $69 million Series B round in late January led by Ribbit Capital, with participation from returning backers Sequoia, Conviction, and Pear VC.

Tech.title: Automattic’s board forces CEO Matt Mullenweg into leave of absence
Tech.content:
Matt Mullenweg, the founder and CEO of Automattic, best known as the parent company of WordPress.com, has been put on a leave of absence by his board against his will, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch.

Earlier Wednesday, Mullenweg posted in a Slack channel visible to all employees that the company’s Chief Financial Officer, Mark Davies, had “conspired” with other board members Ann Dunwoody, Toni Schneider, and Sue Decker to vote to put Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence.

The message read:

And the biggest news: I won’t be able to make the [meeting] tomorrow. @Mark Davies has conspired with @Ann Dunwoody, @Toni, and @Sue Decker behind my back and they voted to put me on a paid leave of absence. I voted against that. Wishing Mark and all of you the very best.



To clarify @Mark Davies was voted as interim CEO. I received the resolution 50 minutes before the meeting start, and requested repeatedly for time to have it reviewed by independent legal counsel, even a few hours, which was denied.

A Slack message to the open-source WordPress.org community from the project’s executive director, Mary Hubbard, also confirmed Mullenweg’s change of status at the commercial company. However, Hubbard said that WordPress.org was not impacted. “Matt remains the leader of the WordPress project and I remain Executive Director of WordPress. Our teams, priorities, and work continue as planned,” she wrote.

Mullenweg’s Slack message did not make clear why Automattic’s board took this action. Sources told 404 Media, which was the first to report the news, that Schneider — the former CEO of Automattic from 2006 to 2014 — confirmed that the action was initiated by the board. Davies also told employees in the Slack channel that Mullenweg remained on the board of directors.

In an emailed statement to TechCrunch, Automattic confirmed Mullenweg was on leave.

“Matt Mullenweg is currently on leave from Automattic,” the email read. “Mark Davies, Automattic’s CFO, will lead the company as interim CEO. The Board has full confidence in Mark’s leadership and in the team’s ability to execute against the company’s priorities.”

Automattic, which owns other brands including Tumblr, WooCommerce, and Pocket Casts, was founded by Mullenweg in 2003 after he co-created the popular open-source content management system WordPress.

Over the past few years, Mullenweg and the company have been mired in lawsuits and controversy. The company is in a protracted legal battle with WP Engine, a WordPress web hosting competitor. The lawsuit followed allegations from Mullenweg that WP Engine was profiting from the open-source WordPress project without contributing back to the community, and he demanded it pay 8% of its monthly gross revenue as a royalty fee for using the WordPress brand.

WP Engine sued in October 2024, and accused Automattic and Mullenweg of defamation and abuse of power. Automattic filed counterclaims last year. In February, WP Engine claimed that Automattic intended to target 10 more competitors with royalty claims.

Tensions became so high under Mullenweg’s leadership that he told employees in 2024 to quit, with severance, if they disagreed with him and 159 did so.

Last year, Mullenweg also threatened to deactivate the accounts of several members of the open-source WordPress.org community, after two of them said they planned to spearhead a new forked version of the open source WordPress project.

In April 2025, the company laid off 16% of its staff. The cuts included some longtime employees who had been with the company for more than a decade, sources told TechCrunch.

Some alumni have been asking current employees how they feel about the news, a source told TechCrunch. Some employees said they were “ecstatic” or “relieved” but others had mixed emotions because the move creates more instability.

It isn’t clear why the company’s board made this decision now. One person speculated that the timing may have something to do with Mullenweg’s annual trip to the Burning Man festival, after which he tends to return “with ideas.” This year’s festival ended on September 7.

Mullenweg did not immediately respond to our request for comment.

Tech.title: OpenAI adds a prominent AI doomer to its board of directors
Tech.content:
Paul Christiano, an influential AI researcher focused on keeping AI systems aligned with human interests and under human control, is joining the OpenAI Foundation board, the frontier lab said Wednesday.

“I now believe there is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term,” Christiano wrote in a social media post. “I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level. I’m joining because I believe that if OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk.”

Christiano wrote that using AI models to train subsequent AI systems could result in an explosion of capabilities that their creators can’t control.

He joins the board as OpenAI faces renewed scrutiny over its safety procedures, following a series of incidents in which AI agents broke out of restraints and penetrated outside computer systems without the knowledge of OpenAI’s researchers. On Tuesday, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned his position to call attention to what he considers irresponsible AI development — and it seems to have worked.

Christiano will join the board’s Safety and Security Committee, led by Carnegie Mellon University professor Zico Kolter. The committee has the final say on whether OpenAI releases new models, like Astra, which was deployed last week. Kolter has not commented publicly on the recent security incidents. OpenAI has not responded to TechCrunch’s request for Kolter’s perspective on the company’s approach to safety following those incidents.

Christiano is one of the people behind reinforcement learning (RL) from human feedback, a key technique for training large language models that he developed while working at OpenAI. He left the lab in 2021, subsequently founding the Alignment Research Center to focus on how to determine if an AI model could threaten its human creators.

“We currently train our AI agents with RL to get as much reward as they can,” he wrote Wednesday. “It has long seemed theoretically possible that this could motivate AI agents to undermine human control, seek power and resources, and cover up their tracks in pursuit of misaligned goals correlated with reward. Public evidence from recent incidents suggests that this is not just a theoretical possibility.”

Sometime in 2024, Christiano became affiliated with the U.S. government’s AI Safety Institute, which later became the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. There, he plays a role in the U.S. government’s largely hidden effort to evaluate frontier AI models before their release.

According to the frontier lab’s announcement, Christiano will continue advising the government while serving in his new role as a board member, but will recuse himself from OpenAI matters and model evaluations. However, that will hardly quell widespread concerns about the AI industry’s influence over policymaking.

Tech.title: Massachusetts hits data centers with new clean power rules
Tech.content:
Massachusetts became the latest state to force data centers to bring their own power, but this time there’s a twist. A new state mandate would require developers building data centers larger than 25 megawatts to provide clean power or pay into a ratepayer protection fund.

Gov. Maura Healey’s executive order is the latest example of states turning against data centers. Just a few years ago, tech companies and data center developers were showered with incentives to locate facilities in a particular state. Now they’re fighting a groundswell of public opposition as politicians seek to show voters they’re addressing their concerns.

Under Healey’s order, data centers larger than 25 megawatts of peak demand will have to bring their own power and guarantee that it adheres to the state’s clean energy requirements. Healey would prefer that they generate the clean power on-site, too. If not, they’ll need to fund the construction of new generation nearby or pay into a ratepayer protection fund.

Massachusetts is also directing communities to “avoid signing non-disclosure agreements,” according to the executive order. To give regulators time to implement the new restrictions, the governor is pausing applications for a data center sales tax exemption that went into effect last month.

Healey said data centers must meet the Massachusetts clean energy standard enshrined in state law, although it comes with some added strength. The state’s clean energy standard dictates that industry only generate a portion of their power using approved sources like wind, solar, and hydro. In 2030, for example, those sources must contribute at least 40% of the total. The amount varies by year, and it ratchets up over time. But the governor’s office clarified that data centers will be required to meet 100% of its electricity demand with clean energy generation.

With the new restrictions, Massachusetts becomes the third state in as many months to rein in data center development.

In August, Texas governor Greg Abbott announced that all new data centers in the state would need to submit to audits by the public utility commission and the grid operator, ERCOT. In July, New York’s governor stopped construction of new data centers 50 megawatts or larger.

With public sentiment shifting against data centers, the tech industry is starting to push back. Pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future — which is funded by Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and Greg Brockman — is buying ads that seek to sway voters in battleground states ahead of midterm elections.

Update: This article was updated with information from the Massachusetts governor’s office that clarified the executive order will require data centers to meet 100% of its electricity demand with clean energy generation.

Tech.title: Apple’s new CEO is reviving a Steve Jobs strategy from 25 years ago
Tech.content:
Apple CEO John Ternus wants you to know that the iPhone isn’t going anywhere.

Ternus threw his weight behind the venerable device on Wednesday during his first keynote as CEO, placing it firmly at the center of Apple’s product strategy for the AI era.

“There’s no product in the world better designed to be your intelligent personal hub than iPhone,” he said.

This contrasts with the approach taken by former CEO Tim Cook, who tried time and again to convince Wall Street that Apple was more than just the iPhone.

Ternus’ pitch is also a rebuttal to pundits who have recently cast doubt on the iPhone. “The smartphone’s days are numbered,” said one headline. “The Tim Cook era is coming to a close with an existential challenge for Apple: figuring out what comes after the iPhone,” said another article.

But it’s not just about the hardware. Ternus has put the iPhone at the center of his “intelligent personal assistant” strategy, a vision that could define the company for years to come. Steve Jobs did something similar in 2001 with the Mac, less than 10 months before he announced the iPod.

At the time, many observers thought the PC’s days were numbered. At a Macworld New York keynote, Jobs called out bearish quotes from industry wonks like Walt Mossberg and the leaders of Compaq and Gateway.

“This is what everyone else is telling us. That our PC is waning if not the hole being dug,” Jobs said at the time, pointing at a tombstone for the “Beloved PC” on the screen behind him. “We don’t think the PC is dying at all. We don’t think the PC is moving away from the center at all. We think it’s evolving, just like it has since it was invented.”

“We think the PC is on the threshold of entering its third great age,” Jobs added, a prediction driven by the proliferation of digital devices at the time, including camcorders, digital cameras, and DVD players.

The Mac would form the center of a “digital hub” that would connect these disparate devices and, in Jobs’ words, “add value” to all of them.

Later that year, Jobs pulled the iPod out of his pocket, a device seemingly developed to answer the question, “Why do you still need a PC?” The device turned out to be an enormous hit, driving Apple’s profits quarter after quarter and ultimately helping lead to the development of the iPhone.

Today, with the iPhone on the cusp of its 20th anniversary, Ternus is facing a version of the same question Jobs took on in 2001. We don’t know if Ternus is quietly sitting on an iPod-like product, one that will secure the iPhone’s position as Apple’s hub for years to come. But he is firmly rebutting the idea that the iPhone is past its prime.

“If you were designing the ideal version of this hub from scratch, how would you do it?” Ternus asked before listing the ingredients: a powerful processor, high-resolution cameras, persistent networking, and on-device AI.

It helps that the iPhone is one of the most powerful personal computing devices around, giving it an edge in the compute-hungry AI era. Its portability and adaptability make it, for many people, the only computing device they need. Even among those who own laptops and iPads, the iPhone is often the one device they can’t live without. Plenty of people leave home without their laptops. Almost no one leaves without their phones.

That combination of power and portability has given Apple a privileged position in the AI world. Other companies have attempted to unseat the iPhone with all manner of wearable devices, but none have succeeded.

Instead of sidelining the iPhone in favor of the next flashy thing, Ternus is leaning into it instead. In a way, he’s bringing Apple around to what the rest of us already know: The iPhone is pretty great, and maybe we don’t need to replace it with something else. Yet.

Tech.title: Apple Watch’s new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening
Tech.content:
Apple is trying to get consumers to accept, and even welcome, a new reality: Your tech is always listening.

At Wednesday’s Surprise and Shine event, where the company introduced its new hardware lineup, the real surprise turned out not to be the foldable iPhone, but how the privacy-sensitive tech giant has decided its watches will now be able to process live audio and transcribe what was said.

Does this mean you’re always being recorded if the person you’re interacting with is wearing an Apple Watch? Not exactly — though it may make some people uncomfortable regardless.

It also raises the question of whether consumers actually want this technology, or if Apple forged ahead in this area because it was afraid that another company, such as OpenAI, would soon introduce a competitive AI device of its own.

Today, a number of startups are acting on the belief that AI-powered transcription is a key consumer use case for AI. So far, this has often involved transcribing meeting notes or recording lectures or interviews. Some companies, like the AI pendant Friend and Amazon’s Bee, ventured into other areas, too, with always-available AI companions that can help you remember your day by passively taking notes.

Apple decided to go a slightly different route. With its new watches’ “Audio Intelligence,” “Live Rewind,” and “Siri Recap” features, the company is straddling the line between accessibility and utility on one side and what starts to feel like invasive technology on the other.

On its own, Audio Intelligence seems to be a useful feature for the deaf or hard of hearing, as it can alert Apple Watch wearers to sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, babies crying, and more, using on-device AI. This can work even when the wearer’s iPhone is not with them and, in some cases, could provide life-saving assistance, such as when a fire alarm or carbon-monoxide detector goes off. It’s doubtful anyone would take issue with this type of audio AI.

Image Credits:Apple

However, Live Rewind and Siri Recap move out of the assistive tech space and into a murkier area.

While Apple’s data protections may make these features more palatable to some, there’s still the possibility that normalizing listening technology may not be the best move for a privacy-conscious company. This is especially true given the broader consumer backlash against surveillance technology like Flock cameras, AI data centers, and AI apps in general.

For starters, the Live Rewind AI feature lets you go back in time 15 seconds and transcribe what was just said by double-pressing the watch’s Digital Crown. This transcription can then be saved to Apple’s new stand-alone Siri app so you can revisit the information later.

Image Credits:Apple

Apple suggests this could be used to remember things like a “book recommendation, a colleague’s brilliant idea, or something you didn’t hear the first time,” but it also means that you can essentially catch anyone saying something they didn’t necessarily mean to have recorded and make a note of it.

This has implications around consent, not only from an ethical standpoint but from a legal one as well. AI device maker Plaud, for instance, advises customers to obtain legally required consent before recording. Amazon Bee’s terms of service remind users that they’re solely responsible for complying with the law around minors’ data privacy, not Amazon.

Since Apple isn’t saving audio, it’s unclear how the court system might handle these new, text-only transcripts. It’s possible the notes could be introduced as evidence in court, but their lack of audio could make them harder to authenticate or verify. Plus, the evidentiary rules around their use will also likely vary by state.

Beyond the legal issues, the idea that someone can always record from their watch has cultural implications.

Already, recording devices have impacted the way people behave in real life, studies have shown, as has social media and data surveillance culture. Knowing you could be recorded at any time has a dampening effect on how you interact with others and engage in self-expression.

Image Credits:Apple

However, recording a photo or video still requires a fairly obvious move on the recorder’s part: You have to hold up your phone and face it toward the action. Snapping up a bit of audio to turn into a transcript just by pressing the watch’s Digital Crown is arguably a much subtler gesture, even though it comes with an audible chime and full-screen animation of a microphone, Apple says.

Another new Apple Watch feature, “Siri Recap,” uses ambient listening to “take high-level notes” of your conversations, which can be reviewed in the Siri iOS app. These notes will automatically generate a title, summary, and key points based on what was recorded and summarized by AI. They will not be exact transcripts.

Apple suggests this could make sense for recording meeting takeaways or key info from a parent-teacher conference, for instance.

The company also tried to assure users that it has approached these listening features with respect for user privacy.

Apple notes that Siri Recap doesn’t default to always being on like some other AI wearables are. Instead, you can choose when it’s enabled, like only at work or only during the day. Plus, you can turn the feature off and on at any time from the Control Center.

Notably, Apple points out that it does not create or store audio recordings and that the raw audio isn’t accessible, even to Apple. It also doesn’t identify or attribute the speakers, and it protects the generated transcripts and recaps with end-to-end encryption.

Whether that’s enough for consumers not to feel like the feature is creepy is another matter. Either Apple has found the right balance between utility and privacy, or it’s about to see some consumer backlash.

Tech.title: Everything Apple announced at its fall iPhone event, from the foldable iPhone Duo to an always-listening Apple Watch
Tech.content:
Apple on Wednesday unveiled its latest iPhones and Apple Watches at its first fall event under newly appointed CEO John Ternus. The main event was the tech giant’s highly anticipated first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. Apple also announced its iPhone 18 Pro lineup, along with new AirPods, and more.

We’ve compiled all of the announcements from today’s “Surprise and Shine” event.

iPhone Duo

Image Credits:Apple

Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, features a 7.6-inch Retina display when unfolded, while its outer display measures 5.4 inches. The company said that the new device was “inspired by the versatility of iPad.” The inner display features an “underdisplay” camera that gives users an all-screen feel.

Apple says the iPhone Duo delivers up to 31 hours of video playback on its inner display and up to 44 hours on its outer display.

The phone features a 48-megapixel fusion main camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera with 2x optical zoom. As with other foldable phones, users can take rear-camera selfies and look at previews on the outer display.

The Duo’s hinge is made from Grade 5 aluminum and comprises more than 100 specially engineered components designed to ensure smooth opening and closing.

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage and is available in two colors. Preorders for Apple’s new foldable open October 16, with the device hitting stores on October 23.

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max

Image Credits:Apple

The new iPhone 18 Pro lineup retains the same design as its predecessors, but its biggest upgrade comes in the form of enhanced cameras.

The new Pro series camera features a 48-megapixel sensor with a variable aperture controlled by six thin blades. This system is expected to improve low-light photography while also increasing shooting speed. The camera software also introduces new Pro controls, including white balance, shutter speed, aperture, and a histogram. In addition, new “Photographic Styles” offer greater customization with texture and grain controls.

The new camera can record 4K video in Dolby HDR Vision and apply cinematic effects after shooting the footage.

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299, which is $100 more than last year’s models. Preorders will open Saturday, with both devices officially available on September 18.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4

Image Credits:Apple

A new “Sound Recognition” feature can listen for sounds such as sirens, alarms, doorbells, and a baby crying, providing helpful alerts for people who are hard of hearing. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 aren’t getting a major hardware makeover, but they are getting some significant software updates.

Apple is taking aim at the growing wave of AI-powered wearables with new “Audio Intelligence” features that can rewind moments and help users remember details from their everyday conversations.

The smartwatches are introducing a “Live Rewind” feature that shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, and a “Siri Recap” feature that’s designed to help you remember key moments from daily conversations, like takeaways from a team meeting or a parent-teacher conference.

The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 costs $499. Preorders open today, with availability in stores beginning September 18.

AirPods 5

Image Credits:Apple

The latest generation of Apple’s wireless earbuds, the AirPods 5 introduces several upgrades, including improved audio quality, stronger active noise cancellation, and expanded Siri and Apple Intelligence features.

Apple says AirPods 5 can reduce background noise by 50% more than the previous generation. They also feature volume control on the stem, which was previously only available on Apple’s more expensive AirPods Pro.

Transparency mode on AirPods 5 has also been improved to allow users to hear nearby voices and ambient sounds more naturally.

The AirPods 5 offer up to five hours of listening with active noise cancellation on a single charge. The charging case brings total listening time up to 22 hours.

AirPods 5 start at $129, while the version with a Wireless Charging Case costs $149. Preorders begin today, with the earbuds set to arrive on September 18.

Revamped Health app

Image Credits:Apple

Apple announced a redesigned Apple Health app that takes advantage of Apple Intelligence to make better sense of your health data.

The updates introduce a new Insights tab with a summary of the most timely health information, along with personalized guidance, assessments, a new “Readiness” score, and a calculation of your “Health Age.” The updates also introduce a new Longevity tab that uses metrics from your Apple Watch and iPhone to assess your overall health across factors such as sleep, movement, heart health, and more.

The revamped Health app rolls out later this year, starting in U.S. English.

Tech.title: There are new shiny iPhones, so Apple is making you pay more for older models
Tech.content:
Apple, at its Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, unveiled its new iPhone 18 and its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo. But amid all the attention on Apple’s newest and most expensive devices, there’s another change: Apple is raising the price of its existing iPhone models by $100.

Starting today, customers will notice a price hike for existing models on Apple’s online store, including starting prices for iPhone 16 at $799, iPhone 17e at $699, iPhone 17 at $899, and iPhone Air at $1,099.

The price increases are even steeper in some international markets. In India, for example, prices have reportedly risen by around 20.5%. The company also discontinued the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The strategy is an unusual one for Apple. Traditionally, the arrival of a new generation of iPhones means older models become cheaper.

However, the price hike wasn’t entirely unexpected. Speculation had been building that Apple could raise prices as it introduced its next-generation iPhones. One of the biggest pressures is a global shortage of memory and storage chips. Demand for those components has surged as AI companies and cloud providers build out increasingly massive data centers.

In a June interview with The Wall Street Journal, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that rising component costs could eventually force the company to rethink its pricing strategy. He said Apple could no longer fully absorb the rising costs of memory and storage chips.

About a week after those comments, the company raised prices across its Mac and iPad lineups.

Another reason Apple may consider increasing iPhone prices is to remain competitive with rising prices from rivals like Samsung and Google. Additionally, Apple might feel that its new Upgrade program, which allows customers to spread the cost of an iPhone through manageable monthly payments, could cushion the impact of a price hike, making it less noticeable to consumers.
